Early results from pioneering works have demonstrated that auto-differentiable NMS models can greatly reduce NMS model calibration time while achieving comparable accuracy compared to traditional calibration methods. The efficient gradient-based optimizers have enabled calibration of increasingly sophisticated human models with a large number of parameters, which seek to narrow the gap between simulation and reality. Several modules have been evaluated separately in different studies, but have never been directly compared within the same study. In this work, these modules are compared on the same differentiable upper limb model with a 3-DoF shoulder, a 2-DoF elbow, and 11 superficial and 5 deep muscles in the calibration to find an optimal pipeline for improving model accuracy. The considered modules include muscle synergy, learnable bone parameters, optimizable geometry of wrap objects, and constraint torque of the differentiable arm model. To evaluate the effect and interplay between the modules on calibration accuracy, one or more modules were used in each of 16 calibration configurations, which were compared in terms of the error between two joint torques calculated by the forward and inverse dynamics with the calibrated model on 9 distinctive testing movements across 4 subjects. Results showed that torque loss was reduced by 23.6% on average using muscle synergy extrapolation to estimate deep muscle activities, and by 10.9% on average through bone dynamic parameter optimization, which are both recommended to be incorporated in the calibration.

items.title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Medical Question Answering on ESC Cardiology Guidelines: Evaluation and Retrieval Optimization
items.summary: Background: Large language models produce hallucinations in medical question answering (QA). Verify-and-revise pipelines that check atomic claims against retrieved guideline evidence are a standard mitigation, but evaluations almost universally treat the verifier's output as ground truth, an assumption rarely tested. Objective: To measure, claim by claim against human judgement, how such a pipeline fails in a guideline-grounded clinical setting. Methods: We built a dataset of 160 questions (100 patient vignettes from 89 de-identified cases, 60 fact-based) over four recent ESC cardiology guidelines, all approved by a practising internist, and a retrieval corpus of 627 hand-verified guideline records at two chunk granularities. A five-stage pipeline was run under four retrieval configurations and three independent runs (1920 arm-runs); all 606 first-pass refuted claims were manually audited, an independent judge re-judged 906 decisions, and the expert blindly reviewed 100 accepted claims. Results: Only 44.7-50.6% of flagged claims were true hallucinations. Correction loops converged in 85.2-95.1% of cases, yet 35% of genuine final errors were introduced by correction. Single-run true-hallucination recall was 35.6-41.2%, the three-run union 71-80%; verifier agreement was moderate (kappa = 0.505). The blind probe estimated the accepted-claim miss rate at 3.2% (95% CI 0.7-6.7%). Final genuine-error rate: 1.7% of answers. Conclusion: Claim-level verification reduces hallucinated content by an order of magnitude, but verifier reliability, not generation, is the limiting factor and must be measured, not assumed.

items.title: A Head-Level Investigative Study of Self-Supervised Backbones for Synthetic Speech Detection
items.summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) speech backbones are the standard frontend for synthetic-speech detection, and layer-wise probing has established which layers carry the most signal. But analysis stops there: which of a layer's twelve attention heads compute the spoof decision is unknown. We present the first head-level study of two frozen backbones, WavLM-base and Wav2Vec2-base, on ASVspoof 5. Per-head ablation shows that only a few heads carry the decision while others actively oppose it; removing those heads lowers equal error rate (EER) with no retraining, by 13% relative in WavLM and 22% in Wav2Vec2. We also find a probe-free signature: spoofed speech draws more focused attention than genuine speech, and this gap alone separates the two almost as well as the full representation, peaking at each backbone's most discriminative layer. Finally, attack identity is decodable from every head, yet heads differ in what they do, not in what they know.

items.title: Can Visual World Models See Force?
items.summary: World models and vision-language-action policy models are increasingly proposed as foundations for robot manipulation. They predict how scenes evolve and which actions to take, yet successful manipulation depends not solely on following observable trajectories but also on the hidden variable of interaction force. Neurophysiology has shown that humans possess a visual prior for this hidden variable, motivating us to ask the question: Do the representations of visual foundation models also capture the forces involved in an interaction? We define force awareness as the ability of representations to (1) indicate when contact force is applied, (2) track how it changes during an interaction, and (3) reflect how large it is. We probe frozen image, video, world- and policy model representations with a lightweight readout trained on synchronized video and force measurements from two manipulation datasets. Our experiments show that most models capture when contact occurs but not how much force is being applied. Surprisingly, robot post-training does not improve this either, highlighting an important gap in current models capabilities.

items.title: DocSEAM: Bidirectional Cross-Page Encoding for Multi-Page Document Understanding
items.summary: Multi-page document vision-language models encode each page independently, creating a feature-level discontinuity at page boundaries: visual tokens are formed without access to content on adjacent pages, and the language model must reason over these page representations formed in isolation. We introduce DocSEAM (Document Selective Enrichment via Anchored Masking), a lightweight module inserted between a pretrained vision encoder and the language model that injects the inductive bias of local cross-page context into visual representations. For each page, DocSEAM forms a local triplet with its two neighbors, applies center-anchored masked self-attention with directional salience gates to fuse information from neighbor pages, and returns only the enriched center-page tokens, leaving the visual token count unchanged. After a supervised cross-page warm-up and multi-page fine-tuning with DocSEAM frozen, our 9B-parameter model achieves state-of-the-art results among the evaluated open-weight models of up to 10B parameters on five multi-page document VQA benchmarks. We further show that under controlled re-pagination, DocSEAM reduces sensitivity to boundary placement and improves cross-page span localization

items.title: Decision-Focused Learning for Multistage Stochastic Programs, with Application to Power Network Repair Scheduling
items.summary: Multistage stochastic programs (MSPs) with discrete decisions are hard to solve due to the curse of dimensionality, non-convex value functions, and scenario trees that grow exponentially with the horizon. We develop a decision-focused learning (DFL) framework for MSPs in which a neural network predicts scores for the part of the decision that drives the state transition. Under structural conditions that make this sub-decision enter the stage objective linearly, the network is trained on labels from offline single-scenario problems, using the Fenchel-Young loss with perturbed optimizers, which need only an optimization oracle. We apply the framework to repair scheduling in power networks under stochastic, time-varying component failures, with and without a per-stage repair budget. On a synthetic 5-bus network and on the IEEE 14-bus network at two repair-cost scales, the learned and baseline policies are compared on common evaluation paths. Without the budget, DFL is the cheapest policy on the 5-bus network; on the 14-bus network it does not outperform a near-sighted model-predictive control (MPC) baseline, but it beats repairing every failed component at the higher scale. Under a binding budget, DFL is the cheapest policy evaluated on both networks and at both scales, 14% to 23% below the next-best policy. On the 5-bus network, the mean cost of DFL is 1.7% (without the budget) and 1.8% (with it) above the exact optimum computed by dynamic programming. Within days of computation, sample average approximation yields costlier policies than DFL and the repair-everything heuristic, and stochastic dual dynamic integer programming remains far from convergence. DFL computes its decisions about as fast as the trivial heuristics and orders of magnitude faster than MPC. Since these conditions are not specific to power networks, the framework extends to other MSPs that share this structure.

items.title: SPGSR: A Small Pixel-Space Generator for One-Step Super-Resolution
items.summary: In one-step super-resolution (SR), vision-only models extract semantic cues directly from the low-resolution (LR) image, keeping those cues spatially aligned with the structures they help restore. Recent models achieve high restoration quality with generators of up to 1.4 billion parameters. Given how much structure the LR image already provides, could a much smaller generator achieve comparable quality? We introduce SPGSR, a vision-only framework that adds a learned RGB correction to the LR image. A frozen DINOv2 guides prediction, and a lightweight block refines the correction locally. SPGSR achieves higher PSNR/SSIM and lower LPIPS/DISTS than VOSR, a leading vision-only SR method, across three benchmarks. Its $31.8\mathrm{M}$-parameter generator is just $6.5\%$ the size of VOSR-0.5B's. SPGSR also achieves competitive quality against T2I-based SR methods. SPGSR's generator uses only $0.60\%$ of the HR pixels used to train and distill VOSR's generator. For $512\times512$ outputs, SPGSR achieves $2.80\times$ and $3.35\times$ GPU-pipeline speedups over VOSR-0.5B and VOSR-1.4B, respectively.

items.title: CHASE: Curiosity-Guided Skill Acquisition for Embodied Task Execution
items.summary: Robots executing tasks in partially observed environments must resolve uncertainty while operating with incomplete skills. Inspired by human curiosity, we investigate how robots can formulate task-relevant hypotheses, seek evidence, and acquire missing skills during task execution. We propose CHASE, a Curiosity-guided Harness for Acquiring Skills from Evidence, which operationalizes curiosity as selecting investigations that resolve task uncertainty and expand executable capabilities. Four modules connect dynamic scene understanding, hypothesis-driven planning, on-demand skill acquisition, and verified execution. The planner balances information value, skill reuse, and acquisition/execution cost. Missing skills trigger bounded exploration, learning from verified segments, and held-out admission during acquisition; separate checks verify physical effects and acquired evidence. Newly admitted skills expand the executable investigation set, closing the loop between resolving uncertainty and acquiring capabilities. Simulation and real-robot experiments evaluate investigation, skill acquisition, and task execution. CHASE achieves 50-80% task success under combined information and capability gaps, with 70-90% evidence resolution.

items.title: SemProxy: Semantic 3D Proxies for Controllable Agentic 3D Modeling
items.summary: Coding agents are increasingly capable of generating 3D models, yet enabling users to effectively control the modeling process remains challenging. Existing workflows rely primarily on text prompts and reference images, which often struggle to convey precise spatial intentions and require iterative corrections. We introduce SemProxy, a lightweight intermediate representation that bridges intuitive human interaction and agentic 3D modeling. Instantiated as labeled 3D bounding boxes, semantic 3D proxies allow users to directly specify object parts and spatial arrangements while leaving geometric details to coding agents. These proxies can be serialized into structured text and rendered as images, making them directly accessible to existing coding agents without additional training or modifications. We further develop ProxyStudio, a user interface that integrates text, image references, and interactive 3D proxy editing into agentic modeling workflows. We demonstrate the versatility of SemProxy across object- and scene-level modeling tasks with different coding agents, and evaluate its effectiveness in supporting controllable human-agent collaborative 3D modeling through a user study.

items.title: Agentic Waterfall: An Intent-Driven Information Discovery Framework for Reclaiming User Control in the Attention Economy
items.summary: We formalize Agentic Waterfall Feed, a new problem of personalized information discovery in which users actively direct recommendations and the system adapts to evolving needs inferred from both explicit requests and browsing behavior. We address this problem with the Agentic Waterfall framework, whose language-model controller maintains persistent user state and coordinates content retrieval, ranking, and state updates. To evaluate systems on this task, we contribute the Agentic Waterfall Dataset and a replay-based evaluation protocol. The dataset combines real content metadata with simulated interaction histories. The protocol compares systems under shared histories using relevance scores and blind judgments of how well recommendations satisfy current user goals and constraints. Agentic Waterfall remains competitive with strong baselines on conventional recommendation tasks across five public benchmarks. On the Agentic Waterfall Dataset, it outperforms the strongest baseline in both evaluations, with relative improvements of up to 16.1%.

items.title: Recoverability policy editing for closed-loop safety in autonomous driving
items.summary: Autonomous driving powered by neural network models lacks safety guarantees. We propose a state-level policy editing technique that guarantees closed-loop safety under recoverable disturbances while reusing the model's existing driving capabilities. Closed-loop safety means that the vehicle remains free of collisions at all future times. We introduce the concept of policy recoverability to characterize whether a vehicle can safely return to the original policy's feasible set in finite time. Our method identifies states that are unsafe in the long term under the original policy but recoverable, and selectively edits policy outputs within this region. The vehicle corrects its actions upon entering this region and resumes the original policy upon recovery. Closed-loop simulations on nuPlan urban driving scenarios show a 48% reduction in safety incidents under the original policy while largely preserving its driving performance.

items.title: Any-Rate: Half-Bit Multi-Precision LLM Quantization with Coded Bit-Planes
items.summary: Nested multi-precision quantization derives multiple precisions from a single checkpoint by reading only the leading bits of each weight, which makes it attractive for on-device deployment under varying memory and energy budgets. However, existing methods offer only integer bits, leaving large accuracy gaps between adjacent precisions and severe degradation at 2 bits. To address this, we propose Any-Rate, which serves 2-8 bits from one checkpoint, in half-bit steps over 2-4 bits. Any-Rate restricts some bit-planes to extended Hamming codewords in 8-weight blocks (0.5 bits per weight), shares one LUT per row across precisions, and encodes all precisions jointly with a separate target for each, reducing the loss from sharing bit-planes. Across four LLMs, Any-Rate achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among multi-precision methods at 2 and 3 bits, keeping 69% of FP16 accuracy at 2 bits, and is within one point of the best at 4 bits. It decodes about as fast as existing kernels, and an LPDDR energy model estimates up to 27% less energy at equal accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/hoonki2002/Any-Rate.

items.title: EvoLink-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Self-Evolving Agents in Long-Horizon Interdependent Task Streams
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from passive chatbots into autonomous systems that operate continuously in dynamic environments. Such agents need not only solve current tasks but also learn from past interactions to improve future performance. However, existing streaming benchmarks often rely on short task sequences or largely independent tasks, providing limited evidence of whether agents can effectively reuse experience when later tasks depend on earlier outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{EvoLink-Bench}, a benchmark for evaluating self-evolving agents in long-horizon, interdependent task streams. It covers daily office work, multi-turn dialogue, and AutoResearch-style workflows, with persistent workspaces and dependencies across tasks. The benchmark includes two complementary levels: \textbf{L1}, which evaluates the acquisition and revision of language-expressible knowledge, and \textbf{L2}, which assesses the development of task-level capabilities through execution and feedback. Its evaluation further distinguishes within-task recovery, persistent-state updates, and experience reuse in later tasks. We evaluate five agent frameworks across three backbone configurations under three persistence conditions, covering 19,635 scored task slots from selected evaluation cohorts. Results show that no framework consistently performs best across both levels, retries recover only a limited proportion of failed tasks, and persistent-state updates do not necessarily improve subsequent performance. Furthermore, the effects of evolution differ between knowledge- and capability-level tasks, suggesting that these two forms of evolution require different learning mechanisms. Performance gains also vary across domains and task streams, with improvements on some tasks not necessarily extending to others.

items.title: When Skills Fail to Compose: Compatibility and Retention in Language Models
items.summary: Skill acquisition alone does not establish a reusable skill library: task proficiency does not specify a compositional interface. Motivated by agents that acquire and refine skills, we study independently learned soft-prompt skills on frozen language models, with skill identities and execution order supplied. Across four digit-task bases and three record-editing models, mean composition accuracy in one call is at most 7.6%, compared with 88.2% to 100% over two calls that add computation and an explicit intermediate output. Neutral-insertion training improves robustness but leaves substantial interference, which block length and per-token norm alone cannot explain on two of four digit bases. Blocks of the same operation need not be interchangeable: after training next to frozen learned partners, a post hoc test on two Qwen bases shows that replacing those partners with independently learned blocks of the same operations lowers median composition accuracy from 98.0% and 95.3% to 12.7% and 0.5%, although every replacement scores at least 90% alone. Repair can improve a composition while impairing the original skill, and rehearsal improves retention while transfer remains limited on Qwen2.5-0.5B. Internal interventions constrain explanations without identifying a shared failure mechanism. These findings motivate evaluating compatibility, retention and transfer alongside acquisition when building skill libraries for self-evolving agents. Code is available at https://github.com/YanLin-Quinne/SkillCompatibility.

items.title: Strong Starts, Simple Recipes: Unified Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation from Multimodal Specialists
items.summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) integrates separately trained domain specialists into a single unified model. Existing methods focus on refining the distillation procedure while initializing the student from a base model or a multi-domain SFT checkpoint, which leaves capability integration largely to distillation itself. Instead, we treat the starting point as a design variable and propose Unified MOPD (Uni-MOPD), which pairs a strong start with a simple recipe: a training-free uniform merge of specialists from the same base model initializes the student, and short MOPD with uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL refines it. Across five multimodal domains and 19 benchmarks, our study establishes three findings. (1) The starting point matters more than subsequent training choices: before any training, the uniform merge already matches the score that the base model reaches after 200 MOPD updates, and after short distillation it matches higher-scoring, search-based starts. (2) Short MOPD recovers most of the capabilities the merge leaves unintegrated; it improves every domain, with the largest gains where the domain teacher still leads. (3) From a strong start, uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL match or exceed every evaluated sampling strategy and divergence, without schedules, per-token weighting, or truncation hyperparameters. Uni-MOPD outperforms Open-MOPD at the same training budget while training 3.3 times faster than its released code. We will release the training framework, specialist checkpoints, and unified student.

items.title: Plausible Is Not Proven: Testing Failure Explanations in Monocular Depth Estimation
items.summary: Failure analyses of monocular depth models often name a cause for each error, such as an occluding boundary, a thin object or a reflective surface, but such labels are rarely tested. We present the Vision Error Observatory (VEO), an audit that finds regions failing the $δ_1$ criterion on sensor-measured pixels, labels each with a likely cause or abstains, and then subjects the labels to four tests: agreement with object annotations on data the label model never saw, agreement with blinded human raters, response to targeted image edits, and value as a training signal. We apply it to eight models on NYU Depth V2, DIODE and iBims-1, with labels also checked on Hypersim, and fix most decision rules before their results. The occluding-boundary label agrees with annotations (AUROC 0.85 on NYU, 0.81 on Hypersim, 0.69 on iBims-1), but a single depth-edge cue does as well, and most boundary failures of the strongest model vanish under a 2-pixel tolerance. The reflection label does not transfer to synthetic data, the textureless label is near chance against annotations, and only one of four edit tests, an exploratory one, supports its label. Evaluated against five blinded raters, VEO's labels matched the human consensus only at chance level (Cohen's $κ$ = 0.05). In addition, an increase in the weight on the diagnosed regions during fine-tuning led to an increase in the error on targeted pixels at every weight tested. The architecture-specific failure fingerprint claimed by an earlier version of this project also failed to replicate across the datasets. Plausible failure explanations, in short, need to be tested before they are trusted; we release the protocol, code, ratings and every result file.

items.title: Linear Single-Source Shortest Path, Almost
items.summary: We give a comparison-addition algorithm for single-source shortest paths in undirected graphs with nonnegative real edge lengths. For each input with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, its expected running time is $O(m+n\log\log\log n)$. It terminates almost surely. Every terminating run returns exact distances and a shortest-path tree on the reachable vertices. The bound is independent of the ratio of edge lengths and is linear whenever $m=Ω(n\log\log\log n)$.

items.title: Robust large-scale approximate solutions of the constrained Kemeny aggregation ranking problem
items.summary: The Kemeny aggregation ranking problem consists of computing the consensus rankings of an election with respect to the well-known Kemeny-Young voting method. These consensus rankings satisfy many fundamental properties and are the geometric medians of the votes in the election under the Kendall-tau distance which counts the number of pairwise disagreements. While having various applications in computational social choice, machine learning, operations research, and biology, the problem of computing the consensus rankings is NP-hard and encounters a severe bottleneck in practice. In this paper, we consider the more general Kemeny aggregation ranking problem under immutable input pairwise constraints and propose robust and scalable approximate methods with provable guarantees. We thus provide an algorithmic solution to the more general constrained problem of incorporating a posteriori immutable pairwise constraints into past rankings (e.g., historical voter ballots or legacy laboratory assays) without incurring the cost of generating new data. Our base algorithm $Γ$-XCC provides a source of rankings with a bounded constant approximation factor. $Γ$-XCC generalizes the Copeland ranking method and satisfies the constrained Condorcet consistency property, an extension of the Condorcet winner criterion for elections with immutable pairwise constraints. Thereby, our methods provide large-scale solutions that address the reliability and explainability issues. Our algorithms are also applicable to weighted tournaments with input pairwise constraints and satisfy similar properties in this larger context.

items.title: Adaptive Control Barrier Functions for Nonlinear Singularly Perturbed Systems
items.summary: Control barrier functions (CBFs) have emerged as a flexible and efficient approach for enforcing dynamic safety constraints. In this paper, we consider a class of uncertain nonlinear systems with singular perturbations and develop an adaptive CBF framework for such systems to enforce safety constraints on both the slow and fast subsystems in the overall singularly perturbed nonlinear system with uncertain parameters. We first develop a robustness property showing that if an adaptive controller for the slow subsystem satisfies the slow CBF condition with an appropriate safety margin, then for sufficiently small values of the singular perturbation parameter $\varepsilon$, the slow subsystem remains within an $O(\varepsilon)$-neighborhood of its safe set. We then consider the more general case of safety constraints on both the fast and slow subsystems and provide conditions under which joint slow-fast safety is achieved despite the parametric uncertainties. The reduced-order slow model and the slow and fast CBF conditions are evaluated using an online parameter estimate and the parameter mismatch between the estimated and true reduced-order models is addressed via a state-dependent robustness margin in the CBF inequalities. To illustrate the proposed framework, we present simulation studies for two systems with parametric uncertainties: a synthetic two-time-scale fourth-order example system and a unicycle with a fast turn-rate actuator and an obstacle avoidance safety constraint.

items.title: Full Structure Recovery of Linearized Reed-Solomon Codes
items.summary: Linearized Reed-Solomon codes (LRS) are optimal sum-rank-metric codes that generalize both Reed-Solomon and Gabidulin codes, and benefit from excellent decoding capabilities, making them potentially interesting candidates for post-quantum code-based cryptography. Previous works have investigated the underlying geometric structure of LRS codes, identifying geometric invariants that distinguish them from random codes. Other works have proposed approaches to recovering the LRS structure from an arbitrary generator matrix, together with additional data. However, both the distinguishers and the recovery techniques proposed so far are either not fully general, or have a prohibitive computational complexity. In this paper, we propose a polynomial-time procedure for the full structure recovery of LRS codes from the sole knowledge of an arbitrary generator matrix. Our results show that, like their Hamming and rank metric counterparts, LRS codes cannot be used as they are for McEliece-like encryption. Our approach combines Overbeck-type attacks with suitable matrix manipulations and shortening techniques to recover the evaluation parameters across different ranges of code dimensions.

items.title: PrO Filtering via Kernel Mean Embedding Dynamics
items.summary: Filtering methods are routinely deployed with misspecified state-space models, where Bayesian filters can diverge and become overconfident. Predictively-oriented (PrO) filtering is a recent, hyperparameter-free alternative that was demonstrated to outperform (generalised) Bayesian filtering methods when either the dynamical model or the measurement model is structurally misspecified. This can be attributed to \emph{hedging} behaviour: when an observation conflicts with the forecast, the PrO update places mass near both. Yet existing implementations of PrO filtering rely on unimodal (Gaussian) approximations, whose ability to effectively hedge is limited. This paper develops the first nonparametric, particle-based implementation of PrO filtering. The key obstacle, that PrO filtering distributions are only implicitly defined, is overcome by constructing a path from the predictive to the PrO filtering distribution whose rate is available in closed form, enabling the use of kernel mean embedding dynamics for measure transport. The resulting algorithm requires only simulation from the dynamical model and evaluations of the likelihood, with neither importance weights nor the predictive density. Moreover, as we prove, the number of pseudo-time steps it requires does not grow with the outlyingness of the observation, in contrast to transport along the Bayesian tempering path. An empirical assessment shows substantial improvement over Gaussian variation of PrO filtering in challenging nonlinear examples where Gaussian approximation is unreasonably limited.

items.title: Time-optimal travel driven by two vector fields on a Riemannian manifold
items.summary: We study minimum-time travel on a Riemannian manifold $(M,h)$ for a kinematic model in which finitely many drift fields contribute additively to the velocity, after independent rescaling of their components parallel and orthogonal to a chosen unit direction $u$. The velocity is then $\mathcal Y_x(u)=(η(x)+h_x(\widehat Z_x,u))u+\widehat W_x$, $u\in UT_xM$, for two effective vector fields $\widehat Z$, $\widehat W$ and a self-propulsion speed $η\geq0$. Let $F$ be the gauge of the radial hull $\mathcal B_x=[0,1]\cdot\mathcal S_x$ of the velocity set $\mathcal S_x=\mathcal Y_x(UT_xM)$. Where $η>0$, we characterize when $F$ is a Finsler metric and give two-sided estimates and representation formulae for it; where $η=0$ and $\widehat Z\neq0$, we recover the Randers, Kropina and strong-wind regimes of Zermelo navigation. Examples include Matsumoto's slope metric, traction-modified slope models, and alternative models for wildfire propagation and microswimmer navigation. Since $F$ need not be a Finsler metric, we treat the minimum-time problem with tools from differential inclusions. For distinct endpoints, the inclusions defined by $\mathcal S_x$ and $\mathcal B_x$ give the same infimum travel time, and so does the convex hull of $\mathcal B_x$ under local controllability at the terminal point. When $F$ is finite, the infimum is attained if $(M,h)$ is complete, $\mathcal Y$ is bounded and each $\mathcal B_x$ is convex. When $F$ is a Finsler metric on $\{η>0\}$, the set $\{η=0\}$ cannot be reached from $\{η>0\}$ in finite time and, on $\{η>0\}$, the minimum time is the Finsler distance; if moreover $(M,h)$ is complete and $η$ is bounded, $F$ is forward and backward complete and the minimum time is attained by geodesics. We also compute the support Hamiltonian directly from the velocity law, for every $η\geq0$.

items.title: On the Convergence of Discrete-Time Primal-Dual Algorithm for Distributed GNE Seeking
items.summary: We investigate the convergence of a discrete-time distributed primal-dual algorithm for generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) seeking in a class of noncooperative games with nonlinear coupling constraints. We establish semi-global convergence of the algorithm under a fixed stepsize, in the sense that convergence can be guaranteed from any prescribed compact set of initial conditions by choosing a sufficiently small stepsize. Under a diminishing stepsize sequence, we further establish global convergence when the constraints are globally Lipschitz continuous. For the special case of affine constraints, global convergence is also guaranteed under a sufficiently small fixed stepsize. Finally, we extend these convergence results to a fully distributed GNE seeking algorithm in a partial-decision information setting, where each agent only has access to the actions of its neighbors. These results complement existing convergence results for continuous-time primal-dual dynamics, and provide new convergence guarantees for the discrete-time counterpart in distributed GNE seeking.

items.title: Min-Plus Products and Dynamic Programming with Few Violations of the Adjacent Monge Inequalities
items.summary: Local rewards can introduce negative adjacent mixed differences into a convex transition cost. If a cost array $B$ has $s(B)$ such differences, we express it as a Monge array minus $s(B)$ weighted rectangles and sweep its columns, maintaining the lower envelope of the active rows. For explicit finite $n\times n$ matrices $A,B$ and $L=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil$, we compute $A\otimes B$ and the smallest minimizing index for every entry in $\mathcal{O}(n^2L+ns(B)L^3)$ time and $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ space, giving near-quadratic time for arbitrary $A$ when $s(B)=\mathcal{O}(n)$, including right factors with $Θ(n^2)$ positive differences. For block costs given by a constant-time Monge oracle and $r$ signed rectangle corrections, the sweep activates each row when its prefix optimum becomes available and computes an optimal contiguous partition in $\mathcal{O}((n+r)L^3)$ time and $\mathcal{O}(n+r)$ working space. The sweep handles convex transitions with interval rules and assigns one rectangle to each internal edge or hyperedge reward in a convex block cost, giving near-linear exact algorithms on sparse inputs for ordered graph modularity, weighted contiguous cluster editing, all-or-nothing HyperLam, and bounded-rank strict hypergraph modularity. Let $c_{\mathrm{APSP}}$ denote the deterministic exponent of all-pairs shortest paths with polynomially bounded integer weights. For fixed $3-c_{\mathrm{APSP}}<α\le1$, any deterministic $\mathcal{O}(n^β)$-time min-plus product algorithm for polynomially bounded integer matrices with $s(B)\le n^{1+α}$ satisfies $β\ge c_{\mathrm{APSP}}-1+α$. The reduction from general integer min-plus multiplication uses right factors obtained from $(j-k)^2$ by at most $n^{1+α}$ interval discounts, with $Θ(n^2)$ positive differences and all remaining differences negative.

items.title: Numerical analysis of a conservative Crank-Nicolson scheme for quasilinear Gross-Pitaevskii equations
items.summary: We propose and analyze a fully discrete Crank-Nicolson finite-difference scheme for one-dimensional quasilinear Hamiltonian Gross-Pitaevskii equations with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions. We establish the existence and uniqueness of numerical solutions and an $H^1$-stability estimate. For sufficiently regular exact solutions, we obtain second-order convergence in both time and space in the discrete $H^1$-norm. The analysis covers the focusing and defocusing cubic nonlinearities and both signs of the quasilinear coefficient $κ$, under a uniform discrete ellipticity condition when $κ<0$. The main difficulty in the error analysis comes from the derivatives introduced by the quasilinear interaction. To overcome this problem, we introduce a discrete action combining the discrete energy and mass, and establish a coercivity inequality in the discrete $H^1$-norm that allows us to control the numerical error. Together with consistency estimates and a discrete Gronwall inequality, this yields second-order convergence. Numerical experiments with bright solitons corroborate the predicted convergence rates.

items.title: Parameter selection procedures for model reduction of a parameterized wave propagation in damaged material
items.summary: In this work, we consider a parameterized version of the classical wave equation that models wave propagation in damaged material. We apply model order reduction to the wave equation using a reduced basis method with the POD-Greedy algorithm. The success of the model order reduction highly depends on the parameter set used in the POD-Greedy algorithm. While a larger parameter set leads to more insight on the behavior of the full order model, it also prolongs the reduction process in the offline phase for constructing the reduced basis. Therefore, subsampling strategies based on Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method, pivoted QR decomposition and Polytope Division Method are applied.

items.title: Uniform Guarded Bootstrapping for Topology-Sensitive Directed Shortest Paths
items.summary: On a source star, every leaf distance is an input weight. Thus computing labeled distances need not reveal their order. For a rooted directed topology, let $K$ be the least worst-case sum of comparisons and additions among finite deterministic programs specialized to that topology and correct for every nonnegative weighting. We give one deterministic program that takes the graph as input. This graph-input-uniform algorithm has total comparison-addition RAM time $O(m+n+KΦ(K)\exp(O(\log_2^*(K+2))))$, where $n$ and $m$ count vertices and arcs, and $Φ$ is a regularized product of successive logarithms. An active core is the small graph remaining after directly recoverable distances are separated. The algorithm chooses its parameters from the core size. Frozen entry ceilings let each interrupted local call be replayed on a small completion, whose complete-run bound controls the stopped work. The cost coefficient satisfies a linear one-step recurrence, yielding at most exponential growth in the number of generations. This permits a depth chosen from the measured core size. For $m=O(n)$, the solver gives $O(n\sqrt{\log n}(\log\log n)^{1/4+o(1)})$ time, improving the sparse directed bound of Duan, Mao, Shu, and Yin. A complementary result uses reusable dominator calibration for changing seed vectors on a fixed weighted graph.

items.title: Sequential Portfolio Optimizer (SPO-CPU and SPO-GPU): C++ Interior-Point Solvers and Differentiable Layers for Quadratic Cone Programs
items.summary: Quadratic cone programs (QCPs) are a practical canonical form for convex optimization, including parametric portfolio problems that must be re-solved to high accuracy as market data change. We present Sequential Portfolio Optimizer (SPO), with SPO-CPU and SPO-GPU the C++ and CUDA realizations of the Clarabel homogeneous-embedding interior-point method. Clarabel is a registered trademark; SPO is our name for these implementations. Each exposes a forward optimizer and an in-solver differentiable layer. The Mehrotra algorithm is unchanged. The contribution is an implementation stack: a reduced two-block vector-Jacobian product with gradients in the original coordinates; a documented variant of the Chen--Goulart--Jones smoothing warm start, applied in equilibrated coordinates; and a GIL-free GPU batch architecture whose isolated throughput is at parity with a warm solver loop up to $B{=}16$. On an RTX A6000, subsequent solves of a $5000$-asset factor-model QP average $24$ ms on SPO-GPU, compared with $98$ ms on Clarabel.rs and $122$ ms on single-thread Gurobi; at $10{,}000$ assets the corresponding GPU time is $59$ ms against $439$ ms for one-thread Mosek. Clarabel.rs, SPO-CPU, and SPO-GPU agree pairwise to $2.2{\times}10^{-7}$ in relative objective on this family. Against a CVXPYLayers baseline driven by Clarabel, the GPU layer reproduces the solution and the return-gradient on a $5000$-asset factor QP/SOCP, while a subsequent forward-plus-backward step is $101$--$137\times$ faster at $5000$ assets (and $17$--$30\times$ at $1000$ assets). The smoothing warm start reduces QP rebalance iterations but can increase them on a large GPU second-order cone. Wall-clock rankings apply to the factor-model family only; an $18$-problem Maros--Mészáros subset is reported as a cross-check. We do not claim a speedup over CuClarabel, and the batch architecture is not a measured throughput improvement.

items.title: Routing and Cache Retention for Multi-Turn LLM Inference: Theory and Implementation
items.summary: Multi-turn AI agents execute iterative loops of large language model (LLM) inference and external tool calls, transforming cluster serving into a dynamic resource-allocation problem where routing and key-value (KV) cache retention jointly govern prefix reuse across inter-turn delays. We formulate a fluid approximation of this system and show that optimal admission, routing, and eviction are governed by endpoint-specific shadow prices for computation and memory together with session continuation values. Building on this structure, we propose an asymptotically optimal buffer-reserve policy that absorbs stochastic fluctuations using a vanishing share of capacity. To handle asynchronous arrivals, delayed load reports, and engine-local memory management in production clusters, we translate these principles into a practical controller named PARK, which pairs online projected subgradient price updates and one-turn migration lookahead with a local KV retention index ranked by expected reuse value per byte-epoch. In real GPU cluster experiments serving a 197-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model on multi-turn software-engineering agent benchmarks (SWE and Terminal-Bench), PARK outperforms all five load-balancing and prefix-aware baselines across contrasting traffic regimes. On 16 H200 GPUs, PARK raises output throughput by $24.2\%$ over the strongest baseline ($336.9\%$ over round robin) on turn-intensive SWE trajectories and by $40.0\%$ over the strongest baseline ($63.3\%$ over round robin) on generation-intensive Terminal-Bench trajectories. Controlled single-replica ablations show that our retention index alone cuts prior-prefix token loss from $13.26\%$ to $2.17\%$ and increases throughput by $36.7\%$ over least-recently-used (LRU) eviction, while 128-GPU scale-up experiments sustain 50,789 to 67,363 output tokens/s across 16~replicas with prefix cache hit rates of $91.3\%$ to $97.4\%$.

items.title: Square-root comparison, Turnpike, and exact semidefinite feasibility
items.summary: Given positive integers $a_i,K$, put $S=\sum_{i=1}^k\sqrt{a_i}$. We construct a realizable Turnpike instance in which the minimum spacing of distinct distances and the smallest nonzero addition residual are both at most $|S-K|$ when $S\ne K$. With approximation oracles, one three-distance realizability query decides $S\le K$. For unordered lists of radical sums with nonnegative rational coefficients, a polynomial-time substitution by integers preserves every normalized ruler. We give the classical reduction of square-root comparison to exact semidefinite feasibility in both threshold directions. The comparison enters through numerical separation and marked sorting; the integer recoding needs no such comparison for unordered reconstruction.

items.title: Convergence of Residual-driven Adaptive Kernel-based Multilevel Approximation
items.summary: Kernel-based multilevel methods combine compactly supported radial basis functions with a residual correction scheme and are known to converge linearly in the number of levels. In this paper we study an adaptive version of the multilevel method, in which the interpolation on each level only uses those sites at which the residual of the preceding level exceeds a given threshold. Although this method has been proposed some time ago and converges in all numerical tests, a convergence proof has been missing so far. We close this gap. We derive an a priori error bound, an a posteriori error bound valid for arbitrary point selections, and extend the analysis to penalized least-squares approximation and to target functions outside the native space of the kernel. For a variant with an additional check-loop per level, we show convergence with the rate of the classical multilevel method. We illustrate our findings with three numerical examples.

items.title: Selecting $2 \times 2$ submatrices with optimally bounded inverses
items.summary: For a matrix $U \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}$ ($n \ge k$) with orthonormal columns, the Goreinov--Tyrtyshnikov--Zamarashkin (GTZ) conjecture asserts that there exists a $k \times k$ submatrix $U_I$ with $\|U_I^{-1}\|_2 \le \sqrt{n}$. The conjecture remains open for $3 \le k \le n - 3$. The existence of such a submatrix in the case $k = 2$ was proved for $n=4$ by Nesterenko (2023) and recently for general $n$ by Sengupta and Pautov (2026). In this paper, we give a short, elementary, constructive proof of a weighted strengthening of this result, which yields a single-pass streaming algorithm that selects a row pair satisfying the $\sqrt{n}$ bound in $\mathcal O(n)$ operations and $\mathcal O(1)$ auxiliary memory. We further give an explicit matrix representation of all equality cases for $k = 2$ characterized by Nesterenko (2026) and use it to construct a single matrix family on which standard selection strategies (including global and local maximum-volume selection, Bischof--Stewart pivoted QR, column-pivoted QR, and LU with partial pivoting) simultaneously fail to attain the $\sqrt{n}$ bound.

items.title: StePPO: Adaptive Step-Size Control for Initial-Value Problems Using Proximal Policy Optimisation
items.summary: ODE solvers are used to model, simulate, and analyse continuous-time systems found in many signal processing applications. Time integration of these initial-value problems is traditionally performed using adaptive embedded Runge--Kutta methods. For proper time-step selection, adaptive solvers accept or reject each candidate step according to a local error estimate. Their efficiency is therefore controlled by the rule that selects the next step size. Classical proportional--integral--derivative (PID) controllers are computationally inexpensive per decision and reliable, but their reactive design can lead to costly numerical solves near stiff transitions. We formulate step-size selection for parametrised IVPs as a Markov decision process and train a continuous-action policy using proximal policy optimisation. The policy processes its observation signals using a deep network while maintaining the embedded solver logic. We evaluate on a decay function, the Van der Pol system, and the Brusselator system at matched tolerances, and compare against a standard PID controller and a multi-scale DeepONet network. We find that the proposed learned policy remains within prescribed error tolerances while reducing the required number of solve steps by up to 60%, achieving a wall-clock time reduction of 58%, for both in- and out-of-distribution settings.

items.title: The Monge Optimal Transport Barycenter Problem with Adaptive Features
items.summary: The data-driven Monge optimal transport barycenter problem seeks a map $y=T(x,z)$ that minimally perturbs an outcome $x$ while removing its statistical dependence on covariates $z$. Numerical implementations approximate the independence constraint through finite-dimensional test-function spaces, making the effectiveness of dependence removal sensitive to the choice of features. This article develops a procedure whereby the features themselves are optimized throughout the procedure. In particular, we adopt a feature space for $f$ consisting of Gaussian radial basis functions (RBFs) with adaptive individual centers and bandwidths. Synthetic experiments show that while fixed nonlinear RBF features can capture dependence structures that are poorly represented by linear features, adapting the RBF centers and bandwidths can further improve dependence removal within a limited feature space and achieve residual dependence comparable to that obtained with a larger fixed basis. We further extend the formulation to multidimensional covariates and evaluate its applicability to real-world problems, including removing age-related dependence in biomedical measurements and dependence on temperature and humidity in bike-sharing demand.

items.title: Exponential Analysis for Trace-Distance Errors in Quantum Information Theory
items.summary: We study the trace-distance error in classical-quantum soft covering, privacy amplification against quantum side information, convex splitting, and decoupling by a Haar-random unitary followed by partial trace. In the independent and identically distributed setting, we determine exact reliability functions and strong converse exponents for soft covering with independent codewords, uniform convex splitting, and Haar partial-trace decoupling. For privacy amplification, we determine the exact reliability function for independent random binning and the exact strong converse exponent for every two-universal hash ensemble. The reliability and strong converse formulas involve sandwiched and Petz-Rényi information, respectively. The proofs connect trace-distance errors to quantum hypothesis testing, using Rosenthal inequalities for sums of random matrices in the reliability analysis and conditional second-moment bounds for the strong converses.

items.title: Functional Factor Graphs and the Functional Sum-Product Algorithm
items.summary: We propose a generalization of factor graphs and the sum-product algorithm (SPA), widely used in the estimation of data, channel state information and sensing parameters, to unknowns that are functions, such as waveforms, time-varying channels and continuous-aperture array currents, which must otherwise be sampled first. In order to mitigate the challenge that functions have no probability density functions (PDFs), the proposed scheme measures densities relative to the prior of each function, not to the flat reference implicit in every PDF. Messages then become likelihood ratios, and the factor-node rule an average over the priors, still exact on trees. For Gaussian models, the proposed functional SPA (FSPA) is Gaussian belief propagation (GaBP) with kernels in place of matrices and a grid-independent convergence condition, whereas scalar GaBP on grid samples provably slows down under refinement, as information hops from sample to sample. Simulations in a multi-user detection setting confirms the latter, and shows that sampling first can also fail for smooth priors.

items.title: Optimal \texorpdfstring{$(1,1)$}{(1,1)}-Criss-Cross Deletion-Correcting Codes with Linear-Time Encoder and Decoder
items.summary: We consider a $q$-ary $n\times n$ array subject to a $(1,1)$-criss-cross deletion, which removes one row and one column. We first derive a sphere-packing type lower bound on the redundancy of codes correcting such deletions. For every $q\geq 2$ and $n\geq 27$, the redundancy is greater than $2n+2\log_q n-2$. For fixed $q$, it is at least $2n-1+2\log_q n-o_q(1)$ as $n\to\infty$. We then present two code constructions. The first construction achieves redundancy $2n-1+2\log_q n+o_q(1)$ by selecting a largest syndrome class. It matches the lower bound up to a vanishing term and admits $O_q(n^2)$-time decoding. The second construction has redundancy $2n+2\log_q n+O_q(1)$ and admits $O_q(n^2)$-time algorithms for both encoding and decoding. For fixed $q$, these running times are linear in the number of array entries.

items.title: Counting Classical Fullerenes VII: Arithmetic Unranking of Fullerene Isomers
items.summary: Given a vertex number $2m$ and a rank, we construct the corresponding ordinary fullerene as a planar adjacency list. Choosing the rank uniformly therefore samples ordinary isomorphism classes exactly from the vertex number alone. We select an integral period by counting lattice points on a quadratic level in polytopes with fixed facet directions. For a fixed positive semidefinite integral form on a box of radius $H$, with a linear term of coefficients $O(H)$, the algorithm computes all level counts simultaneously in $O(H^2\operatorname{polylog}(2m))$ bit operations when $H=O(\sqrt m)$ and the facet offsets have $O(\log(2m))$ bits. A signed decomposition into orthogonal simplices gives this bound. For fullerenes we use deterministic $O(m^2\operatorname{polylog}(2m))$ bit work to construct an index of $O(m\log(2m))$ bits. With this index a rank costs $O(m\operatorname{polylog}(2m))$ bit work, uniformly in the rank. Two families of recuts let energy descent escape self-contacts in the slit polygon. The decoder then writes the graph from its selected period in $O(m)$ arithmetic word operations.

items.title: Structure-preserving finite element method for the 2D MHD-$α$ turbulence system
items.summary: We propose a structure-preserving finite element method for the two-dimensional MHD-$α$ turbulence model, which filters the transport velocity at a length $α$ while retaining the ideal invariants of the original MHD equations, with the energy replaced by an $α$-dependent energy. The scheme preserves mass conservation and the magnetic Gauss law pointwise and satisfies discrete dissipation laws for the energy, the cross helicity and the mean square magnetic potential, which reduce to exact conservation in the ideal limit. The discrete systems are solved by an augmented Lagrangian preconditioner with monolithic geometric multigrid, observed to be robust with respect to the filter width $α$ and the Reynolds numbers, and to the mesh size for small time steps. The scheme converges at the optimal rates and agrees with a Fourier pseudo-spectral direct simulation of the original MHD equations at the large scales. In under-resolved flows, the unfiltered scheme has no numerical dissipation and accumulates energy at the grid scale. Filtering relieves this accumulation and a larger $α$ gives a more compact spectrum. Long-time simulations reproduce selective decay, including relaxation toward the Arnold-type bound and the inverse cascade of the mean square potential.

items.title: Non-Intrusive Least-Squares Reduced Basis Methods: Black-Box Snapshots and Exact Residual Certificates
items.summary: For a parametrized linear first-order system, the least-squares functional at a conforming pair is the squared norm of the residual of the continuous problem, and it can be computed exactly. In this paper, we use this least-squares residual as the error certificate of reduced basis methods whose snapshots are computed by black-box solvers. The output of the solver is first made conforming by a reconstruction, and a flux is recovered by least-squares if the solver does not provide one. The online reduced problem minimizes the least-squares functional over the product of the space spanned by the snapshot fluxes and the space spanned by the snapshot potentials. It needs no inf--sup condition on the reduced spaces, and its certificate needs no stability constant. We discuss second-order elliptic equations, the Stokes equations, where only the velocity of a black-box solver is used, and linear transport equations with a moving inflow boundary. In the numerical experiments, the snapshots are computed by least-squares, conforming, nonconforming, stabilized, finite volume, and finite difference solvers. With adaptive meshes and the same tolerances, the greedy algorithm stops at the same or nearly the same reduced dimension for all solvers that accept a mesh.

items.title: On Bramble-Pasciak-type preconditioners and their properties
items.summary: Bramble and Pasciak (Math. Comp., 1988) discovered a preconditioning method for linear algebraic systems in saddle point form, which under certain conditions transforms a symmetric indefinite saddle point matrix into a nonsymmetric matrix that is positive definite in some non-standard inner product. Thus, the method "removes" the indefiniteness of the problem, while retaining the property that the preconditioned system can be solved using an optimal Krylov subspace method with three-term recurrences. Since this well-known method has some limitations, several variants with potential improvements have been proposed in the literature. In this paper, we attempt a systematic assessment of the mathematical properties and practical efficiency of Bramble-Pasciak-type preconditioners. Our goal is to close some gaps in the understanding of these techniques. We identify and analyze the three main methods in this context, highlighting a variant that offers additional flexibility but has received little attention to date. We perform detailed spectral analyzes of the preconditioned matrices and illustrate our theoretical results on several numerical examples.

items.title: A Counterexample to Single-Control Null Controllability of Stochastic Heat Equations
items.summary: We disprove the conjecture that a single localized drift control suffices for null controllability of stochastic parabolic equations with bounded adapted coefficients. On a bounded interval with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions, we construct a deterministic, nonnegative smooth noise coefficient supported at positive distance from the control interval. One fixed nonzero smooth initial state cannot be driven to zero almost surely at any positive time by any progressively measurable control with finite expected $L^2$ energy. The proof uses products of Brownian increments in the adjoint terminal data to keep the initial pairing bounded away from zero while the observation norm tends to zero. On the flat torus, the construction yields counterexamples in every Gevrey class of order $s>1$ whenever the complement of the control set contains an open ball. Thus Gevrey regularity above order one cannot replace analyticity as a general sufficient condition for null controllability.

items.title: Variational Principles and Machine Learning: a Numerical Analysis and PDE perspective
items.summary: Variational principles have played a fundamental role in the development of modern mathematics, physics, and scientific computing. From the principles of least action in mechanics to the calculus of variations and the variational formulation of partial differential equations, they have provided a powerful framework for understanding complex problems and designing reliable numerical methods. In recent years, Machine Learning has introduced a new computational paradigm, in which highly expressive nonlinear function spaces and large-scale minimisation problems play a central role. In these notes, we explore the connection between these two frameworks. We develop a variational and numerical-analysis perspective on Machine Learning algorithms, focusing in particular on their formulation as nonlinear minimisation problems. We investigate how classical concepts such as stability, consistency, approximability, and compactness acquire new interpretations in this setting, and how the variational structure of the underlying continuous problem can govern the behaviour of neural-network approximations. This perspective provides a mathematical framework for understanding existing ML algorithms while also suggesting new approaches to their design. In particular, alternative and strongly coercive variational principles can lead to more stable, reliable, and potentially more efficient computational methods.

items.title: Parameterized Algorithms for Minimum Sum Vertex Cover on Dense Graphs
items.summary: The \textsc{Minimum Sum Vertex Cover} (MSVC) problem asks for a linear ordering of the vertices of a graph that minimizes the sum, over all edges, of the position of the earlier endpoint. We study its parameterized complexity on graphs that become a clique, cluster graph, or a split graph after deleting a small set of vertices, called the Modulator. We prove that MSVC is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized jointly by the cluster modulator size and the maximum clique size in the remaining cluster graph, while allowing arbitrarily many cliques. For the clique modulator parameterization, we present a combinatorial algorithm that avoids the integer quadratic programming used in prior work [Aute, Panolan, Theoretical Computer Science, 2025]. We also introduce a vertex-weighted formulation of MSVC and obtain an XP algorithm parameterized by the clique modulator size. Using this algorithm as a subroutine, we develop an XP algorithm parameterized by the split modulator size. These results extend the known structural parameterizations of MSVC and highlight weighted MSVC as a promising direction for further research.

items.title: The $k$-disjoint paths problem for group-labelled graphs
items.summary: A $Γ$-labelled graph is an oriented graph with edge labels in a group $Γ$. Fix a finite abelian group $Γ$ and a positive integer $k$. We give a polynomial-time algorithm that finds $k$ vertex-disjoint paths joining prescribed pairs with a prescribed gain on each path, or determines that none exist. The result previously appeared only in the author's 2009 PhD thesis. This proof uses a reduction to unbreakable graphs and recent structure theorems for graphs drawn on a surface, and was found with the help of AI.

items.title: Computing Optimal Graph Mappings
items.summary: The weak graph distance is a distance measure for comparing two embedded graphs, which takes into account both the topology and the geometry of the graphs. The algorithm for computing this measure produces a mapping from one graph to the other that minimises the maximum distance; however, it maps all other distances only well enough to ensure that the maximum distance is not exceeded. In practical applications, it may be of interest to map the parts of the graph beyond the bottleneck as accurately as possible. We propose two different criteria for optimal mappings and also provide algorithms to compute them.

items.title: Polynomial-degree-robust saturation on triangular meshes
items.summary: We prove a polynomial-degree-robust ($p$-robust) saturation property for conforming finite element approximations of the Poisson equation on shape-regular triangular meshes. Previously, a $p$-robust saturation estimate for the spectral method on a square was proved in [C. Canuto et al., A saturation property for the spectral-Galerkin approximation of a Dirichlet problem in a square, ESAIM Math. Model. Numer. Anal., 53 (2019), pp. 987--1003]. For every fixed $λ>1$, increasing the polynomial degree from $p$ to any $q\geq\lceilλp\rceil+3$ reduces the energy error by a factor $α_λ\in(0,1)$ independent of $p$ and the mesh size, up to a data oscillation term.

items.title: The confined discrete DLSS equation: gradient flow structure and long-time asymptotics
items.summary: We propose and analyse a structure-preserving discretization of the fourth-order DLSS equation in dynamically rescaled variables leading to a linear confinement on the one-dimensional real line. The scheme is obtained as a discrete analogue of the Carrillo--Toscani splitting. It allows for a new interpretation of the DLSS equation as gradient flow of the relative entropy with respect to a combined diffusive and transport metric, extending the structure of the discretization introduced in our earlier work with Giuseppe Savaré for the unconfined equation. We prove global existence of positive solutions and, as the main analytical result, exponential decay of the relative entropy towards the discrete Gaussian equilibrium. The decay rate is obtained via a discrete modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality. The resulting rate is consistent with the continuum rate and converges to it from below in the vanishing mesh-size limit. Numerical results illustrate and confirm our findings.

items.title: Simultaneous Inversion of Drift and Potential in the Fractional Magnetic Schrödinger Equation
items.summary: We study the Calderón problem for the fractional magnetic Schrödinger equation with drift in the bivariate additive framework. When the magnetic potential $A$ is known and fixed, we prove that the drift $b$ and the scalar potential $q$ can be simultaneously and uniquely determined from exterior Dirichlet-to-Neumann measurements. When $A$ is unknown, we prove that the triple $(A,b,q)$ can only be recovered up to a natural gauge equivalence class, and that the drift $b$ is a gauge invariant, hence uniquely determined. The proofs rely on the Alessandrini identity, Runge approximation, and the unique continuation property for fractional magnetic operators. Furthermore, we have developed a numerical reconstruction framework that combines finite difference discretization, radial basis function surrogate modeling, and smoothed TV regularization. One-dimensional and two-dimensional numerical examples have verified the effectiveness of the proposed method and supported the theoretical uniqueness result.

items.title: A Local-Counting Approach for Distributed Induced Path Detection
items.summary: A well-known application of the celebrated color-coding technique is fast detection of paths in a distributed setting with limited bandwidth, by propagating a signal along colorful paths [Even et al., DISC 2017]. However, since vertices of the same color are indistinguishable by this procedure, it cannot detect induced paths, as they appear the same as cycles. We make the following observation. If, for a given edge, we \emph{count} the number of such signals over all permutations of the random coloring that terminate at that edge, then we can separate an induced path from a cycle: an induced path contributes one to that count, while a cycle contributes two. Refining and generalizing this observation gives our \emph{local-counting approach}, which allows us to separate induced paths from any other subgraph. We establish the following end results, all improving upon the state of the art in their round complexities and refined detection variants. * An $O(1)$-round algorithm for induced $P_4$ detection. * $O(Δ)$-round algorithms for detection of induced $P_5$ and $P_6$. * An $\tilde{O}(n^{1/3})$-round algorithm for detection of induced $P_5$ in induced-$C_4$ free graphs.

items.title: FoundSurface: Feedforward Ray-Based 3D Scene Surface Reconstruction from Unposed Images
items.summary: Accurate 3D surface reconstruction from unposed images remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. Recent feed-forward pointmap methods eliminate the need for camera poses but inherently produce discrete, sparse representations. In this paper, we present a generalizable pipeline that directly recovers continuous, high-fidelity 3D surfaces from unposed images by seamlessly integrating pointmap- and ray-based representations. Our approach first extracts explicit geometric priors using a pre-trained pointmap model. A query-view-centric selection module then identifies geometrically relevant reference views via a robust surfel voting mechanism. Next, a cross-attention regressor bridges target query rays with reference features to estimate a continuous coarse surface. Lastly, a raylet-based module aggregates local 3D features to carve out high-frequency details and analytical normals. Trained as a single foundation model on 9 diverse datasets, our method demonstrates exceptional zero-shot generalization on 6 unseen datasets, clearly surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in geometric accuracy and detail preservation.

items.title: Scaled Coordinate Descent for Convex Quadratic Programs
items.summary: We study a modification of coordinate descent for unconstrained symmetric positive definite quadratic programs that combines a coordinate correction with an exact scaling of the current iterate. For a selected coordinate, the method minimizes the objective function over the two-dimensional subspace spanned by the current iterate and the corresponding standard basis vector. Closed-form expressions are obtained for the two update parameters and for the resulting objective decrease. The scaling produces a state-dependent effective curvature that is no larger than the diagonal curvature used by standard coordinate descent, so the exact scaled update makes at least as much progress for the same selected coordinate. We discuss initialization, numerical stability, randomized coordinate selection, experimental comparisons with ordinary two-coordinate descent, and a block coordinate extension. In the spirit of previous theoretical results, we give a probabilistic linear convergence result. Finally, we provide experimental results to show the effectiveness of the proposed method on synthetic data.

items.title: A Robust Optimization Framework for Energy System Capacity Expansion under Line Outage Uncertainty
items.summary: Capacity expansion models are widely used in climate and energy policy analysis to find optimal investments in generation, storage, and transmission. As the share of renewable generation grows, these models rely more on transmission lines to balance supply and demand across regions. Transmission lines, however, can fail due to aging, extreme weather, or accidents. Models that represent outages as time-dependent events come mainly from electrical engineering and are applied to small-scale systems, as they quickly become computationally intractable for inter-regional capacity expansion. We develop a capacity expansion model in which the risk of line failures shapes the investments in all parts of the system. We formulate it as a two-stage, scenario-based robust optimization problem that samples time-varying outage scenarios from a Markov model and hedges the investments against the most severe ones. To solve the model, we propose a memory-augmented Benders decomposition algorithm combined with Monte Carlo simulation that can handle thousands of scenarios. The selected plan is then evaluated with an out-of-sample simulation to bound the Value-at-Risk (VaR) of its system cost. In a 25-node case study of Germany and its neighboring countries, the gap between the lower bound and the simulated VaR bound is below 1%. We compare the robust plans with a deterministic plan, which assumes all lines are always available, and with a reserve-margin heuristic, which requires local firm capacity to be above peak demand. Like the heuristic, the robust plans nearly eliminate loss of load in 1000 simulated outage scenarios. Their mean system cost is within 0.2% of the deterministic plan and about 4.5% below the heuristic. Instead of adding more generation capacity, the robust approach mainly changes the type and location of capacity, for example, by spreading storage across the network.

items.title: Tropical and maximum colorful matchings in vertex-colored graphs
items.summary: A subgraph of a vertex-colored graph istropical if it contains every color. We study matchings by the number of colors they cover. A matching is maximum colorful if no matching covers more colors. When a tropical matching exists, the maximum colorful matchings are exactly the tropical matchings. We give polynomial-time algorithms for two problems: a maximum matching that covers the most colors, and a tropical matching with the fewest edges. Both algorithms rest on a counterpart of Berge's theorem: a matching is optimal if and only if it admits no tropical augmentation, or no tropical reduction. These are chains of alternating paths linked by relays, and each one is found by a single augmenting-path search in an auxiliary graph. The same tools give a maximum colorful matching with the fewest edges, and show that all maximum matchings that are maximum colorful are connected by flips. Finally, the sets of colors that a matching can cover form a matroid. The greedy algorithm then computes a matching of maximum color weight. This paper extends the conference version and the PhD thesis of one of the authors.

items.title: Concavity of cardinality-constrained interval stabbing and interval cover problems
items.summary: We consider the cardinality-constrained interval stabbing problem, in which the goal is to maximize the total weight of intervals hit by at least one of at most $k$ selected points. Although this problem does not admit a simple greedy solution, we show that its optimal value is a concave function of $k$. We establish this result using a linear programming formulation whose relaxation always admits an optimal solution with integer values. This allows us to prove concavity for the original problem. We further extend the result to the related interval cover problem. These concavity properties provide a basis for applying Lagrangian optimization using algorithms for the corresponding unconstrained problems.

items.title: Feature Engineered Reinforcement Learning for S-pair Selection in Buchberger's Algorithm
items.summary: Selecting the order in which to process S-pairs is a crucial decision in Buchberger's algorithm for computing Groebner bases: this choice can change the cost by orders of magnitude. Recent work has shown that reinforcement learning agents viewing exponent vectors of the polynomials outperform classical heuristics on binomial ideals. We extend this line of work to general polynomial ideals by using statistical features. We introduce a 17-dimensional feature vector to describe a polynomial and use PPO to train policies on five distributions of random ideals. We find that using S-polynomial features significantly outperforms S-pair features on all five distributions. The new policies also outperform the retrained RL baseline on all five distributions, reducing algorithmic work by 41--53\% relative to the degree heuristic on four distributions where learning helps. The additional cost of the feature engineering means that wall-clock cost remains similar to the baseline, but our new approach benefits from easier transfer to unseen distributions.

items.title: Exact Integration of ReLU-type Neural Networks for Solving PDEs
items.summary: Developing robust training methodologies for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with neural networks is crucial for reliable scientific computing. Piecewise-linear activations such as the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) are a convenient choice in this setting as their structure resembles classical piecewise-linear approximations. However, when the loss functional incorporates the spatial gradient of the network, as in the Deep Ritz method, numerical integration becomes problematic. Specifically, relying on standard integration techniques (e.g., Monte Carlo sampling) during training yields incorrect gradients, even as the number of integration points approaches infinity, leading to optimization failure. To overcome this limitation, we present an integration framework for single-hidden-layer ReLU networks that computes correct gradients when using Deep Ritz for PDEs or PINNs for first-order problems. Our approach employs the Sutherland-Hodgman algorithm to partition the physical domain into subdomains according to breaking hyperplanes underlying the ReLU network. By finding these hyperplanes exactly, our method can correctly integrate the gradients, ensuring the optimizer receives correct information. In this work, we further assemble the energy in matrix--vector form that allows all neuron interactions to be computed efficiently with vectorized operations, introduce an alternative approach termed Conforming Monte Carlo that is a stochastic version of the proposed method, and propose two stochastic training strategies to reduce complexity. Numerical results on two-dimensional domains demonstrate that our framework recovers optimal PDE solutions that standard stochastic sampling and other existing quadrature methods fail to capture.

items.title: Conjugation-preserving polynomial and rational interpolation for limited-memory matrix-function actions
items.summary: Approximating $f(A)b$ for a large nonsymmetric matrix can require substantial storage if a long Krylov basis is retained. We develop polynomial and rational interpolation schemes that use a fixed number of large recurrence vectors and preserve conjugation symmetry. Starting from a prescribed scalar approximation region, the schemes organize real nodes and complex-conjugate pairs into Newton-like bases with real interpolation coefficients. The polynomial and single-real-pole recurrences use real arithmetic in the matrix-action stage; the multi-pole construction also exploits conjugate pole pairs. A conjugation-preserving AAA procedure supplies interpolation data for the latter. We establish the interpolation and basis properties and compare the resulting realizations with Leja, Taylor, and Krylov methods on matrices from differential equations, model reduction, and networks. The experiments demonstrate arithmetic savings relative to complex-arithmetic counterparts and identify the influence of shifted solves and orthogonalization requirements. The methods are intended for memory-constrained computations in which useful approximation-region information is available.

items.title: Model and higher-order structure-preserving scheme for the chemotaxis equations modeling the growth of bacterial colonies
items.summary: In this paper, we study the model and higher-order structure-preserving numerical scheme for the chemotaxis equations modeling the growth of bacterial colonies. By using a new variational analysis method, we first rigidly derive the nonnegativity for two solutions of the chemotaxis equations. Then, utilizing the finite element method with mass-lumping in space and the BDF scheme with the positivity-preserving extrapolation to deal with the nonlinear terms in time, we propose a high-order fully discrete framework for the chemotaxis equations by combining with the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) shift and the Lagrange multiplier method, which preserves the mass conservation of the discrete system and the nonnegativity of two approximation solutions. Moreover, apart from confirming the existence and uniqueness of the nonlinear equation generated by the Lagrange multiplier method, by classifying its structure in detail, we prove that the secant iteration method for this nonlinear equation is locally convergent. Finally, we show some experiments to verify the theoretical prediction and efficiency of the proposed scheme, including consistent simulations of the growth of the colonies under different nutrient concentration and agar hardness.

items.title: Directed $k$-Disjoint Shortest Paths in Polynomial Time
items.summary: The $k$-Disjoint Shortest Paths problem asks for pairwise vertex-disjoint shortest paths connecting $k$ prescribed terminal pairs in a graph with positive edge weights. Eilam-Tzoreff [DAM 1998] asked whether it is polynomial-time solvable for every fixed $k$. Lochet [SODA 2021] answered this for undirected graphs, while for directed graphs it has remained open for every $k\ge3$. We give a polynomial-time algorithm for directed graphs and every fixed $k$, resolving this open problem for all graphs.

items.title: Certified Outage Bounds for RIS-Assisted NOMA with Source-Side Thermal Energy Harvesting
