items.summary: Gaussian useful-gain and mean-interference approximations can cause opposite power-sizing errors in reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA). We extend a source-side thermal energy harvesting model with Poisson interference and certify two-sided outage bounds. In a tested environment, the combined required signal-to-noise ratio error has opposite signs at 20 and 24 elements per user. Under another power convention, mean or moment-matched Gamma-distributed interference can predict false feasibility with exact useful gain. In the Gamma case, the Gaussian gain approximation can mask this false feasibility. Propagated Chernoff bounds give sufficient designs. Results concern the specified model and tested regimes.

items.title: Structure Preserving Iterative Solution of Linear Systems Arising in Gauss Collocation for port-Hamiltonian DAEs
items.summary: This work presents structure-preserving computational techniques for the pencil Padé approximation arising in the numerical integration of port-Hamiltonian differential-algebraic equations (pH-DAEs) via the Gauss-Legendre schemes. We first extend the concept of the diagonal Padé approximation and introduce a generalized framework characterizing the $s$-stage Gauss method. We further examine its structural properties and the role of the full orthogonalization method (FOM) in approximating the discrete solution. Building on this, we analyze the iterative approximation of the pencil Pade approximation and establish conditions on the search space in Petrov-Galerkin-type approximations which guarantee that structure-induced properties, such as dissipativity or energy preservation, are inherited by the Petrov-Galerkin approximations. In particular, we show that FOM-based Krylov subspace methods preserve these properties iterate-wise. The presented results provide a new insight into the interplay between Krylov subspace methods and energy preservation in the numerical integration of pH-DAEs. Finally, we conclude with numerical examples illustrating the convergence and the conservation of the physical properties.

items.title: Algebraic Diversity of Switching Functions
items.summary: Algebraic Diversity generalizes averaging over many observations to averaging one observation over a group of transformations matched to its structure. This paper develops the framework on the Boolean cube $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ for the translations, the coordinate permutations, the hyperoctahedral group, and the general linear and affine groups. It determines the commutant of each action and gives closed forms for the group-averaged second-order statistic of one truth table, which collapses to the Walsh periodogram for the translations, to per-weight averages for the hyperoctahedral group, and to the weight up to complementation for the affine group. Bent functions are exactly those whose translation average is white, the Haar transform along an input order is the multiplexer tree of Shannon's expansion, and higher-order averages see only the weight below a first informative order, two for the translations and four for the affine group. A matched stabilizer stands in for repeated observations, since a vote over orbits of $s$ points divides by $s$ the number of noisy truth tables a target error requires. The same viewpoint gives the affine hull of a function as matched coordinates, an exact variance identity for XOR hashing, and matched hashes whose variance never exceeds that of a pairwise independent hash. Applications on public benchmarks include hash choice for approximate model counting, the decision of parity-structured formulas and the refutation of counting formulas modulo 3 and 4 from the spectra of clause blocks, separation of NPN classes by canonical spectra, tested on ISCAS-85 cut functions and all five-input classes, correction of noisy truth tables and protection of lookup tables by voting over symmetries, blind group matching, and an analog of the CLEAN algorithm that writes a truth table as the XOR of atoms in the fixed spaces of groups. All proofs are given in full.

items.title: Near Optimal Pure Stepsize Adaptation Acceleration for Gradient Descent on Nonconvex Optimization
items.summary: Existing accelerated first-order methods for nonconvex optimization typically rely on momentum or extrapolation, requiring auxiliary vectors beyond the current iterate and gradient. On the other hand, memory-free stepsize scheduling alone can accelerate certain convex problems, while no guarantee exists for nonconvex problems. This paper closes this gap by proposing Nonconvex Adaptively Clipped Chebyshev (NACC) gradient descent method, which achieves near optimal acceleration while keeping the vanilla gradient descent update. NACC combines an adaptive selection of reversed fractal Chebyshev stepsizes with an epoch-wise clipping mechanism to control the aggressiveness of stepsizes. For nonconvex problems with Lipschitz continuous gradients and Hessians, we establish a near-optimal $\widetilde O(ε^{-7/4})$ complexity. If the problem is convex in addition, then, without modification, NACC automatically achieves an $\widetilde O(ε^{-3/4})$ accelerated complexity. Importantly, NACC guarantees the standard quadratic sufficient descent at every iteration, even when the stepsizes are substantially larger than the conventional choice. These monotonicity properties further facilitate practical implementations that adaptively adjust the estimated gradient and Hessian Lipschitz constants, demonstrating significant advantages in numerical tests against the existing nonconvex acceleration benchmarks.

items.title: Almost Tight Hardness of Approximation for $0$-Extension
items.summary: In the $0$-Extension problem, we are given an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with non-negative edge weights $w: E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$, a collection $T \subseteq V$ of $k$ terminals, and a metric $D$ over terminals $T$. The goal is to find a retraction $f:V\rightarrow T$ that maps every terminal to itself, while minimizing the sum over all edges of the product of the edge's weight and the distance in $D$ between the terminals to which its endpoints are assigned, i.e., \[ \sum_{\{u,v\}\in E} w_{\{u,v\}} \cdot D(f(u), f(v)). \] Fakcharoenphol, Harrelson, Rao, and Talwar achieve the best known approximation ratio of $O(\log k / \log \log k)$, while the known approximation hardness is $Ω(\sqrt{\log k})$ assuming the unique games conjecture. In this work, we establish an $Ω(\log^{1-\varepsilon}k)$ hardness of approximation for every constant $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$ and arbitrarily large fixed $k$, almost matching the upper bound in the exponent of $\log k$. The main technical contribution is an $Ω(\log^{1-\varepsilon}k)$ integrality gap for the earthmover relaxation. Our construction is inspired by randomized extensions of expanders introduced by Schwartz and Tur for the metric relaxation. The result then follows from an existing theorem by Manokaran, Naor, Raghavendra, and Schwartz that translates the integrality gap for the earthmover relaxation to the approximation hardness for every fixed $k$.

items.title: Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao Reconstruction of Discrete space Population Dynamics
items.summary: Reconstructing the continuous time dynamics of cell state evolution from sparse snapshot observations can be formulated as an unbalanced optimal transport problem. To study such dynamics at a coarse grained cell type level, unbalanced optimal transport must be extended to discrete state spaces. Inspired by discrete flow matching, we extended the dynamic Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) problem to discrete spaces, and derived a closed form for its solution. For particularly large state spaces or more general models, we proposed an unbalanced discrete flow matching as a numerical approximation method, which provides a Markovian reconstruction of the optimal WFR flow. Our discrete WFR framework also stays stable across different coarse grain resolution. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed approach, and applications to real biological data supported the plausibility of the reconstructed dynamics.

items.title: Data-driven framework for invariant manifold identification in multiscale systems
items.summary: Multiscale dynamical systems often exhibit fast transient behavior followed by slow evolution on a low-dimensional attracting manifold, on which their long-term dynamics unfold. Identifying this structure directly from data remains challenging when the governing equations, Jacobians, and fast-slow variable partitions are unknown. In this work, we propose a fully data-driven framework for timescale decomposition, slow invariant manifold (SIM) approximation, and reduced-order model identification. A sparse-regression surrogate of the vector field is reconstructed from the data, and its Jacobian, estimated with a matrix-free Krylov method, is analysed with Computational Singular Perturbation diagnostics. The resulting fast-slow partition guides the learning of explicit SIM algebraic representations through regression, and the reduced model follows by restricting the dynamics to it. For a linear stochastic system, this regression agrees with the Mori-Zwanzig projection at leading order in the timescale ratio. We demonstrate the validity of the framework on an illustrative linear system, the Michaelis-Menten model, a biofilm growth model, and a five-dimensional target-mediated drug disposition (TMDD) model. The method accurately identifies fast variables, reconstructs slow invariant manifolds, and generates accurate reduced models. Furthermore, we map the performance boundaries of the framework under sparse sampling and measurement noise, showing robust recovery for low-dimensional systems and highlighting data-requirement limits in higher dimensions. These results demonstrate that interpretable multiscale reduction can be achieved directly from time-series data, without requiring explicit prior knowledge of the underlying fast/slow timescale separation.

items.title: Geary-type expectation identities for Mardia's sample skewness and kurtosis
items.summary: Under multivariate normality, we establish exact Geary-type expectation identities for Mardia's sample skewness and kurtosis. A polar decomposition of the centered Gaussian data matrix shows that each of these statistics is independent of the sample covariance matrix. This independence allows the moments of each statistic to be expressed as ratios of expectations involving polynomial numerators and powers of the determinant of the sample covariance matrix. The identities hold in arbitrary dimension $p$. To illustrate their use, we give exact expressions for the variance of Mardia's sample skewness and the third central moment of Mardia's sample kurtosis for $p=2$ and $p=3$. As an application of the exact variance formulas, we construct a moment-matched chi-square approximation to the null distribution of Mardia's sample skewness and compare its performance with Mardia's classical and mean-corrected approximations.

items.title: VoroPlex: A Python Framework for Multi-Threaded and Differentiable Voronoi Tessellation
items.summary: Voronoi tessellations are widely used in computational physics, for example to measure local structure in particle systems and to generate meshes. We present VoroPlex, an open-source Python package for computing Voronoi tessellations in two and three dimensions. VoroPlex is built on the multi-threaded version of the C++ library Voro++, so that large tessellations can be computed in parallel. The package also makes the tessellation differentiable. Each Voronoi vertex is labeled by the generators that define it, and VoroPlex uses these labels to compute the derivative of the vertex with respect to the positions of these generators. PyTorch can therefore compute gradients of quantities such as cell areas, volumes, and interface areas with respect to the generator positions, so that these quantities can be optimized using standard gradient-based methods. The package also includes tools for extracting interfaces between groups of cells and for exporting meshes. For one million points using 28 threads, VoroPlex is 46 times faster than SciPy in 2D and 39 times faster in 3D. We demonstrate the package with three applications: centroidal Voronoi tessellations with a variable density, meshing of 2D shapes defined by signed distance functions, and the design of foams with a preferred cell orientation.

items.title: Quantization and Codebook Stability of Euclidean and KL Lattice Quantizers
items.summary: Small edits to raw data can cause large changes in the compressed version, which can be costly in applications such as data synchronization and incremental backup. We study quantization stability, the probability that two perturbed distributions map to the same representative, and codebook stability, the probability that the resulting Huffman codebooks are the same. We first quantize the empirical distribution and then construct a Huffman code from the quantized distribution, which can improve codebook stability at the cost of some compression efficiency. We study two quantizers based on a shifted and scaled lattice in the probability simplex: the Euclidean Lattice Quantizer (ELQ) and the KL Quantizer (KLQ). For ELQ, we derive bounds on quantization stability and KL distortion. For KLQ, we show that its quantization cells can be determined by comparisons with adjacent lattice codewords and use the distances to the cell boundaries to derive a quantization stability bound. For a symmetric codebook of positive types, we obtain the exact worst-case KL distortion over the full probability simplex. We also give a heuristic choice $α^\star$ of the minimum codeword probability and compare it with the minimum coordinate of a Lloyd-optimized codebook. Simulations using canonical Huffman coding compare ELQ and KLQ with an existing compander-based quantizer and show the trade-off between KL distortion, codebook stability, and encoded length under random deletions.

items.title: BGPNP: A Non-Euclidean Gradient Projection Newton Pursuit Method for Sparsity-Constrained Optimization
items.summary: A non-Euclidean gradient projection Newton pursuit method is proposed for solving sparsity constrained optimization problem via the Bregman distance. The method is also denoted as BGPNP. The method firstly constructs a gradient projection step based on the Bregman distance to ensure that the iterates satisfy the sparsity constraint. Then, when the support set becomes stable or the gradient norm is sufficiently small, a Newton pursuit step is introduced to improve local convergence efficiency. The BGPNP is proved to possess a sufficient descent property and the non-increasing monotonicity of the objective function values. The full convergence and linear convergence rate of the BGPNP are established under appropriate conditions, which do not involve the symmetry coefficient of Bregman distance and the $θ$-uniform condition. Moreover, the locally quadratical convergence rate of the BGPNP is also obtained. This method provides an effective algorithmic framework for sparse optimization in non-Euclidean setting. Numerical experiments on sparsity-constrained compressed sensing problems validate the competitive performance of BGPNP compared with existing leading solvers.

items.title: A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for ARRIVAL
items.summary: In ARRIVAL, a token moves through a directed graph from a specified starting vertex, alternating between the two outgoing arcs of each vertex on successive departures. The problem asks whether the token ever reaches a given destination. Although the walk can be exponentially long, we give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, resolving an open problem. We first average the local routing rules and then restore the original rules on selected periods. The number of refinement rounds is at most the number of nonterminal vertices. The algorithm extends to explicitly given cyclic successor lists. It also computes exact departure counts when every nonterminal vertex has a path to an absorbing terminal and recovers the configuration of the walk at any binary-encoded time.

items.title: A Nonlocal Allen--Cahn Model for Volume-Constrained Wetting and Its Multi-Structure-Preserving Discretization
items.summary: At finite interface thickness, small droplets can shrink or disappear during wetting relaxation even when the phase-field mass is conserved. We develop a nonlocal Allen--Cahn model that couples a nonlinear diffuse-volume constraint to dynamic wall relaxation through Onsager's principle. The constraint gradient vanishes at the pure-phase values and does zero work in the energy balance, preserving the original bulk and wall dissipation structure. We construct a Compatible Variational Chain-Rule (CVC) scheme using the same discrete derivative of the volume density in the correction and in the volume increment. The scheme exactly conserves the nonlinear diffuse volume and reproduces the bulk--wall dissipation identity for the original discrete energy. Under a coercivity condition, the energy also yields a mesh-dependent maximum-norm bound. Numerical tests show second-order convergence in space and time. In flat-wall tests, the proposed model improves small-droplet retention and geometric-volume preservation and reproduces equilibrium cap shapes and contact angles. Additional tests illustrate wetting on chemically heterogeneous and rough substrates.

items.title: Toggle Tree: A New Data Structure for Efficient Parallel Graph Processing
items.summary: We present the Toggle Tree, a parallel data structure for frontier-based graph algorithms. A Toggle Tree is used to represent a subset of vertices using hierarchical bit vectors, enabling efficient parallel updates, traversal, and set-wise reductions without global packing. It provides an IndexSet interface that unifies a wide range of parallel graph algorithms under a common abstraction of frontiers and active sets, and an IndexMap interface that also incorporates priority-queue semantics. Specifically, the Toggle Tree aims to combine the advantages of traditional sparse and dense frontier representations, offering both provable theoretical guarantees and high efficiency in practice. Using Toggle Trees, we implement five fundamental graph algorithms, including breadth-first search (BFS), k-core, degree-based graph coloring, single-source shortest paths using Bellman-Ford, and weighted-BFS (wBFS). Across a diverse set of large real-world graphs and the five graph problems, our implementations outperform state-of-the-art baselines, including GBBS and PASGAL, achieving substantial speedups. Our code is publicly available.

items.title: Improved Quantum Algorithms for TSP and More
items.summary: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) is a canonical NP-hard optimization problem. For general edge weights, the classical dynamic programs of Bellman and of Held and Karp solve TSP on $n$ cities in $O^*(2^n)$ time. To date, no $\Oh(c^n)$-time classical algorithm is known for any $c<2$. Combining Grover search with the dynamic programming technique, Ambainis et al. (SODA 2019) introduced a quantum algorithm with running time $O^*(1.7274^n)$, which is still the best known quantum time bound. In this work, we improve the running time to $O^*(1.70961^n)$. The core idea of our algorithm is to combine the framework of Ambainis et al. with the extremal set-system framework, which was recently used for classical space-time tradeoffs of TSP by Jabal Ameli, Nederlof and Wang (FOCS 2026) and Dallant and Kozma (FOCS 2026). To obtain our upper bound, we decompose the optimal tour into four consecutive subpaths of different sizes, for which, based on the idea of set-systems, the optimal values are computed using dynamic programming with small success probability and use amplitude amplification. Using the same idea, we also give a new quantum space-time tradeoff for TSP, improving the previous results of Caroppo et al. (ESA 2026) and Dallant (arXiv:2607.12374). Finally, we obtain the same quantum upper bounds for several other related problems.

items.title: A nonequilibrium-capturing unified gas-kinetic scheme II: multi-frequency radiation transport
items.summary: Conventional discrete ordinate methods are widely used for thermal radiative transfer, but their fixed number of angular degrees of freedom (DoFs) incurs unnecessary computational cost near equilibrium. We therefore develop a nonequilibrium-capturing unified gas-kinetic scheme (NCUGKS) for multi-frequency radiation transport. The scheme preserves the mul tiscale capability of UGKS through interface evolution that couples transport and collision. Radiation intensity is expanded in an orthonormal basis of the discrete angular space. The expansion coefficients serve as angular DoFs, with their number adapted independently to local nonequilibrium in each cell, frequency group, and quadrant. At each time step, the coefficients to be evolved are selected using the exponentially decayed contribution from the previous step and the requirements of interface transport. The selected coefficients are advanced by the finite volume scheme and corrected to match the macroscopic radiation energy before higher-degree coefficients are discarded according to the prescribed relative tail tolerance. Therefore, in the optically thick limit, the resulting representation retains only one angular DoF per quadrant. Numerical tests spanning different optical regimes show close agreement with reference solutions, validating its accuracy. Furthermore, in terms of memory and computational efficiency, the proposed method reduces memory by factors from 21.7 to 154.0 and achieves speedups from 24.87 to 257.9 compared with the original discrete ordinate UGKS. NCUGKS thus provides the ability to accurately simulate multiscale ra diative transfer with reduced memory and computational costs. The proposed approach also offers a framework for adapting angular degrees of freedom in other discrete ordinate methods.

items.title: CAMPS: Composable Adapters for Mixed-Precision Solvers
items.summary: Mixed-precision solvers usually assign a fixed precision to each algorithmic component. This makes it hard to reuse a lower-precision solver at different depths inside a higher-precision solver. We introduce CAMPS (Composable Adapters for Mixed-Precision Solvers), a framework that uses iterative refinement to connect solvers across precisions. An adapter computes residuals and updates in the precision of its parent and passes each correction solve to a child solver in a lower precision. The child can be a direct solver, an iterative solver, or another adapter. The adapter checks every correction and keeps it if the residual does not increase. We prove three results. Adapters can be placed at any compatible set of precision boundaries in a solver tree without breaking the solver interface. Every output that the root solver reports as successful satisfies a backward-error bound set by the stopping tolerance and the root precision. Convergence follows from one sufficient condition per boundary, computed from the leaves of the tree to its root. We test five configurations on dense and sparse systems in 64-bit, 32-bit, and 16-bit floating-point arithmetic (FP64, FP32, and FP16). On dense well-conditioned systems, CAMPS is up to 9.6x faster than an FP64 direct solver for a single solve that includes the factorization. On sparse nonsymmetric systems, a three-precision hierarchy is the fastest method we tested. Compared with our implementation of the nested solver F3R, CAMPS is as fast and uses about 3.4x less peak memory. CAMPS does not always win. Plain conjugate gradient is faster on sparse symmetric positive definite systems. On very ill-conditioned systems, FP32 corrections fail, and the adapter detects the failure and switches to an FP64 fallback.

items.title: SAT-Driven Exact Treewidth via Safe Separators and Structure-Aware Encodings
items.summary: Treewidth is a standard measure of graph structure, but computing it exactly is NP-hard. SAT- and MaxSAT-based approaches provide a uniform way to solve treewidth by encoding it in conjunctive normal form and delegating the search to modern Boolean solvers, thus directly benefiting from continued progress in SAT technology. This report studies how to strengthen such SAT-driven solvers with structural reasoning and low-overhead guidance, both at the meta-algorithmic level and within the encoding itself. Starting from a baseline SAT/MaxSAT formulation, we investigate structure-based simplifications that reduce solver effort while preserving exactness, and we evaluate practical heuristic enhancements (fast upper/lower bounds and solver guidance) within iterative SAT and MaxSAT workflows. Experiments show consistent speedups on instances with exploitable structure, and clarify where SAT-based approaches remain limited.

items.title: Two 3-Dimensional Coefficient Inverse Problems for Wave-like Equations With a Single Location of the Point Source
items.summary: In this paper two long standing open questions are addressed for the first time. Those questions are about Lipschitz stability estimates and uniqueness theorems for two Coefficient Inverse Problems (CIPs) for 3-Dimensional wave-like Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) with formally determined input data. We assume that a certain associated PDE is written in finite differences with respect to time t. The unknown coefficients depend on all three spatial variables. The key novelty here is that the input data for these CIPs are generated by only a single location of the point source at the moment of time {t = 0}. In the first CIP (CIP1) the unknown coefficient is the potential of a wave-like PDE. The second CIP (CIP2) is concerned with a far more challenging case when the unknown coefficient is involved in the principal part of the hyperbolic operator. In addition to Lipschitz stability and uniqueness results, numerical methods are developed for both CIPs. Their convergence analysis establishes the global convergence property of both numerical techniques. The latter is unlike the local convergence of conventional numerical procedures for CIPs. The method for CIP1 is tested computationally. Its extensive numerical testing for complicated media structures consistently demonstrates a very accurate performance of this method for noisy input data. The authors declare that artificial intelligence was not used for any part of this work.

items.title: A fast tangential rational Krylov subspace method with randomized sketching for large Lyapunov matrix equations
items.summary: We propose a tangential rational Krylov subspace method augmented with randomized sketching for solving continuous-time Lyapunov equations $AX + XA^T + BB^T = 0$, where $A$ is large and sparse and $B$ has a rank much higher than one. Numerical solutions require high-dimensional rational Krylov subspaces (e.g., of dimensions up to $\sim 1000$), leading to substantial computational cost and long runtime. Building on the adaptive strategies of [SIAM\,J.\,Matrix\,Anal.\,Appl., 35\,(2014), pp.\,476--498], which expand the subspace using the most relevant directions, we introduce several enhancements: selective orthogonalization of basis vectors and fast residual-norm estimation enabled by randomized sketching, and the option to use either adaptive distinct poles or a small set of repeated poles. We derive a new computable error bound for the approximate solutions and show that sketching does not degrade the convergence rate relative to the standard (non-sketched) algorithm. Numerical experiments demonstrate improved robustness and efficiency, with reduced runtimes and often higher accuracy than the standard tangential method.

items.title: Online Network Design with Batch Processing
items.summary: An online service chooses which waiting jobs to start together. Each finishes after its own processing time, and the longest determines the next possible launch. We charge network cost plus either total flow or the sum of per-batch maximum flows. For TCP acknowledgment with a fixed fee per launch, the optimal deterministic total-flow ratio is \(1+ρ\), where \(ρ\) is the processing-time spread. For batch maxima, a union of intervals on the release-time axis gives the exact offline cost when batches may overlap. It yields an offline \(2\)-approximation and pays for an online timer of ratio five. The optimal deterministic ratio is two at equal lengths and lies in \([2+2\sqrt2,5]\) at unrestricted spread. How often can later batches incur the same blocking delay? Rooted purchases can be combined, giving a polynomial-time \(3+2\sqrt2\) guarantee for batch maxima on undirected Steiner networks. A mobile server can concatenate walks in order, transferring an instantaneous maximum-wait ratio \(α\) to a batch-maximum flow ratio \(3α+6\). With \(k\) ephemeral facilities sharing one processor and one site per launch, separate openings can each incur the wait. The optimal deterministic batch-maximum ratio is then \(Θ(k)\) at unrestricted spread. The upper bound uses exact assignments, computable in polynomial time for fixed \(k\).

items.title: Anderson-Accelerated Landweber Iteration with Regularization Guarantees for Nonlinear Ill-Posed Problems
items.summary: Anderson acceleration (AA) can markedly reduce iteration counts for fixed-point solvers, but its unrestricted signed history extrapolation need not preserve the stability required for iterative regularization of ill-posed problems. We introduce a regularization-guaranteed Anderson-accelerated Landweber method (\RG) in which finite-memory AA generates a proposal while the committed iterate is a controlled perturbation of a certified Landweber anchor. Under a local tangential cone condition and a scale-normalized localization condition, we prove strong convergence of the exact-data trajectory to a solution, stability at every fixed iteration, finite discrepancy stopping, and strong convergence of the discrepancy-stopped noisy reconstructions to the same exact-data limit; local uniqueness is needed only if that selected limit is to be identified with a prescribed solution $x^\dagger$. Under the additional benchmark source condition $x^\dagger-x_0=F'(x^\dagger)^*λ^\dagger$ and a standard range-invariance condition, we obtain the discrepancy-principle rate $\norm{x_{k_δ}^δ-x^\dagger}=O(δ^{1/2})$. The rate proof controls data-dependent Anderson coefficients through fixed memory, a fixed-reference ridge in the small AA least-squares problem, and an outer correction budget with an $O(k^{-1})$ tail. The numerical examples verify the efficiency of the proposed method.

items.title: Node Differential Privacy via Node-Stable Graph Projections
items.summary: Node-differentially private algorithms enable learning on network-structured datasets in which records reflect interactions among individuals. They protect the privacy of each individual's information, including all their associated records. A key challenge in the design of such algorithms is to exploit the structure of realistic graphs---where most nodes have low degree---to achieve high accuracy, without compromising on the worst-case privacy guarantee. In this work we give two new tools for designing accurate, computationally efficient node-differentially private algorithms. First, we give a nearly linear time, randomized, node-stable graph projection: the projection leaves graphs of maximum degree $D$ unchanged, maps arbitrary graphs to subgraphs of maximum degree $\hat D \approx D$, and ensures that changing one node of the input graph has only a small effect on the distribution of the edges selected among the remaining vertices. Unlike prior approaches, which abstain when the input violates the degree bound, our projection acts as degree clipping: even when $D$ is set well below the true maximum degree (trading truncation bias at high-degree outliers for lower privacy noise), it retains at least as many edges as a maximal $D$-bounded subgraph. Second, for graphs with bounded edge weights, we give a deterministic nearly linear time Lipschitz extension for the total edge weight that agrees with the original sum on graphs of maximum degree $D$ yet is $D$-Lipschitz on all graphs. Finally, we show how to apply these methods to design node-private algorithms for high-dimensional vector summation and gradient descent on datasets where records are associated with graph edges, such as email threads.

items.title: Physics-Informed Learning for Multiplayer Differential Games
items.summary: Computing per-player feedback strategies in $N$-player adversarial differential games is challenging as the associated coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman system is high-dimensional and generally lacks classical solutions. We address this by approximating viscosity solutions using physics-informed neural networks within a policy iteration scheme with a vanishing-viscosity annealing schedule. Theoretically, we establish an explicit $\varepsilon$-Nash guarantee by bounding per-player regret via computable residuals and prove our method reaches this stopping criterion in finite time. For two-player zero-sum games, we further establish a computable bound on the approximation error of the value function. Numerical experiments on pursuit-evasion scenarios illustrate the tightness of these computed bounds and the framework's scalability to high-dimensional environments.

items.title: Learning from Natural Images Untangles Number Sense
items.summary: Numerical cognition is a simple yet fundamental ability that remains challenging for modern vision-language models. Meanwhile, number sense is already present in numerically naïve animals, suggesting that it can emerge without explicit numerical learning. Deep neural networks provide a related observation, with numerosity-selective units appearing after training on unrelated natural-image tasks and even before any training. However, these findings leave unresolved whether visual learning contributes beyond the spontaneous emergence of numerical selectivity. Human development provides a clue, as children become better at making judgments in which numerosity and proportion conflict. Here, we introduce a geometric framework to trace how representations of these two quantities change across learning. Although untrained and pretrained networks exhibited similar unit-level numerosity selectivity and basic comparison performance, natural-image pretraining increased the angle between numerosity and proportion subspaces while reducing their overlap, supporting more robust readout under conflict. Direct manipulation of these geometric properties further demonstrated their functional contributions to decoding accuracy and functional independence. Importantly, conventional supervised pretraining was not essential for quantity separation, which also emerged through self-supervised learning without category labels and synthetic-image training without natural-image exposure. Together, our findings suggest that structured visual learning can refine spontaneously emerging number sense into robust and functionally independent quantity representations without explicit numerical training.

items.title: Solving the capacitated vehicle routing problem with polygonal neighborhoods using a metaheuristic enhanced with block coordinate descent
items.summary: We study a capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) in which customers are represented by planar regions, called customer neighborhoods, rather than fixed points. Visiting a customer consists of selecting a point within its neighborhood. Therefore, besides determining the sequence of customers visited by each vehicle, one must also determine the corresponding visit points. To better reflect practical applications, customer neighborhoods are allowed to be simple polygons, either convex or non-convex, and distances are measured using the Euclidean norm. Applications include aerial reconnaissance, wireless sensor data collection and inspection, and two-stage delivery systems. We propose a general variable neighborhood search framework in which each neighbor is represented by a collection of routes. Constructing a route involves two stages, defining a customer sequence and then determining the associated visit points. The latter task is solved by a block coordinate descent (BCD) procedure, the central methodological contribution of this work, which computes high-quality visit points at a cost low enough to be used repeatedly inside the search. In extensive experiments on newly generated and adapted benchmark instances, within the time limits considered, the proposed framework matches all solutions proven optimal by CPLEX and matches or improves the best solutions found by CPLEX in the remaining instances. For the instances adapted from the CVRP literature, it also improves, in every instance, a CVRP-based upper bound given by the solution of the original CVRP instance reported in the literature, which is feasible for the problem with neighborhoods.

items.title: PACL: Patch-based Admissibility and Conservative Limiting framework for bound-preserving compact single-step DG methods for hyperbolic conservation laws
items.summary: We develop a Patch-based Admissibility and Conservative Limiting (PACL) framework for compact single-step discontinuous Galerkin (DG) discretizations of hyperbolic conservation laws. The key idea is to establish admissibility of weighted averages over overlapping cell patches after a complete high-order time step. Continuous patch weights cancel interior numerical flux contributions, yielding admissibility estimates for weighted patch averages under suitable time-step conditions. A conservative patch correction uses these averages as reference states to obtain admissible physical cell averages, and a subsequent cellwise scaling enforces whole-cell or nodal admissibility in the original DG space. The framework requires neither a strong-stability-preserving decomposition nor auxiliary first-order discretizations, and all limiting is performed at the end of each time step. For scalar conservation laws, we prove a patchwise weak maximum principle for compact Runge--Kutta DG (cRKDG), ADER-DG with converged or fixed-Picard predictors, and Lax--Wendroff DG. We also prove that, under the stated local mesh and scaling assumptions, a single application of the scalar limiter preserves approximation order at active bounds, including flat extrema. For the compressible Euler equations, we establish patch admissibility for cRKDG and fixed-Picard ADER-DG under time-step conditions that maintain positive predictor density while allowing nonpositive predictor pressure. The analysis covers both exact spatial integration and compatible quadrature. Numerical experiments demonstrate high-order accuracy and bound preservation, including problems with near-vacuum states and strong shocks.

items.title: Two-timescale variational Q-learning for ergodic risk-sensitive control of Markov chains
items.summary: We propose a variational Q-learning algorithm for the ergodic risk-sensitive control of a discrete-time Markov chain with finite state and action spaces and an unknown transition kernel. The proposed algorithm is a two-timescale stochastic approximation algorithm, where the slow iteration solves for the fixed point of the multiplicative Bellman equation cast in a variational form, while the fast iteration solves the associated optimization problem over the probability simplex that stems from the variational representation. We prove that the iterates converge almost surely to the risk-sensitive Q-function and maximizing transition kernel. The proof adapts the ODE method for two-timescale stochastic approximation, where we analyze the global asymptotic stability of the equilibria of the corresponding fast and slow ODEs as well as bound the trajectory of the fast ODE away from zero. The main challenge lies in proving that, almost surely, the slow iterates are norm-bounded and the fast iterates are bounded below away from zero on the support of the transition kernel. We address this by using a fluid scaling approach for the slow iteration combined with tailored estimates for the fast iteration to control a certain fluid-scaled relative entropy error that arises in the ODE approximation. Numerical experiments illustrate the performance of the proposed algorithm and compare it with the existing risk-sensitive Q-learning algorithms.

items.title: FokasNets: Completing missing boundary data in Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Operators via the Global Relation
items.summary: We introduce FokasNets, a framework that combines Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and operators (PINOs) with the Global Relation (GR) formulation of the Fokas method (also referred to as the Unified Transform), for mixed boundary problems. The general framework considers lifted representations of the neural network models, where the Dirichlet boundary conditions are imposed by construction and the neural network learns the interior correction. The Global Relation is used as an additional solve during training that provides the missing boundary conditions to the lifted neural network, making training more efficient and accurate in the interior and on the boundary. We develop the construction of FokasNets for elliptic and evolution PDEs (Fokas-PINNs), and the corresponding PDE solution operator problems (Fokas Operator Networks - FONets), using the Global Relation formulations for these PDE classes. Furthermore, we develop the necessary theoretical framework for FokasNets, including error and stability analysis and show that FokasNets are universal approximators. We provide comprehensive numerical experiments, using examples with manufactured solutions and literature benchmarks. Compared to standard PINNs and Physics-Informed DeepONets and their lifted versions, FokasNets achieve significant improvements in solution accuracy in the interior and boundaries, both for single PDEs and particularly for solution operators, where the improvement reaches multiple orders of magnitude and fixed threshold errors are reached faster during training.

items.title: Stochastic Optimization for Switch-System Identification under Errors-in-Variables
items.summary: In this paper, we address the identification of switched dynamical systems under errors-in-variables, where both input and output measurements are corrupted by noise, and the number of operating modes and subsystem orders are unknown. We propose a unified identification framework that simultaneously estimates the subsystem parameters, latent switching sequence, and model structure. The proposed formulation combines a variance-normalized data-fitting criterion with temporally regularized soft mode assignments and sparsity-inducing penalties for selecting the active modes and relevant input-output lags. To solve the resulting nonconvex optimization problem, we develop an alternating algorithm that incorporates convex mode-assignment updates and proximal stochastic variance-reduced gradient optimization for parameter estimation. While the existing approaches in the literature require exhaustive searches over candidate structures, the proposed method performs structure selection within a single model. Numerical experiments demonstrate accurate recovery of the underlying system structure and favorable computational efficiency compared with a generalized total least squares and dynamic programming approach, particularly as the number of candidate structures increases.

items.title: Adaptive Blockwise Tensor Trains for Stochastic Finite-Volume Methods with Uncertain Geometry
items.summary: Stochastic finite-volume (SFV) methods extend conservative, shock-capturing discretizations to hyperbolic systems with uncertain inputs by partitioning the parameter domain into finite-volume cells. However, their memory and computational cost grow exponentially with the number of uncertain parameters. Tensor-train (TT) formats can remove this exponential dependence, provided the ranks of the discrete solution remain small throughout the simulation. This requirement is frequently violated when the uncertainty is geometric. Mapping each realization onto a common reference domain introduces parameter-dependent metric factors, so that shocks and contacts propagate at different reference speeds and come to occupy different cells across realizations. The resulting rank growth is spatially localized - a structure that neither a single global TT nor a separate TT for each physical cell is able to exploit. We propose an adaptive blockwise TT representation in which the SFV solution is partitioned along its physical mode into contiguous blocks, each stored as an independent TT for every conserved variable. Blocks are split near discontinuities and in regions of large variance or rank, and merged where the solution is smooth. The mesh itself is never changed; only the grouping of cells into trains adapts. We embed this representation in a TT-based SFV solver combining WENO3 reconstruction in the physical and stochastic directions, positivity-preserving limiters, and strong-stability-preserving Runge-Kutta time integration, with nonlinear steps evaluated via cross approximation. A mean-conservative rounding that adds no rank, together with single-valued interface fluxes, conserves the parameter-mean mass and energy to round-off for any partition. The approach is demonstrated on a Sod shock-tube problem with uncertain wall positions.

items.title: Representing and Animating Piano-Hinged Solids as Non-Manifold Cell Complexes: The Magic Photo Cube
items.summary: Piano-hinged solids are articulated structures consisting of rigid solid components connected along edges, allowing relative rotations while preserving their connectivity. We propose representing such structures as a class of edge-connected non-manifold cell complexes, in which the components and their hinge relationships are encoded through cell incidences rather than separate geometric hinge elements. This representation provides a unified framework for describing the geometry, connectivity, and admissible motions of articulated solids. We demonstrate the approach using the magic photo cube, an assembly of eight cubical cells connected by eight edge hinges. Each cell maintains a persistent identity and local coordinate frame, while successive folding operations transport hinge axes through rigid transformations. We reconstruct two distinct three-stage folding sequences and analyze their resulting configurations. Although the sequences produce compact cubes at different positions and orientations in a fixed reference frame, numerical analysis demonstrates that their terminal configurations are rigidly equivalent as labeled, oriented assemblies under a single proper rigid transformation. The example illustrates how an edge-connected non-manifold representation can support geometric modeling, animation, and configuration analysis while preserving the identities and incidence relationships of the constituent cells. An accompanying interactive web-based simulator, implemented in JavaScript and WebGL, is publicly available at https://people.tamu.edu/~ergun/software/magic_cube.

items.title: Fast Algorithms for Permanents of Permutationally-Dominant Matrices
items.summary: We establish a fast algorithm for approximating the permanent of permutationally-dominant matrices. In particular, we obtain a fully polynomial randomised approximation scheme whose runtime is quadratic in both the dimension of the matrix and the inverse of the approximation error. Our approach is based on a polymer model representation of the permanent and importance sampling of the logarithm of its partition function via the theory of heaps of pieces of Viennot.

items.title: Stochastic Optimization with Network Distribution Dynamics via Local Jacobian Approximation
items.summary: Network systems feature complex interactions among agents, whereby local decisions can influence the state distributions observed by other agents through coupled network dynamics. Such endogenous distribution shifts across large-scale networks pose significant challenges and call for distributed and adaptive decision-making pipelines. To address these challenges and collectively optimize a steady-state performance objective, we propose a distributed network-aware decision-response (D-NAD) gradient algorithm. This algorithm enables each agent to approximate network-response sensitivity using only local information (i.e., the Jacobians of local dynamics and objectives) and neighborhood communication. We establish a non-asymptotic closed-loop convergence guarantee and quantify the impact of the Jacobian approximation errors therein. Numerical experiments on a semi-synthetic networked electric-vehicle price--demand problem demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

items.title: PAC Learning to Sample: On Computational Aspects of Language Generation
items.summary: The success of language models has motivated theoretical work on learning to sample from distributions on discrete domains. A prominent abstraction is the model of language generation in the limit, introduced by Kleinberg and Mullainathan (NeurIPS 2024), in which the algorithm must generate from the target language after some finite but unspecified number of positive examples. While its positive results are surprisingly general, most guarantees are qualitative. In this work, we seek quantitative guarantees on sample and time complexity, inspired by statistical and computational learning theory. To this end, we study a PAC model of language generation, proposed (in a different context) by De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio (SODA 2015), in which a Boolean concept class $C$ over $\{-1,1\}^n$ defines the target languages: given uniformly random positive examples of an unknown concept $f \in C$, the learner must output a sampler whose output distribution (conditioned on the training data) is close in total variation to the uniform distribution over $f^{-1}(1)$. Their work implicitly gives an efficient algorithm for PAC learning to sample $C$, given three primitives for $C$: an online learner, approximate sampling and counting oracles, and an SQ learner. We ask whether these ingredients, in particular online learnability, are necessary. First, we construct a Boolean concept class $C$ for which online learning is cryptographically hard, yet PAC learning to sample is computationally efficient. Then, we develop new algorithms that use offline ERM oracles instead of online learners, together with approximate sampling/counting oracles for intersections of concepts in $C$ and an SQ learner for $C$. We view our results, together with the work of De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio, as a first step towards understanding the computational complexity of language generation.

items.title: APEX: Agentic Platform for Ensemble eXploration
items.summary: Ensemble-based methods provide a practical framework for history matching, prediction, and optimization of subsurface models. In methodological studies, however, performance is rarely assessed from a single run. Comparisons typically span cases, configurations, and random seeds, while each evaluation may require an expensive external simulator. Keeping such studies computationally bounded, auditable, and reproducible therefore requires more than implementing a numerical method: experiments must be validated before execution, computational costs estimated, repeated runs organized consistently, and configurations and outputs made traceable. To address these needs, we developed APEX (Agentic Platform for Ensemble eXploration), an open-source Python platform that provides a common framework for configuring, validating, executing, recording, and comparing ensemble-based experiments. APEX is organized around three concepts: an experiment defines what is executed, a run records a single execution, and a study coordinates and compares multiple experiments or runs. Experiments are specified through validated configurations, which can also be generated by a planner agent. Before execution, APEX estimates the maximum number of forward simulations required. If the estimate exceeds a user-defined threshold, submission is held for approval. Each run records provenance information, while studies repeat problems across variants and paired replicates and compare results using paired statistical analyses. Scientific and computational components, including methods, simulators, metrics, and optimizers, are implemented as plugins. A command line interface, Python client, REST service with a web interface, and tools for language model agents access these capabilities through a common service layer.

items.title: Using block coordinate descent for solving the close enough traveling salesman problem
items.summary: The Close Enough Traveling Salesman Problem (CETSP) is a variant of the Euclidean Traveling Salesman Problem in which the salesperson must visit some point within a disk associated with each customer. Evaluating a visiting sequence requires determining an optimal visit point within each disk. This building block of virtually every CETSP algorithm is typically computed either by solving a second-order cone programming (SOCP) problem with a general-purpose solver, which can be expensive, or by discretizing the disks, which sacrifices optimality. We propose a block coordinate descent (BCD) method that computes these visit points exactly, without discretization, optimizing one visit point at a time. We show that the resulting single-disk subproblem reduces to a one-dimensional minimization, and we characterize its stationary points through the roots of a quartic polynomial. Of the three resulting solution strategies, which agree up to machine precision, Newton's method is the most efficient. Compared with an off-the-shelf SOCP solver, BCD evaluates fixed tours more than an order of magnitude faster. Embedded in an iterated local search (ILS-BCD), it finds the known optimal solutions of 720 small benchmark instances and, on 62 large ones, outperforms all heuristics of their original study in 47 and matches the best of them in 11 others. Within the memetic algorithm MA-CETSP, replacing the general-purpose SOCP solver with BCD and adding an exact local search based on the single-disk solver yields a method that, over the best of 20 runs, is better than the original algorithm in 20 of the 62 large instances and equal in the others, and improves on its best published values in 21. BCD is a fast and exact building block for evaluating visiting sequences that can replace general-purpose SOCP solvers within CETSP algorithms and enables searches that would otherwise be computationally prohibitive.

items.title: A block coordinate descent method for nonconvex multiobjective optimization under Hölder continuity
items.summary: In this paper, we propose a block coordinate descent method for unconstrained multiobjective optimization problems with possibly nonconvex objectives and Hölder continuous gradients, intended for large-scale instances, in which updating all the variables simultaneously is expensive. In each iteration, only one block is updated along a descent direction common to all objectives, obtained by minimizing the maximum of their regularized quadratic models. We show that, unlike the single-objective case, stationarity on each block does not imply Pareto stationarity, and that no method that updates only the blocks of a partition of the variables and is monotone in all the objectives reaches, in general, an $ε$-Pareto stationary point. Therefore, when none of the blockwise stationarity measures exceeds the tolerance, the algorithm performs a joint step across all coordinates and terminates only at $ε$-Pareto stationary points. We establish a complexity bound of $O(ε^{-(β+1)/β})$ iterations, where $β$ is the smallest Hölder exponent, the same order as that of methods that update all the variables, as well as bounds on the numbers of function and gradient evaluations, which also hold with one regularization parameter per block.

items.title: The Traveling Salesman Problem with non-convex polygonal neighborhoods: A hybrid Iterated Local Search--Block Coordinate Descent approach
items.summary: The Traveling Salesman Problem with Neighborhoods (TSPN) generalizes the classical TSP by requiring a tour to visit a set of regions in the Euclidean plane rather than fixed point coordinates. It has applications in last-mile delivery, surveillance, and remote sensing in precision agriculture. In this paper, we address the Euclidean TSPN with arbitrary, non-convex polygonal neighborhoods---a highly complex setting due to the joint continuous and combinatorial optimization challenges. To solve the continuous subproblem of determining optimal visit points for a given visiting sequence, we propose a Block Coordinate Descent (BCD) method based on solving fast one-dimensional geometric subproblems. Computational experiments demonstrate that BCD computes optimal visit points for a fixed sequence in almost all instances in which optimality is certified, more than six orders of magnitude faster than a commercial solver solving the equivalent Mixed-Integer Quadratically Constrained Programming (MIQCP) formulation. This efficiency enables an effective hybrid Iterated Local Search metaheuristic (ILS-BCD) that thoroughly explores the combinatorial search space at low computational cost. Extensive computational tests on 235 benchmark instances derived from the Generalized TSP (GTSP), with up to 100 neighborhoods, show that ILS-BCD matched or improved upon the best-known GTSP tours in all cases, obtaining strictly shorter tours in 234 instances. On the 80 instances for which optimality is proven, ILS-BCD attains the optimal tour length in all of them, within a relative difference below 0.001%. On 60 larger instances, with as many as 6,325 neighborhoods, ILS-BCD remains competitive up to about 220.

items.title: Improved Exact Algorithms and Parameterized Results for Monopolar Graph Problems
items.summary: A monopolar graph is a graph whose vertex set can be partitioned into a cluster graph and an independent set. Deciding whether such a partition exists is Monopolar Recognition. We also study three related problems: Monopolar Extension, where a partial assignment of vertices to the two sides is given and must be extended to a full monopolar partition; List Monopolar Partition, where each vertex comes with a list of allowed sides; and Monopolar Vertex Deletion, which asks for a minimum-weight vertex set whose removal makes the graph monopolar. All four problems are NP-hard, which motivates the study of faster exact algorithms for these problems. We design a new exact branching algorithm for Monopolar Extension running in O*(1.29803^n) time, improving upon the previously best-known O*(1.3734^n)-time algorithm of Philip and Sridhara [WG 2025]. The O*(.) notation suppresses factors that are bounded by a polynomial in the input size. The same bound applies to List Monopolar Partition, which is an equivalent formulation, and to Monopolar Recognition, which is a special case. It also gives an O*(2.29803^n)-time algorithm for Monopolar Vertex Deletion. We further present the first explicit fixed-parameter algorithms with concrete single-exponential dependence on treewidth for these problems. We show that Monopolar Extension, and hence also List Monopolar Partition and Monopolar Recognition, can be solved in 3^tw*n^O(1) time. For Monopolar Vertex Deletion we obtain a running time of 5^tw*n^O(1), which improves to 4^tw*n^O(1) when the weights are integers bounded by a polynomial in n.

items.title: Error estimates for a structure-preserving finite-element scheme of quasi-incompressible Navier-Stokes-Maxwell-Stefan systems
items.summary: A conforming finite-element scheme for quasi-incompressible Navier-Stokes-Maxwell-Stefan systems in a bounded domain with periodic boundary conditions is presented. The system consists of the Navier-Stokes equations, together with a quasi-incompressibility constraint, coupled with the cross-diffusion Maxwell--Stefan equations. The numerical scheme preserves the partial masses and the quasi-incompressibility constraint and dissipates the discrete energy. First-order error estimates in space and time are shown for a diffusion-augmented mobility matrix by using the relative energy method and suitable projection error estimates. Numerical experiments in two space dimensions illustrate the convergence of the scheme and indicate second-order convergence in space in the $L^2$ norm.

items.title: What Must LLM Agents Communicate? From Information Loss to Communication Failures
items.summary: When evidence is distributed across LLM agents, a team may collectively possess all the information needed for a decision yet fail to use it effectively. What must agents communicate for accurate joint predictions, and when does interaction help? We study three requirements for effective communication: sufficiency of the information conveyed, selection of relevant evidence, and utilization of received information. Drawing on information theory and communication complexity, we develop a framework that combines theoretical benchmarks with controlled experiments and message-level analyses. We find that local probability reports can discard essential information, with theoretical information loss closely matching observed performance penalties. Query-first interaction improves predictions when relevant evidence depends on a private query, but compact one-shot representations can eliminate this advantage. Even when sufficient information is communicated, agents may fail to select or use it correctly. Together, these findings distinguish fundamental communication limits from failures in how LLM agents communicate and use information.

items.title: The involute function and its inverse in IEEE 754 double precision: measured and proved accuracy, and its effect on gear inspection
items.summary: Almost every spur and helical gear calculation uses the involute function inv(a) = tan(a) - a or its inverse. Near a = 0 the two terms almost cancel: at a = 10^-3 the textbook formula in binary64 keeps about 9 correct digits, and far fewer in binary32, binary16 or fixed point, and the result can depend on the platform's tan. We report the accuracy of a proprietary implementation that avoids these problems. On 50,000 committed test angles the forward function's largest error against an 80-digit reference is 0.4999681 ulp, so every tested result is correctly rounded (measured, not proved). The inverse is proved faithfully rounded, with error at most 0.6 ulp, for 10^-200 <= y < 2, using interval arithmetic and the SMT solvers z3 and cvc5 with a short, named list of trusted inputs; its largest measured error on 50,000 points is 0.5555115 ulp. A separate bracket around the root is proved to contain it for 0 < y <= 10^6, and did so at all 47,083 test points. Both functions return identical bits on x86-64 and aarch64 Linux, Apple-silicon macOS, AWS Lambda and an NVIDIA DGX Spark, in Python and Node.js, on every finite test input. Against public inverse methods on nine runtimes, our inverse returned the same bits on all of them and stayed within 0.54 ulp on 12,017 targets from 0.5 to 60 degrees, while textbook Newton iterations differed between runtimes on up to about 10% of inputs and kept only 12 correct digits. For external and internal spur gears with 5 to 500 teeth and pressure angles from 14.5 to 30 degrees, all inputs fall inside the tested and proved ranges. Against ISO 1328-1 tolerance classes, we give in micrometres the errors that shortcut inverses cause in pin measurement and centre distance, and how far circular-arc CAD teeth (SolidWorks Toolbox) depart from the involute. Drawing an involute is easy; accuracy matters in inspection.

items.title: Feedback Rounds and Query Costs in Sparse Product Pure Exploration
items.summary: How much can one more round of feedback save when a measurement combines several settings into a single noisy reading? We study a product decision with $K$ blocks and $m$ nonbaseline labels per block. At most $s$ blocks have nonzero effects, of arbitrary sign. Each query tests labels in at most $b$ blocks. The final assignment must have total loss at most $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-δ$. On the benchmark $K=s^2$, $1\le b\le s$ and $s^ν\le m\le s^ζ$ for fixed $0<ν\le1\leζ$, we characterize two minimax costs for sufficiently large $s$. The optimal orders are $(Km/b)χU_B$ readings and $KmχU_B$ settings for $B\ge1$ batches, where $χ=σ^2s^2/\varepsilon^2\ge1$ for noise proxy $σ^2$ and $δ\le1/16$. The factor $U_B$ is obtained by applying $B-1$ logarithms to $\log(es)$, clipping each iterate at one and imposing a floor of $\log(1/δ)/s$. One algorithm attains both bounds. For general dimensions, a polynomial-time algorithm attains the optimal setting cost. When $K=s^2$, $m=b=s$ and $\log(1/δ)=s$, both fully adaptive orders are attainable in polynomial real-arithmetic time when $χ=Ω((s/\log(es))^{1/3})$. With identical budgets and decoder, four batches succeeded on 1,070 of 1,200 paired simulated instances and two batches on 779.

items.title: hp-Adaptive Finite Element Modeling of Static Cracks in Density-Dependent Media
items.summary: The elastostatic crack-tip fields within a density-dependent continuum are numerically investigated under several macroscopic loading configurations. The governing nonlinear boundary value problem is formulated using an algebraically nonlinear hyperelastic constitutive relationship in which the material moduli are intrinsically coupled to volumetric strain. Existence and uniqueness of the weak solution to the nonlinear displacement-based variational formulation are rigorously established at the continuous level via the Minty-Browder theorem. The variational formulation is then linearized at the partial differential equation level to construct a continuous damped Newton-Raphson scheme. To accurately capture the severe field gradients and internal singularities inherent to this model, the resulting sequence of linear operator equations is discretized and solved via a conforming finite element method within an $hp$-adaptive framework. A comparative analysis is conducted across five distinct boundary loading profiles (encompassing uniform, piecewise-slope, and concentrated point loads) applied to a stationary cracked geometry. Within each configuration, the density-dependent constitutive parameter is systematically varied to assess its regulatory impact on the fracture process zone, focusing on the spatial evolution of normal stress, normal strain, and strain energy density near the crack tip. Numerical results demonstrate that local kinematic deformability is strictly bounded by the strain-limiting nature of the continuum, whereby static equilibrium is sustained through severe, localized stress amplifications. Furthermore, the mechanical influence of the modeling parameter is fundamentally dictated by the topological interplay between internal crack geometry and the spatial distribution of applied macroscopic loads.

items.title: VibeVideoAgent: Closing the Perceptual Loop for Code-Driven Video Generation
items.summary: Code-driven video generation asks a coding agent to write and run rendering programs. This gives exact control over typography, data visualizations, synchronized audio, and multi-shot scenes, and it leaves an editable project behind. A program that exits cleanly can still render overlapping labels, a camera aimed away from its subject, broken object interactions, or narration that drifts out of sync, and none of these raise a runtime error. Feeding rendered frames and audio back into the coding session bloats its long-horizon context, while critiquing only the finished full-resolution render turns early design mistakes into costly rewrites. We introduce VibeVideoAgent, a training-free framework that lets coding agents inspect their drafts throughout production. Multimodal perception runs in short-lived contexts kept apart from the coder and returns compact, grounded Findings. Seven primitives operate on a unified multi-clock representation of assets and drafts: they explore media from coarse to fine, verify quoted requirements with evidence from every required modality, compare a draft with a reference or an earlier revision on separate clocks, and measure stream signals locally. A lightweight staged protocol has the agent test its riskiest decision on a minimal preview first. On all 239 VibeVideoBench tasks, with matched agent runtimes and a fixed perception model, VibeVideoAgent improves holistic audiovisual quality (L3) for Claude Opus 5.5 (4.03 -> 4.43, while L2 rubric compliance rises from 98.87% to 99.35%), GPT-6 Astra (4.03 -> 4.27), and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (3.97 -> 4.10), with the largest gains in audio-visual synchronization (up to +0.56). Controlled ablations show that each component contributes, and trajectory audits show that the granularity of code edits governs the trade-off between rubric adherence and perceptual quality.

items.title: PyRUA-Dex: Learning Programmatic Policies for Dexterous Bimanual Manipulation with Coding Agents
items.summary: Learning for dexterous manipulation is limited by the scarcity of high-quality demonstrations: retargeting from human video is imprecise, teleoperation gives no force feedback to the operator, and exoskeleton-based collection is hard to scale up. We present PyRUA-Dex, a framework that enables coding agents to develop dexterous manipulation through programmatic policy, without the need of demonstrations. The programmatic policy is developed in two stages: during exploration, multiple agents explore in parallel for task skills and ways to compose them, and a distilling agent condenses the successful attempts into a task library and one program. During refinement, this program is improved through randomized layouts for enhanced robustness and execution efficiency. In simulated environments, PyRUA-Dex achieves SOTA on Bench2Dex with a score of 72.9 and reaches 81.0% success on DexJoCo under full randomization, ahead of every trained policy on both benchmarks. In real world experiments on a bimanual platform with two 22-DoF hands, PyRUA-Dex learns to play piano, write calligraphy, and other tasks efficiently: learning a new piece from sheet music takes as little as 30 minutes. These results suggest that PyRUA-Dex is an effective framework for developing dexterous manipulation policies with coding agents in the absence of high quality dexterous manipulation demonstrations.

items.title: AIRIS: Benchmarking Social Embodied Intelligence in Egocentric Streaming Videos
items.summary: Embodied agents operating around people must not only recognize social cues, but also decide when the available evidence is sufficient, whether to intervene, and how to respond without violating social norms. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate these abilities in isolation or with access to completed videos, obscuring where an online social decision fails. We introduce AIRIS, a causal streaming benchmark that formulates social embodied intelligence as a time-anchored chain of Attention, Intention, Reaction, and Interaction (A-I-R-I). AIRIS contains 8,000 expert-curated questions grounded in 357 egocentric clips across 11 context categories and 36 capability dimensions. At each query, models receive only the observation prefix available at that time; decision-aware metrics reward calibrated waiting and complete reactions while penalizing premature commitment. Evaluating 45 proprietary and open-source general-purpose, embodied, streaming-video, and omni-modal models reveals fragmented and temporally miscalibrated competence. General-purpose VLMs excel at passive cue grounding and intent recognition, whereas embodied specialists lead on isolated reaction sub-decisions; yet across all families, models frequently guess intents before sufficient evidence emerges and fail to jointly align intervention timing, action domain, and concrete execution within the same episode. AIRIS thus provides a diagnostic foundation for bridging the gap between passive social perception and reliable embodied interaction.

items.title: Target-Part Preference Optimization for Part-Aware 3D Generation
items.summary: Part-aware 3D generation requires not only globally plausible objects but also complete, well-separated semantic parts, yet high-quality part decompositions remain too scarce to support large-scale supervised fine-tuning. We study whether preference fine-tuning based on Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) can adapt a pretrained part-aware generator from limited part-annotated data without architectural changes. We rank candidates generated with different random seeds against ground-truth (GT) geometric metrics, and select the (object, target-part) examples with the largest across-seed quality gap. Each selected example stores a seed pair whose two flow trajectories share one clean GT compositional latent and differ only in Gaussian noise. We derive a reference-relative target-block preference loss from FlowDPO that compares the two trajectories against a frozen reference model. GT flow-matching losses on the target block and complete part set provide absolute supervision, while only the diffusion transformer (DiT) is updated. Human-ranked controls test an alternative ordering source, and synthetic cropping provides controlled loser targets that are incomplete by construction. Among the three training-set scales, the medium-scale setting gives the strongest result on held-out Objaverse and outperforms both the pretrained generator and the reported direct supervised fine-tuning baseline on the multi-part aggregate. Further analysis shows sensitivity to pair ordering, target-part coverage, and the balance between pairwise and GT supervision. Cross-dataset experiments show less consistent gains under distribution shift.

items.title: Playfulness as Feedback for Agentic Game Development
items.summary: Coding agents can generate runnable games from natural-language descriptions. However, a runnable game does not guarantee an excellent gameplay experience for players. In our view, a playful game should provide 1) reliable core functionality, 2) appealing visual design and assets, and 3) rich gameplay that supports exploration and progression. How agents can improve these aspects of playfulness remains underexplored. In our work, we propose Play2Evolve, a recursive game development framework with three stages: Initialization, Refinement, and Evolution. Using playfulness as feedback, agents playtest the game and diagnose issues in its functionality, visual presentation, and gameplay. Their feedback guides bug fixes and asset improvements. It also helps agents propose new gameplay and aesthetic goals for continued game evolution. To enrich game materials, we combine a video generation model with code to create appealing static and dynamic assets and integrate them into interactive gameplay. Finally, Play2Evolve achieves state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods, scoring 60.05 on GameCraft-Bench compared with 50.81 after Game Initialization and 52.46 for Play2Code. Human overall-quality ratings reach 3.67, compared with 2.38 and 2.43, respectively. Our code will be released at https://github.com/showlab/Play2Evolve.

items.title: What Is Redundant at High Resolution? Efficient Attention and Feed-Forward Design for All-in-One Image Restoration
items.summary: Multi-scale architectures are widely adopted in all-in-one image restoration (AIO-IR) to capture larger-scale context at low-resolution stages and refine details at high-resolution (HR) stages. However, processing spatially large feature maps at HR stages incurs substantial computational costs and memory traffic, making efficient HR processing challenging. To address this challenge, we propose High-resolution Global-Local Restoration (HiGLR), an efficient multi-scale AIO-IR network grounded in an analysis of spatial redundancy in self-attention and convolutional feed-forward networks (ConvFFNs). Specifically, this analysis identifies three key redundancies: per-query readout at the finest-scale stage, key routing across neighboring queries at intermediate stages, and spatial mixing in the expanded feature spaces of ConvFFNs. Accordingly, HiGLR replaces costly self-attention at the finest-scale stage with a learned input-independent kernel. At intermediate stages, we propose a Block-Routed Hybrid Attention, which combines coarse-scale dense attention with fine-scale block-sparse attention over value residuals relative to coarse summaries, and shares routing indices across neighboring queries. We further introduce a Dual-Space FFN that performs spatial mixing in a compact space and pointwise nonlinear transformation in an expanded space, enabling efficient kernel fusion. Combining these designs, HiGLR achieves state-of-the-art performance while delivering up to a 4.24times inference speedup over existing methods.

items.title: Beyond the Happy Path: Generalizing Robot World Models from Simulated Failures
items.summary: Robot world models are increasingly used to evaluate and plan policies, yet robot training data are dominated by successful demonstrations. Off the happy path, when a grasp is misaligned or mistimed and the object is pushed, tilted, or slips, their predictions break down. Across five pretrained action-conditioned models, object-motion error is at most 10.4% lower than that of a static baseline that copies the first frame, and two models are worse than this baseline. We present WorldReforge, which teaches world models what happens when manipulation goes wrong. We construct the Reforge dataset of 62k simulated trajectories by perturbing reference grasps in position, orientation, and closure timing, recording each resulting push, slip, or failed pickup with ground-truth object pose, contact, and surface points. WorldReforge turns this ground truth into two training signals without additional inference cost. Interaction Alignment focuses reconstruction on the small object and contact regions that a global loss underweights, and Surface Correspondence trains backbone features to follow the same physical surface points across frames. On Cosmos3 Nano, WorldReforge reduces object trajectory error by 28.2% overall and by 35.0% on unseen objects, and it lowers the error in predicting how two actions' outcomes diverge by 43.3%. Although trained only in simulation, it also improves reconstruction on DROID and on real failure videos. Controlled data studies show that failed contact and successful holding teach complementary physics: failed contact teaches how objects respond, and holding teaches how a grasped state persists. Our code, data, and models are available at aim-uofa.github.io/WorldReforge/.

items.title: SEEK: Self-Evolution through Execution Knowledge for Agentic Robot Manipulation
items.summary: General-purpose multimodal foundation models enable robots to adapt during deployment from observations and execution feedback, without task-specific demonstrations or training. However, the robot retains what it learns only in the model's working context. Once the task ends, it loses this execution knowledge, such as how to carry a bowl between two grippers.
