Across 75 configurations of five hand models, maximum discrepancy between source and exported palm-frame vertex sets was approximately 1.3 micrometers against a 100-micrometer geometry tolerance. We isolated reference-angle and collision-component effects through controlled ablations and validated 1,920 directional task-wrench capacity calculations against independent Cartesian-force linear programs. In a common GraspIt! workload, median reset-close-score-state cycle latency through direct Python was 10.7% lower than through persistent ROS 1 services. An executable export-plan-reconstruct workflow and grasp examples on six hand models demonstrate how the contact, score, and joint representations support numerical analysis and command reconstruction.

items.title: The coordinate dependence of numerical rank: charts adapted to level sets
items.summary: Sampling a smooth field on a grid can give an array of high numerical rank even when the field is simple. A Gaussian ridge rotated off the grid axes is the standard example: in coordinates which follow the ridge, the same field has rank one. The rank therefore depends on the chart, that is, on the coordinates in which the field is sampled. We ask which properties of a chart control this rank. For a field which depends on position only through a function $φ$, a chart whose coordinate lines follow the level sets of $φ$ gives rank one. Building on this, we show four things. First, mesh quality does not control rank: a chart whose cells have perfect size and shape can still give infinite rank. Second, when a chart follows the level sets of an estimate of $φ$, the extra rank depends on a single quantity, the defect, which measures how much the true field varies along each coordinate line. Its size matters only logarithmically, its complexity through a count which cannot be improved in general, and when the defect is simple across the level sets the cost stays small. Third, whether the defect is simple can be checked by differentiating the true level function along the flow which builds the chart. Fourth, rank and invertibility fail differently. When the curve behind an offset chart is perturbed, the rank grows slowly, but the chart stops being invertible abruptly, once the offset exceeds the distance at which neighboring normals of the curve first cross. A chart built from the level sets of a field estimate stays invertible when the gradient of the estimate does not vanish on the band and the coordinate lines along each level set do not cross themselves. Pre-registered experiments in two dimensions show how far the bounds are from the observed ranks, and suggest when each kind of chart is preferable; two choices in the last comparison were made after the experiments.

items.title: A Principled Framework for PDE-Based Shock Capturing in High-Order Discontinuous Galerkin Methods
items.summary: PDE-based artificial viscosity (AV) captures shocks in high-order discontinuous Galerkin (DG) methods by solving an auxiliary PDE for a smooth viscosity field. The behavior of that field is set by how the terms of the AV PDE scale with the element size $h$ and polynomial degree $p$, and by how its coefficients are parametrized. This work derives both choices from analysis and studies the impact these choices have on the implicit steady-state solver. First, an $L^2$-projection analysis shows that the thinnest shock a polynomial space can represent monotonically scales with the resolution length $\bar h = h/p$, and a scaling analysis of the AV PDE gives concrete conditions on its diffusion and source terms for the solution to be self-similar in $\bar h$. Prior formulations satisfy them only under $h$-refinement at fixed $p$; the AV PDE is scaled so that they hold under $hp$-refinement, and the captured shock thins accordingly. Second, a Green's-function analysis of the steady AV PDE gives closed-form expressions for the width and magnitude of the AV. In the standard parametrization the two are coupled: raising the diffusion coefficient widens the AV but lowers its peak. An alternative parametrization of the decay coefficient removes the coupling in the Green's-function response and inverts it in the coupled state-AV problem, so that widening the AV raises its peak instead of lowering it. Third, a parameter study on a Mach 5 viscous flow over a half-cylinder characterizes how the choice of solution variables and the AV PDE's time, width, and magnitude coefficients affect the robustness and cost of the implicit solve. The choice of variables dominates robustness, with entropy variables converging over the largest region of the width-magnitude parameter space. Together, the three contributions make PDE-based AV more predictable to tune and its implicit solve more robust.

items.title: Achievable Rate and Reconstruction Fidelity of FeFET-Based Compute-in-Pixel Arrays
items.summary: Compute-in-pixel (CiP) image sensors such as MACPix weight each photodiode voltage by a conductance stored in a ferroelectric FET and sum the currents on a column bus, so that $N$ pixels are read as $M<N$ weighted sums before digitization. We model the column bus as a Gaussian multiple-access channel and derive its achievable rate under thermal and shot noise, device variation, and ADC distortion. Conductance variation acts as noise proportional to the scene energy, which limits the rate to $4.5$ bits per readout and makes a 6-bit ADC sufficient. End-to-end simulations recover natural images at $26.3$ dB from 2 bits per pixel and, for sparse scenes, reduce the edge-node energy by up to $6.4\times$ against raw 8-bit readout.

items.title: Portable Extended-Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic for Scientific Computing Kernels
items.summary: Many scientific computations need more accuracy than IEEE double precision, but arbitrary precision is often too costly on CPUs and GPUs. Multi-float arithmetic fills this gap by representing each value as an unevaluated sum of IEEE numbers. Existing implementations are generally confined to a CPU, CUDA, or language-specific programming model. We present MultiFloats.cpp, a header-only C++17 library that uses Kokkos to compile the same extended-precision kernels for Serial, OpenMP, CUDA, and HIP. The library supports Float64x2 through Float64x4 (106--212 bits) and the corresponding Float32-based types. We evaluate it using seven SHOC-style kernels and compare against QD, CAMPARY, MPFR, and Julia MultiFloats.jl on A100, GH200, and AMD RX 780M systems. On A100, Float64x4 addition sustains 15,700 MOps/s, or 1.5 times CAMPARY; on CPU, vectorized Float64x4 operations are 4.2--6.6 times faster than QD's qd_real. Addition and multiplication produce 0 ULP error over 10,000 inputs, while Float64x4 division and square root remain within 1.71 and 17.9 ULP, respectively. Thus, extended precision can remain practical and portable without separate backend implementations.

items.title: Exact edge cover by strict and non-strict temporal walks
items.summary: Exact edge cover asks whether the edges of a temporal graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges can be partitioned into time-respecting walks with a prescribed number of walks starting at each vertex and, in the fixed-end variant, ending at each vertex. For non-strict walks, we prove that the problem is polynomially solvable by a new approach based on M-convexity, which also closes a gap in the proof sketch of an earlier static reduction. An orientation of the edges is realizable by walks exactly when walk counters stay non-negative and every snapshot component contains a walk, and only components with all degrees and counters even can violate the latter condition. Once a dead state is removed, the states of each such component form an M-convex set. This yields an augmenting path algorithm that returns walks or an infeasibility certificate, using at most $m/2$ augmentations and $O(n+nm^2)$ arithmetic operations with path-reversing re-orientation. The implementation was validated on small instances. For strict walks, we prove that the problem is NP-complete, already with six time labels for prescribed ends and two for free ends.

items.title: Towards a faster parameterized algorithm for Chordal Vertex Deletion
items.summary: The \textsc{Chordal Vertex Deletion} (\chvd{}) problem asks whether an input graph $G$ can be made chordal by removing at most $k$ vertices. When $k$ is taken as parameter, this problem is known to be fixed-parameter tractable \cite{M10,CM16}. However, it is still open whether \chvd{} admits a single-exponential FPT algorithm, i.e. an algorithm with running time $O(α^k |V(G)|^c)$ for some constant $α$ independent of $k$. Towards this goal, we describe an FPT algorithm for the compression version of \chvd{} with the following specification. Given an instance $I = (G,k,X)$ of the disjoint \chvd{} compression problem such that $|X| = k+1$, $G - X$ is chordal and its longest chordless path has length $L$, we solve $I$ in time $O((L+1)^{3k} k^2 |V(G)|^4)$.

items.title: Robust Pair--Restricted Lipschitz Regression with Global--Local Transfer
items.summary: We develop a robust pair-restricted Lipschitz regression framework for grouped longitudinal data represented as finite trajectories in a space equipped with a prescribed or learned pseudometric. For a fixed geometry, latent responses and a Lipschitz bound are estimated jointly through a convex optimisation problem with constraints imposed on selected trajectory pairs. We show that the choice of fidelity loss leads to different structural behaviour: Huber regularisation strictly reduces the pair-restricted Lipschitz seminorm whenever the exact interpolant has a finite positive seminorm, whereas $L^1$ fidelity can preserve exact interpolation below a data-dependent threshold. For grouped observations, global and local Lipschitz structures are combined while keeping group identity outside the trajectory geometry. The global component draws on observations from other groups, while the local component uses each group's history to account for group-specific behaviour. We also characterise when group-specific observations can be fitted exactly under a shared Lipschitz bound and establish a regularity bound for the combined predictor. We describe a computational implementation based on constraint generation and illustrate the framework through an application to longitudinal sow-production data.

items.title: JAX-Nano: A GPU-Accelerated Differentiable Phonon Boltzmann Transport Solver for Nanoscale Heat Transfer
items.summary: As semiconductor device dimensions approach phonon mean free paths, heat transport enters ballistic and quasi-ballistic regimes where Fourier's law becomes inadequate. The phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) describes these nonequilibrium effects but presents significant computational challenges. This work introduces JAX-Nano, a GPU-accelerated, end-to-end differentiable phonon BTE solver for nanoscale heat transport. The solver integrates steady-state and transient BTE formulations within a unified finite-volume framework, supporting structured and unstructured meshes, mode-resolved transport, phonon scattering, volumetric heat generation, and multiple boundary conditions. Automatic differentiation enables gradient computation with respect to transport properties, boundary conditions, heat-generation rates, and geometric parameters without separately derived adjoint equations. Numerical predictions are validated against analytical solutions and established BTE solvers across diffusive-to-ballistic regimes. Applications to complex three-dimensional geometries are demonstrated using single-fin, double-fin, and arrayed fin field-effect transistor (FinFET) configurations. Gradient-based inverse learning enables single- and multi-parameter identification, including simultaneous recovery of mode-resolved phonon relaxation times and spatially distributed heat-generation rates in steady-state and transient problems. GPU performance and scalability are evaluated with respect to spatial resolution, angular discretization, and phonon bands, including comparisons with an MPI-based BTE solver. JAX-Nano provides a unified computational framework for three-dimensional phonon transport, automatic differentiation, and inverse parameter identification, enabling sensitivity analysis and optimization of nanoscale thermal systems.

items.title: Kemeny median rankings with ties under constraints on the buckets
items.summary: The median ranking is the ranking that minimizes the sum of the Kemeny distances from the rankings expressed by a set of judges. In many applications the consensus requires a prescribed structure: a given number of buckets, given sizes of all or some of the buckets, as in the forced distributions of Q methodology, or the form of a top-$k$ list. We show that all these problems are a single problem, the search for the median ranking among the rankings whose pattern of bucket sizes is admissible, and that they depend on the data only through the combined input matrix, defined by Emond and Mason in 2002. On this matrix we build BOLT, a deterministic heuristic that combines a set of starting solutions, a local search that moves one object at a time and can create or remove ties, and the exact best partition of a fixed order of the objects into buckets with an admissible pattern. We also provide an exact solution for the median top-$k$ list. The solutions of BOLT are assessed, on real and simulated data, against the optimum certified by a binary linear programming formulation, adapted to the Kemeny distance and to the constraints on the buckets, and against the methods available in the literature. Applications to Q-sorts, top-$k$ lists and large and sparse data sets of ratings show how the constrained problems arise in practice, and how the treatment of the objects not ranked by the judges changes the solution.

items.title: Semantic Communication via Federated Learning with Knowledge-Enhanced Networks and Privacy
items.summary: This paper presents a novel privacy-preserving semantic communication framework that combines Federated Learning (FL) with Knowledge-Enhanced Networks (KE-NET) for distributed wireless systems. Unlike centralized semantic communication approaches that require data aggregation, our method enables multiple clients to collaboratively train a knowledge-enhanced model while keeping their data and knowledge graphs private. We develop a multi-objective federated optimization strategy that balances semantic fidelity, knowledge integration, channel robustness, and reconstruction accuracy. Theoretical analysis reveals that federated aggregation improves effective SNR for $N$ clients through noise averaging. Numerical results with AWGN and Rayleigh fading channels demonstrate that multi-client federated learning consistently outperforms both single-client and centralized baselines across all SNR conditions, with particularly significant gains in low-SNR scenarios.

items.title: A Class of Monotone Quasi-Newtonian Flows Coupled to Nonlinear Equations: Analysis and Finite Element Approximation
items.summary: We analyze a monotone quasi-Newtonian flow coupled with nonlinear heat and concentration equations. In the model, the viscosity depends on the temperature, the concentration, and the velocity gradient, and the diffusivities depend on the temperature and the concentration. We show the existence of weak solutions without smallness assumptions on the data, and their uniqueness under suitable smallness and regularity assumptions. For the numerical approximation, we consider the Taylor--Hood and mini elements. We prove that the discrete solutions converge, up to a subsequence, to a weak solution, and we derive a quasi-best approximation result and convergence rates. We present numerical experiments in two and three dimensions that illustrate the theory.

items.title: An Efficient Long-Time Stable Second-Order Ensemble Method for the Parameterized Navier--Stokes Equations
items.summary: Ensemble simulations for uncertainty quantification, ensemble forecasting, and long-time statistics require stability over arbitrarily long horizons without time-step restrictions. We develop a second-order ensemble method for parameterized incompressible Navier--Stokes equations that uses a common, time-independent Brinkman (shifted Stokes) operator for all members. The scheme combines BDF2, a mean-reverting scalar auxiliary variable (mr-SAV) treatment of convection, and viscosity splitting with a shared viscosity $\barν$ treated implicitly and memberwise deviations explicitly. For constant viscosities satisfying $0<ν_j<4\barν/3$, we establish unconditional, uniform-in-time dissipativity under uniformly bounded forcing, including an absorbing bound independent of initial data and time-step size. We show that the upper viscosity threshold is sharp for fixed $\barν$. For spatially varying random viscosities, unconditional long-time stability holds under a signed pointwise condition that confines $ν_j$ to $(\barν/3,4\barν/3)$ uniformly away from the endpoints; for proportional spatial profiles, it holds over the full range $0<ν_j<4\barν/3$. Under the full-range constant-viscosity condition and sufficient regularity in two dimensions, we prove second-order temporal error bounds for velocity, the auxiliary variable, and the discrete time primitive of the pressure error. Numerical tests corroborate long-time stability at large time steps and the sharpness of the viscosity threshold, demonstrate accurate individual solutions and ensemble statistics, and show that mean reversion prevents long-time drift. Reusing the shared operator reduces computing time by about half relative to member-by-member solves.

items.title: A feasible point method for derivative-free linearly constrained optimization
items.summary: This paper presents a framework for linearly constrained derivative-free optimization (DFO) in which the original objective function is evaluated only at feasible points. The method first analyzes the linear constraint system using certificates of infeasibility and implied activity to detect infeasibility or a singleton feasible set, or, when the feasible set has positive dimension, to identify the affine subspace spanned by the feasible set and obtain an equivalent reduced representation with a strictly feasible base point. It then transforms the resulting reduced problem into an unconstrained optimization problem by means of a pointed feasible retraction and an exact penalty function. The retraction maps arbitrary trial points to feasible points by an explicit scaling in the reduced coordinates, so that no constrained optimization or projection subproblem is required during objective evaluations. This construction permits a broad range of unconstrained DFO methods to be used as inner solvers while preserving feasibility of the original objective evaluations. Numerical experiments compare several such variants on linearly constrained test problems of different dimensions. The results show that the choice of inner solver affects robustness, the number of problems solved, function-evaluation efficiency, and computational time, and that relative performance changes with problem dimension.

items.title: Layered soft-output MLSE architecture for PAM4 short-reach optical interconnects
items.summary: The rapid growth of data traffic driven by artificial intelligence demands high-speed data-center optical interconnects, where soft-output maximum-likelihood sequence estimation (SMLSE) provides reliability information for soft-decision forward error correction. However, conventional SMLSE suffers from a latency bottleneck because sequential state-metric recursions cause latency to increase linearly with the number of symbols. Here, we propose a layered SMLSE architecture that reduces latency from linear to logarithmic order. Downward branch-metric accumulation combines adjacent interval metrics in parallel, while upward state-metric propagation reconstructs forward and backward state metrics at successive interval midpoints. Experiments with 112-Gbit/s PAM4 transmission over 2-km standard single-mode fiber demonstrate identical soft-output performance for layered and conventional SMLSE, while the total latency decreases from 26 to 10 processing cycles. The proposed layered SMLSE provides a low-latency architecture while preserving soft-output performance for high-speed optical interconnects.

items.title: Fast likelihood evaluation for multivariate sensory discrimination models
items.summary: Sensory discrimination is often measured by fitting statistical models with likelihood functions that are computationally challenging to evaluate. In the standard triangle and duo-trio tests, a subject is presented with three stimuli, two of one kind and one of another, and is asked to identify the odd one out (the triangle test) or which of two stimuli matches a reference (the duo-trio test). In a Thurstonian model, the subject's internal representation of each stimulus is a Gaussian whose mean and covariance depend on the stimulus, and the probability that the subject's response is correct is an integral over a $3d$-dimensional Gaussian with no closed form for $d > 1$, where $d$ is the dimension of the stimulus space. To fit a statistical model to data collected from triangle or duo-trio tests, the likelihood function, and often its gradient, need to be evaluated many times, making statistical inference inefficient. Here, we introduce fast algorithms for evaluating certain classes of likelihood functions for the triangle and duo-trio tests. The algorithms rely on reducing the dimension of these functions. The triangle probability, a function of $2d + d(d+1)$ arguments, reduces analytically to a function of $2d$ arguments, and the duo-trio probability, when the two stimuli have equal covariances, reduces to a function of a single scalar for any $d$. After reducing the dimensionality of those functions, we use neural networks and Chebyshev expansions to evaluate the lower-dimensional functions efficiently. Our algorithms demonstrate orders of magnitude speedups over existing approaches at comparable accuracy, both for a single evaluation and when used to compute the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate of a model of color discrimination. The dimensionality reduction we use generalizes to non-Gaussian noise models with elliptical level sets, and to tests with more than three stimuli.

items.title: Learning the Boltzmann Collision Operator with Structural Constraints for Fast Kinetic Simulation
items.summary: The high-dimensional integration in the Boltzmann collision operator is a major computational bottleneck in deterministic kinetic simulations. We develop a structure-preserving neural operator that provides an efficient approximation of this nonlinear collision mapping. The operator maintains the gain-loss structure of the original Boltzmann collision operator, and, by construction, is proportional to the square of the gas density. Conservative moment projection and entropy correction enforce conservation of mass, momentum, and energy, as well as entropy dissipation. By construction, the collision term also vanishes at all Maxwellians. In the numerical scheme for simulations of gas dynamics, we establish nonnegativity of the distribution function with the learned collision operator and prove exponential relaxation to the moment-matched equilibrium when a positive spectral gap is imposed. Numerical experiments for a constant collision kernel demonstrate a favorable accuracy-cost tradeoff relative to Fourier spectral evaluations. Although trained on smooth distributions, the same operator handles discontinuous distribution functions and is embedded without retraining in steady Couette flow, normal-shock, and two-dimensional lid-driven cavity solvers. These results demonstrate a reusable approximation for repeated collision evaluations that retains kinetic structure and supports accurate deterministic simulation.

items.title: Random Projection Neural Networks for Phase-Field Models: Model Reformulation, Scaling, and Network Architecture
items.summary: Phase-field models, particularly the Allen-Cahn(AC) and Cahn-Hilliard(CH) equations, are widely used to describe interfacial dynamics, but resolving their sharp transition layers and stiff dynamics presents substantial numerical challenges. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) offer a mesh-free approach, yet optimizing large numbers of network parameters can be computationally demanding and may still yield limited accuracy. We develop a random projection neural network (RPNN) framework that combines first-order PDE reformulations with independent random-feature representations of the unknowns. By fixing randomly initialized hidden-layer parameters and optimizing only the output coefficients, RPNNs reduce training to least-squares problems amenable to Newton-type solvers. Introducing auxiliary variables eliminates higher-order derivatives from the PDE residuals, while separate random feature bases in the unknowns provide flexibility in approximating fields with different scales and regularity. For the CH equation, we scale the chemical potential to address the disparity between its magnitude and that of the phase field. We compare the first-order and corresponding higher-order formulations and systematically examine the effects of initialization distributions, the random feature range $R_ξ$, seven activation functions, and dense versus separable space-time bases. We also evaluate gradient-based adaptive sampling, residual reweighting, and mild spatial derivative-penalty regularization. Across the reported benchmarks, the proposed framework reduces relative $L^2$ and absolute $L^\infty$ errors by nearly one to three orders of magnitude compared with the various PINN baselines. These results demonstrate the potential of first-order RPNNs for accurate approximation of phase-field dynamics with sharp transition layers.

items.title: Perturbed QMC designs and reduced QMC strength
items.summary: Small errors in sampling locations can change the convergence rate of a cubature rule. We study this effect for equal-weight integration on spheres and determine how accurately the nodes must be realized to retain optimal Sobolev rates. Under an average energy condition on the reference nodes, we establish sharp perturbation bounds and characterize how the decay of node errors affects quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) strength, which measures the smoothness range over which optimal rates hold. We identify when this strength is preserved and when it can decrease, and show that sufficiently slow decay of node errors can destroy all optimal Sobolev rates. For a reference rule with optimal convergence, we further establish a necessary and sufficient condition on node accuracy for retaining the optimal rate uniformly over all permitted perturbations. Numerical experiments with spherical designs, Fekete points, and Coulomb-energy points illustrate the different stability regimes.

items.title: Worst case tractability of weighted linear tensor product problems under the absolute error criterion
items.summary: This paper studies weighted linear tensor product problems in the worst case setting. We consider algorithms that use finitely many evaluations of arbitrary continuous linear functionals. We investigate algebraic and exponential tractability under the absolute error criterion in the case $λ_1>1$, where $λ_1$ is the square of the univariate maximal singular value. We obtain necessary and sufficient conditions for various notions of algebraic and exponential tractability on weights and univariate singular values. Our approach is to convert algebraic tractability of the problems for the absolute error criterion with $λ_1 > 1$ to exponential tractability of the normalized problems. Specifically, we solve Open Problem 27 as posed by Novak and Woźniakowski (2008).

items.title: Simplified Plotkin-type Bounds for Function-Correcting Codes with b-Symbol and Sum-Rank Distances
items.summary: Function-correcting codes (FCCs) are a coding framework that enables reliable communication with minimal redundancy while ensuring the recovery of specific functions of transmitted messages. FCCs have been studied recently under the $b$-symbol distance and the sum-rank distance. Existing general Plotkin-type bounds on the optimal redundancy of FCCs under these distances require computing the pairwise distances between vectors that map to different function values. As a result, these bounds are often computationally difficult to determine. In this paper, we derive simplified Plotkin-type bounds on the optimal redundancy of FCCs under the $b$-symbol and sum-rank distances. These bounds depend only on the number of message vectors corresponding to each function value and the sum of pairwise distances among vectors mapped to the same function value. The proposed bounds apply to arbitrary functions and are considerably easier to evaluate than existing Plotkin-type bounds. The known simplified bounds for linear functions under the $b$-symbol and sum-rank distances are subsumed as special cases of the proposed bounds. Furthermore, we obtain a tighter bound for linear functions under the sum-rank distance than the existing bound.

items.title: AdapToC: A Unified Framework for Multi-Task Visual Token Communication
items.summary: Pretrained discrete visual tokenizers supply compact latents for synthesis, recognition, and embodied perception, yet wireless token streaming remains fragile. Under fading and noisy pilots, hard cyclic redundancy check (CRC) erasures turn corrupted blocks into missing tokens while frozen decoders amplify edge errors, which can collapse unequal error protection (UEP) into a binary choice between strong coding and omission under severe fading. Soft bit posteriors break this collapse. We present AdapToC, a single-pass transceiver that restores multi-tier rate-distortion tradeoffs without altering tokenizer weights or differentiating through pixel decoders. We align codebook geometry to the channel via offline frequency-weighted Pseudo-Gray relabeling and Halton dispersion to contract bit and burst errors with zero overhead. Because soft recovery pulls intermediate rates onto the three-tier convex hull, our unit-gated AdaLN sender schedules protection tiers across channel budgets, while our pilot-calibrated receiver feeds factorized codebook posteriors into a ConvNeXt-attention restorer with CRC bypass. We co-train AdapToC solely in latent space via counterfactual utility estimation and codebook cross-entropy regularization. On identical VQGAN-f16 tokens, AdapToC outperforms TONIC and adaptive TokenCom+AMC, cuts multi-SNR Rayleigh LPIPS from 0.6551 to 0.3312 within the frozen-tokenizer PSNR ceiling, and saves 43.8% Rician-K6 symbols at matched quality. Our single-pass restorer runs 8.3x faster than iterative resampling, raises accuracy while accelerating decoder-free recognition 20.6x, and improves fidelity plug-and-play across TiTok, VAR, and zero-shot NuPlan.

items.title: R2WM: Recursive Reasoning Wireless Model for Long-Horizon mmWave Beam Prediction
items.summary: Long-horizon beam prediction aims to extend beam-training intervals while supporting beam alignment in mobile millimeter-wave systems. Although pretrained large models can improve prediction over compact recurrent baselines, their large backbones impose substantial storage and computing requirements. To address this limitation, we propose a recursive reasoning wireless model (R2WM). Given a fixed history of beam indices and angles of departure (AoDs), R2WM repeatedly updates coupled latent and prediction states using a shared causal-attention backbone before jointly decoding the future beam indices. Backbone reuse increases computational depth at fixed parameter count. In the standard 10-step DeepMIMO setting, R2WM achieves an average normalized beamforming gain of 0.9597, compared with 0.8629 for the prompt-as-prefix large language model, with 99.1% fewer parameters and 59.1% fewer counted floating-point operations. Transfer experiments show that R2WM retains normalized gain under the tested carrier-frequency and antenna-count changes, while its beam-index-only variant retains gain under the tested base-station change. Component ablations show higher gains with historical AoD conditioning and causal attention. Recursion analysis reveals a gain-computation trade-off across separately trained configurations with the same parameter count. An additional comparison with a nonrecursive Transformer of similar parameter count shows higher gain for R2WM at greater computational cost. These results support accurate long-horizon beam prediction without a large pretrained backbone.

items.title: The Complexity of Oracle-Efficient Realizable Transductive Learning
items.summary: In realizable transductive online learning, the learner knows the entire sequence of $T$ instances in advance, and the labels are consistent with one of $N$ hypotheses. With explicit access to the hypothesis class, the halving algorithm makes at most $\log_2 N$ mistakes. Can a comparable guarantee be achieved using only polynomially many empirical risk minimization (ERM) queries? We answer this question negatively, even for a weighted-ERM oracle that optimizes arbitrary real-valued linear objectives and returns a complete maximizing hypothesis. For every fixed $β\in(0,1)$ and every randomized learner making polynomially many oracle queries, there exists a fixed realizable instance with exactly $N=2^{\lfloor T^β\rfloor}$ hypotheses on which the learner makes $Ω_β(\sqrt{T\log N})$ mistakes in expectation. This matches the agnostic-rate upper bound achieved by random playout using $O(T)$ oracle calls. The separation persists for much smaller classes as well: along a sequence with $\log N=Θ((\log T)^2)$, we establish a mistake lower bound of $\exp(Ω(\log T/\log\log T))$. Our main technical contribution is a composition lemma that combines two realizable prediction problems such that their mistake lower bounds add, up to a small loss, while their hypothesis class sizes grow only additively. Iterating this lemma yields a family of hard instances spanning the desired parameter regimes, establishing a sharp separation between information-theoretic and oracle-efficient mistake guarantees.

items.title: String Indexing for Maximal Gap-Bounded Occurrence Clusters
items.summary: Repeated occurrences of a pattern can form groups that reveal where repetition is concentrated in a text. We study how to find such groups efficiently when both the pattern $P$ and the distance threshold $G$ between occurrences are specified as query parameters. A maximal $G$-cluster of $P$ is a maximal block of at least two occurrences of $P$ whose consecutive starting positions differ by at most $G$. In this paper, we present indexes for reporting all cluster intervals and counting the clusters. For a text of length $n$ and a pattern of length $m$, we propose an $O(n\log n)$-space index that reports all maximal cluster intervals in $O(m+\log\log n+\mathit{output})$ time, where $\mathit{output}$ is the number of reported intervals, and that counts the clusters in $O(m+\log\log n)$ time. Restricting occurrences to those fully contained in a query substring preserves the reporting time using $O(n\log^2 n)$ space. Our indexes combine suffix-tree decompositions with geometric reporting queries on consecutive gaps.

items.title: PopMelodyGen: A Copyright-Aware Platform for Controllable Pop-Melody Generation
items.summary: Large-scale redistributable symbolic pop-melody data remain scarce due to copyright restrictions, creating a bottleneck for both practical deployment and reproducible research in music generation. We present PopMelodyGen, a copyright-aware platform for controllable pop-melody generation that combines rule-based synthesis with neural generation. Our approach first uses an expert synthesizer to produce large-scale labeled synthetic melodies from explicit musical knowledge and templates, providing scalable pretraining data with auditable provenance. A neural model is then pretrained on this corpus and adapted with a small licensed real-pop corpus to improve melodic naturalness while preserving controllability. The platform supports interactive melody creation with accompaniment playback and export for creators, as well as batch construction of annotated symbolic datasets for researchers. PopMelodyGen demonstrates a practical training and deployment paradigm for creative AI when large-scale reusable real-world data are limited.

items.title: Structure-preserving active flux method for the compressible Euler equations with gravity
items.summary: In this paper, we propose a structure-preserving active flux method for the compressible Euler equations under gravitational fields, ensuring exactness for the generalized hydrostatic equilibrium state and the preservation of positivity for both density and pressure. This approach entails the update of the cell average and the point values simultaneously. To obtain the equilibrium preservation of the scheme for the cell average, the strategy pursued is to reformulate the gravitational term using the steady state solution, followed by the application of a decomposition algorithm. For the point values, we introduce minor adjustments to the Lax-Friedrichs flux vector splitting, coupled with the same finite difference operator performed on the flux and source term to restore the well-balancedness. Furthermore, a posteriori Multi-dimensional Optimal Order Detection (MOOD) paradigm is adopted for achieving positivity preservation and oscillation control near strong discontinuities. A series of numerical experiments are performed to verify the high-order accuracy of our proposed method, along with its exact equilibrium and positivity preservation, and its ability to capture small perturbations at or close to steady flow without spurious oscillations.

items.title: Well-balanced nodal finite volume WENO scheme with flux localization for hyperbolic balance laws
items.summary: In this paper, we develop a general framework for constructing arbitrarily high-order well-balanced ``nodal" finite volume weighted essentially non-oscillatory (WENO) schemes, specifically tailored for hyperbolic balance laws. To handle complex systems involving nonconservative products and steady-state solutions with global integral quantities, we introduce a flux localization technique. This technique defines the numerical fluxes, incorporating the entire source term and nonconservative products, locally within each computational cell. By exactly preserving the nodal equilibrium state and conservatively updating the cell averages within a finite volume framework, the method avoids both reference-state reconstruction and the use of ODE solvers. The well-balanced property is achieved by performing high-order WENO reconstruction and employing a linear segment path in terms of equilibrium variables, rather than conservative ones. A rigorous theoretical analysis confirms that the scheme exactly preserves all the targeted stationary solutions. The effectiveness and versatility of the proposed method are demonstrated through a series of numerical experiments on various systems of hyperbolic balance laws.

items.title: Interface-aware dynamic mode decomposition with control for partitioned multiphysics systems
items.summary: We develop an interface-aware dynamic mode decomposition with control (DMDc) formulation for multiphysics systems, within an optimization-based partitioned coupling framework. The finite-element interface-input operator is projected onto the reduced space and kept fixed during identification, while the unknown state-dependent local dynamics are learned from trajectory data. The common interface control is recomputed online by minimizing the mismatch between the reconstructed physical interface quantities. The formulation accommodates local subproblems governed by ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and differential--algebraic equations (DAEs). For a DAE subproblem, tangent projection identifies the state dynamics, whereas a residualized normal regression identifies the pressure balance and provides an algebraic pressure reconstruction. We further propose regularized quadratic correction DMDc to enrich the tangent dynamics and, for DAEs, the normal pressure balance through jointly fitted linear and compact quadratic operators. Feature normalization and block-dependent regularization control the enlarged regression while retaining the prescribed interface operators and identified DAE geometry. The proposed framework is evaluated on problems involving both ODE--ODE and DAE--ODE couplings. The numerical results demonstrate accurate predictions and stable long-time behavior.

items.title: Quantitative Convergence of the Spherical Brownian Motion collisional particle system for the Maxwellian Landau Equation
items.summary: In this paper, we establish the quantitative convergence of the spherical Brownian motion (SBM) collisional particle system for the Maxwellian Landau equation via Wasserstein distances. When used as numerical method, it enjoys linear complexity $O(N)$ in particle number $N$, and conserves the momentum and energy almost surely. Moreover, only random grouping and sampling are needed for simulations without further numerical discretization. In the first part, we identify the large particle mean field limit of the system, and the Wasserstein convergence to the limit is justified through a coupling similar to the recent work for the Nanbu type Monte Carlo method \cite{BorghiPareschi2025}. The key difference is that the particles in our coupled shadow system are not i.i.d. due to the perfect matching. In the second part, the convergence of the mean field dynamics to the Landau solution is justified by the relative entropy with a bound $O(τ^2)$, being $τ$ the stepsize. This results in an $O(τ)$ bound for the Wasserstein distance error. A crucial technical tool in the convergence in relative entropy is to provide suitable bounds on the derivatives of the logarithmic density or score function in the mean field dynamics. The combination of these estimates leads to the full convergence of the squared Wasserstein distance with order $O(N^{-1/2}+τ^2)$ for the numerical scheme in $d=3$.

items.title: Numerical approximation of the Hilfer fractional derivative using orthogonal Quasi-Polynomials
items.summary: A numerical approach based on a composite Gaussian quadrature for the Hilfer fractional derivative is presented. This approach employs quasi-polynomials that are orthogonal with respect to the weight function on the interval $(0,1)$. As special cases, the Riemann--Liouville and Caputo fractional derivatives are obtained. Error bounds for the approximation are derived. To confirm the convergence rates as well as the high efficiency of the new approach, numerical examples are provided.

items.title: Finite-difference neural policy iteration for high-dimensional degenerate Hamilton--Jacobi equations
items.summary: We develop a finite-difference neural policy iteration method for high-dimensional degenerate Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman and Isaacs equations. Artificial viscosity yields a monotone finite-difference operator, and neural networks approximate the linear equations of semi-discrete policy iteration using local stencil values. This avoids global tensor-grid storage. For measurable feedbacks, we bound the propagation of evaluation, terminal, gradient, and control optimization errors by a geometrically weighted sum. Discrete comparison, consistency, and vanishing viscosity relate the approximation to the original degenerate equation. On coupled manufactured problems with rank-deficient diffusion, the method achieves lower mean errors than direct physics-informed neural networks at every tested dimension from five to fifty under equal training time. At fifty dimensions and $900$ seconds, the mean relative $L^2$ error over three paired seeds is about $40\%$ lower. Two-dimensional refinement attains $0.297\%$ error against the original degenerate solution, with independent grid references separating approximation error from viscosity bias. In a twenty-dimensional game with finite control sets, reusing policies reduces the measured time to a relative error of $5\%$ by $24.3\%$ compared with direct minimization of the same discrete residual with fresh samples at every update.

items.title: KernelMix: Bayesian kernel machine regression in Python
items.summary: Exposures measured together can have nonlinear associations with an outcome, and the association with one exposure may depend on another. Bayesian kernel machine regression represents these patterns through a flexible exposure-response function. We implement this approach in KernelMix, a Python package. To handle different outcome types, KernelMix combines the exposure function with continuous, binary, count and survival models, including selected extensions for clustered observations and censored event times. For fitted models, it returns posterior summaries, uncertainty intervals, joint predictions and sampling diagnostics. Fitting and prediction use NumPy and SciPy without requiring R. To assess the implementation, we compare selected Gaussian and probit posterior summaries and conditional calculations with installed R bkmr 0.2.2 and check additional model components against independent mathematical calculations. A daily ozone analysis illustrates how these components form an analysis workflow.

items.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Sample Complexity of Natural Policy Gradient with a Matching Information-Theoretic Lower Bound
items.summary: A fundamental question in reinforcement learning is how many sampled transitions are needed to learn a near-optimal policy, and whether direct policy optimization can attain this statistical limit. To answer this question, we consider natural policy gradient (NPG), a widely used policy optimization method. We study tabular finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) with known rewards and unknown horizon-dependent transition kernels, accessed through a generative model. Our sample-based NPG algorithms update the policy by backward sweeps and do not estimate transition probabilities. Under three different batch-size and step size schedules, we establish last-iterate guarantees with sample complexity $\widetilde O(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$, where $S$, $A$, and $H$ denote the number of states, the number of actions, and the horizon length, respectively. In this setting, horizon-dependent transition kernels contribute a factor of $H$ to our transition-query bound. Our information-theoretic lower bound of $Ω(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$ shows that the resulting $H^4$ dependence is unavoidable in the worst case, even for agents that select their queries adaptively. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first last-iterate guarantees for NPG whose sample complexity matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, our results demonstrate that direct policy-space optimization through NPG can achieve the fundamental statistical limits of reinforcement learning while guaranteeing the performance of the final policy. Furthermore, for known kernels, we prove that exact NPG with a constant step size $η=1/H$ requires $Ω(H^2/\varepsilon)$ iterations in the worst case, matching the known upper bound for that step size.

items.title: Neural Schrödinger Bridge via Yasue Action with Applications to Generative Modeling
items.summary: We propose a novel neural solver for inferring the continuous state evolution of the Schrödinger bridge problem. The proposed solver builds on a saddle point formulation involving the Yasue action functional. This allows us to realize the continuous state evolution by learning the optimal velocity for an ordinary differential equation, as opposed to learning the optimal drift for a stochastic differential equation. The proposed solver only uses the source and the target samples, and not the source and target distributions per se, which makes it particularly suitable for high dimensional applications arising in generative modeling. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed solver using several numerical experiments in low and high dimensions, using both real and synthetic datasets.

items.title: Deterministic regularisation of the nonsymmetric eigenproblem
items.summary: We give a deterministic algorithm for pseudospectral shattering in exact arithmetic. This resolves an important open problem in the complexity of the nonsymmetric eigenproblem. Given a complex contraction $A$ of order $n\ge2$ and $0<δ<1/2$, we compute a perturbation $E$ with $\|E\|<δ$ such that $A+E$ has simple spectrum. The ratio of its eigenbasis condition number to its minimum eigenvalue gap is at most $C(n/δ)^{20/3}$. The algorithm also computes an exact eigensystem of $A+E$. It uses $O(n^3\log^d(n/δ))$ real-field operations and comparisons, where $C$ and $d$ are absolute constants. We choose the rank-one perturbations using a lower bound on the circle mean of the logarithm of the discriminant modulus. A quadratic penalty controls how far the accumulated updates move the matrix. By using the same reference eigenbasis for several updates, we can estimate all the current projector norms while recovering only the directions needed for the next perturbation.

items.title: Multi-location Newsvendor: An Interpretable Inventory Policy
items.summary: We study a multilocation newsvendor problem in which inventory is chosen before demand is observed and surplus stock can subsequently be transshipped to locations with shortages. The objective is to minimize expected holding, backlog, and transportation costs over a metric network. Under uniform transportation costs, the optimality conditions balance local and aggregate demand coverage and reduce to a scalar search under mild regularity conditions. We use this structure to develop an interpretable iterative heuristic for general metrics. The heuristic calibrates effective transportation costs from lateral shipments under independent stocking and uses them to construct location-dependent pooling weights. These weights have a direct operational interpretation through the cost of serving demand at other locations. Under the stated assumptions, the heuristic recovers the exact uniform-metric solution. Numerical experiments on structured and random networks show costs close to the sampled optimum on average and substantial savings relative to independent stocking.

items.title: Tight Bounds for Rank Estimation in Turnstile Streams
items.summary: We study rank estimation in turnstile streams. A frequency vector $f$ over the universe $[U]$ receives insertions and deletions. Given a query $x\in[U]$, the goal is to estimate the rank $\sum_{u<x}f_u$ within additive error $ε\|f\|_1$ with constant probability. The standard approach is Dyadic CountSketch by Luo, Wang, Yi and Cormode, using $\tilde{O}(ε^{-1}\log^{3/2}U\log n)$ bits, where $n$ is the final $\ell_1$ norm of $f$. Bulánek, Kumar, Meka, Nelson, and Sarlós placed this approach in a matrix-factorization framework. They improved the space of Dyadic CountSketch to $O(ε^{-1}\log^{3/2}U)$ words, and proved a lower bound of $Ω(ε^{-1}\log^2(εU))$ bits for all streaming algorithms when $U\le n\le U^{O(1)}$ and $ε=U^{-1+Ω(1)}$. This leaves a gap of $\sqrt{\log U}$. In this work, we fully determine the space cost of rank estimation up to an absolute constant. Our main result is a space lower bound for all streaming algorithms: for $0<ε\le 1/8$ and $n\ge\log^2 U$, the space is at least $Ω(\min\{ε^{-1}L^{3/2}\log(2+nε/\sqrt{L}), ε^{-2}\log U\log n, \log\binom{U+n}{n}\})$ bits, where $L=\log(2+Uε)$. When $U\le n\le U^{O(1)}$ and $ε=U^{-1+Ω(1)}$, this simplifies to $Ω(\min\{ε^{-1}\log^{5/2}U, ε^{-2}\log^2 U\})$ bits. Our proof uses a surprising hard distribution and novel information-theoretic techniques. The above bound matches Dyadic CountSketch when $n\ge U$ and $U^{-1+Ω(1)}\leε\le O(1/\sqrt{\log U})$. The lower bound is also tight in the remaining regimes. For $ε\ge(\log U)^{-1/2}$, there exists an algorithm that uses $O(ε^{-2}\log U\log n)$ bits using $\ell_1$ samplers. For $ε\le U^{-1+o(1)}$, we refine Dyadic CountSketch so that its space in bits matches the first term of the bound.

items.title: The Gerards-Schrijver conjecture on the Edmonds-Johnson property is false
items.summary: An integral matrix $A$ has the Edmonds-Johnson property if, for all integral vectors $b,c,l,u$, the first Chvátal closure of $\{x: b\le Ax\le c,\ l\le x\le u\}$ equals its integer hull. Gerards and Schrijver conjectured that a totally half-modular matrix has the Edmonds-Johnson property if and only if it has no minor equal to one of two specific matrices, of size $3\times3$ and $3\times4$. We disprove this conjecture. We give a totally half-modular $5\times6$ matrix that does not have the Edmonds-Johnson property and has no minor equal to either matrix. It is a minimal obstruction: every proper minor has the Edmonds-Johnson property. The proofs work on a graph whose edges are the rows and bounds of the matrix, and on which the minor operations act by deleting, contracting and halving edges. For minimality, we reduce every proper minor to two classes of matrices known to have the Edmonds-Johnson property.

items.title: Tight Mistake-Abstention Tradeoffs for Sequential Prediction under Adversarial Injections
items.summary: We study the sequential prediction problem introduced by Goel et al. (2023), where an adversary can inject arbitrarily many corrupted instances in an i.i.d. stream from a clean distribution $μ$, while the learner is allowed to abstain from making a prediction at no cost if the current instance was indeed injected. When $μ$ is unknown, Yu and Blanchard (2026) show a polynomial tradeoff between mistakes and false abstentions for classes with finite VC dimension and oblivious adversaries, but still leave open a significant gap between upper and lower bounds in their tradeoff landscape. In this paper, we propose the weighted shattering potential, and based on variants of this potential, provide gap-closing algorithms that essentially characterize the tradeoffs under various settings of interest: When $μ$ is known, our algorithm improves over Goel et al. (2023) and achieves their conjectured $O(d\log T)$ mistake bound; When $μ$ is unknown, for oblivious adversary, our guarantees are tight both in $T$ and in terms of the VC dimension $d$, which completely characterizes the abstention-mistake tradeoff in this setting and gives an $O(\sqrt{dT})$ balanced rate. For adaptive adversary, our results are tight up to $\operatorname{poly}(dD\log T)$ factors for structured classes with finite so-called reduction dimension $D$. Our guarantees also extend to censored feedback, where the label is hidden after an abstention.

items.title: An ADMM-Based Approach to the Large-Scale Geomagnetically Induced Current Blocker Placement Problem
items.summary: We propose an Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM)-based approach for addressing the challenge of determining placements for geomagnetically induced current (GIC) blocking devices on large-scale transmission networks. Traditional formulations of this placement problem lead to mixed-integer nonlinear programs (MINLPs) that are difficult for state-of-the-art MINLP solvers, which often struggle to exploit problem structure and fail to produce high-quality solutions on large systems. To overcome these challenges, the proposed method employs a three-block ADMM decomposition enhanced with (i) partial linearization of the GIC-related nonlinearities, supported by conditions guaranteeing exactness, and (ii) heterogeneous penalty parameters that significantly accelerate convergence to high-quality local solutions. Numerical experiments on newly constructed large-scale benchmark systems (up to 10,000 buses) demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods by several orders of magnitude in runtime while producing solutions whose objective values closely approach the ideal all-blocker lower bound. These results highlight the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed approach for mitigation planning efforts in large transmission networks.

items.title: A hybrid high-order discretization of a volume integral formulation for eddy currents on unstructured polyhedral meshes
items.summary: Volume integral formulations are attractive for eddy-current simulation because they require a mesh only of the conducting region. However, their dense interaction matrices make it important to control the number of unknowns needed for a prescribed accuracy. We propose an arbitrary-order Hybrid High-Order discretization of a current-based volume integral formulation on general unstructured polyhedral meshes. The method combines high-order polynomial approximation with local mesh refinement around defects and material interfaces. For bounded positive spatially varying resistivity and magnetic permeability uniform throughout space, we establish well-posedness and a priori error estimates using a constructive right inverse of the discrete divergence. Numerical experiments demonstrate convergence for smooth solutions and compare mesh refinement with increasing the polynomial degree. Selected comparisons show that higher degree on coarser meshes can reduce the number of current unknowns coupled by the Green operator and the associated storage for a prescribed accuracy. Finally, a three-dimensional eddy-current testing benchmark assesses the predicted impedance against experimental measurements, using local refinement around a narrow slot and reusing the system matrix and its factorization throughout the probe scan.

items.title: Data-driven discovery of sparse governing equations with parameterized operators
items.summary: We study parameterized SINDy (pSINDy), an extension of the Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) framework for the discovery of parsimonious governing equations involving operators with unknown parameters such as fractional-order Caputo derivatives, fractional Laplacians, and parameterized kernel operators. The framework jointly identifies the unknown operator parameters and sparse library coefficients through a sparsity-promoting optimization problem. To solve this problem, we develop and analyze the parameterized sequentially thresholded least-squares (pSTLSQ) algorithm. In each iteration, it removes terms with small coefficients, updates the operator parameters by a fixed number of optimization steps that improve the fit of the remaining library terms, and refits their coefficients by least squares. Under suitable assumptions, we prove that pSTLSQ converges locally to a local minimizer and give sufficient conditions for identifying the terms present in the governing equation. Numerical experiments demonstrate recovery of governing equations from noisy synthetic data for fractional ODEs, fractional PDEs, and nonlocal diffusion equations. We also examine the influence of the hyperparameters, discretization scheme, and noise, and compare pSTLSQ with two benchmark methods. All three methods identify the correct terms at low noise levels, but differ in parameter accuracy, cost, and sensitivity to initialization and the candidate library.

items.title: A $(3/2+\varepsilon)$-Approximation for Weighted 3-Set Packing
items.summary: We give a deterministic $(3/2+\varepsilon)$-approximation for weighted $3$-set packing, for every fixed rational $\varepsilon>0$, improving on the 1.6908-approximation reported by Tong and Xu (2026). The algorithm has two phases. It first performs bounded local search using a rounded $12/7$-power potential. It then combines compatible exchanges that insert at most three sets and increase the original weight. The analysis relates the gap left by the first phase to the gain available to the second phase. We prove a structural inequality that bounds the weight of a comparison packing by $3/2$ times the current weight plus one sixth of a sum of small-exchange gains. Each gain accounts for all sets that the exchange must delete. A greedy rule recovers enough of these gains to obtain the approximation guarantee. We derive the structural bound from local optimality by analyzing finite computation trees and averaging the error caused by their limited depth. The running time is $n^{4^{O(1/\varepsilon)}}\operatorname{poly}(L)$, where $n$ is the number of input sets and $L$ is the input encoding length. The same guarantee holds for maximum-weight independent set in induced $K_{1,4}$-free graphs.

items.title: Hierarchical Sub-Array Beam Training for Flexible Intelligent Metasurface-Enabled Hybrid Near-Far-Field Multiuser Communications
items.summary: Low-resolution discrete phase shifters (PSs) are attractive for extremely large-scale arrays, but phase quantization distorts near-field (NF) beam patterns and degrades beam training and multiuser transmission. Moreover, the distinct codebook structures required by NF and far-field (FF) users complicate hybrid NF-FF beam training and codeword switching. To address these challenges, we introduce flexible intelligent metasurface (FIM) surface shaping as an additional geometric beamforming degree of freedom. We establish the hybrid NF-FF channel and beam pattern models, characterize the grating lobes induced by discrete PSs, and develop a phase-quantization compensation method. A deformation-range analysis shows that wavelength-scale shaping can achieve beam patterns comparable to those obtained with continuous PSs. We further propose a hierarchical sub-array beam training (HSABT) scheme that progressively doubles the activated central aperture according to the beam-width and beam-depth characteristics. A beam-intersection-based sampling strategy improves the angle-distance resolution, while a measurement-driven adaptive NF-FF beam-switching mechanism selects the final codeword without relying on the Rayleigh distance or prior user-location information. HSABT is also extended to multi-path channels through adaptive peak detection and inter-level energy-consistency-based candidate tracking. For high-gain multiuser transmission, we develop an alternating-optimization-based design and a complementary non-iterative key observation method, and analyze their convergence, computational complexity, and steady-point properties.Simulation results demonstrate continuous-phase-comparable beam patterns, reduced training overhead, more accurate main-path acquisition than exhaustive polar-codebook training, and higher multiuser sum rates than conventional rigid-array benchmarks.

items.title: Accelerating wave-scattering simulations with learned search directions
items.summary: Wave-scattering simulation requires solving a dense boundary-element system for every frequency, incidence and design. Krylov solvers build each search space from scratch, and it grows with problem size. Here we present BEMFormer, a solver that learns to generate search directions across systems of one integral equation and supplies geometry-specific directions through a coarse-grid correction. BEMFormer generalizes to unseen geometries, meshes and excitations, and to acoustic scattering after fine-tuning on eight geometries. It reproduces the measured radar cross-sections of benchmark targets. On a quadcopter with 1.04 million unknowns, 38 times the largest training problem, BEMFormer solves each system 30 times faster than a preconditioned Krylov solver. Both reach a radar cross-section deviation of about 1 dB, comparable to the difference between independent measurements and acceptable for engineering applications. These results show that solving million-unknown scattering problems in minutes is possible when the search space is learned rather than built from scratch.

items.title: Approximate Map Matching under Realistic Assumptions
items.summary: Given a graph $G=(V,E)$ and a polygonal curve $P$ of complexity $n$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we study the map matching problem of computing a path in $G$ that minimises the Fréchet distance to $P$. Chen, Driemel, Guibas, Nguyen and Wenk (ALENEX 2011) gave a near-linear time $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for the case when $G$ is $λ$-low-dense and $P$ is $c$-packed. We show that these assumptions can be relaxed, and we give efficient $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithms under the weaker conditions. First, if $P$ is $c$-packed and $G$ is an arbitrary graph, we obtain an $\tilde{O}(cn + c^2|E|)$ time algorithm. Second, if both $G$ and $P$ are $λ$-low-dense, we obtain an $\tilde{O}(λ^2((n|V|)^{1-1/d}+n+|V|))$ expected time algorithm, which becomes $\tilde{O}(λ^2(n+|V|))$ in the plane.

items.title: Optimal User-Level Private Stochastic Convex Optimization and Mean Estimation with Heavy Tails
items.summary: We study stochastic convex optimization with heavy-tailed stochastic gradients under $(\varepsilon, δ)$-user-level differential privacy, which protects each user's entire collection of samples. Instead of assuming a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant, we only assume bounds on the second- and $k$-th moments of the random sample Lipschitz parameters. This allows for unbounded, heavy-tailed stochastic gradient distributions and can lead to sharper excess risk bounds. We characterize the minimax optimal excess population risk up to logarithmic factors. Our algorithm achieves the optimal rate with only $\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon)$ users. As a byproduct of our algorithmic developments, we obtain tight bounds for user-level private mean estimation under norm-moment assumptions, improving over the guarantees of Esfandiari et al. (2022) and Zhao et al. (2024). Finally, for mean estimation under the directional-moment assumption of Agarwal et al. (2025), we close their remaining approximate-DP gap by removing the additional $d/\varepsilon$ user requirement and attaining the optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors.

items.title: A Generalized Framework for Structured Low-Rank Approximation and Completion
items.summary: We formulate a generalized version of SLRA, consisting of general affine constraints, which subsumes the problems of structured low-rank matrix approximation and completion as special cases. We characterize its critical points and propose an algorithm to approximately solve the general problem. Finally, we demonstrate the performance of the proposed algorithm for stock-price forecasting, computing approximate gcd of polynomials with noisy coefficients, and time-series denoising.

items.title: Sub-Riemannian flow matching
items.summary: We study sub-Riemannian conditional flow matching (SRCFM) for generative transport with prescribed velocity constraints. Training uses paths between sampled source and target points whose velocities lie in the allowed horizontal directions at each state. A neural network takes time and the full state as input and predicts the coefficients of these directions, and the horizontal frame then determines the full velocity used for generation. We describe constructions based on Heisenberg geodesics and joint endpoint equations in free step-two Carnot groups. We propose a scalable piecewise algorithm that computes horizontal paths directly from their endpoints. A straight segment sets the horizontal coordinates, and a loop in those coordinates corrects the remaining vertical displacement. We verify the algorithm's endpoint accuracy to numerical precision in high-dimensional tests. Synthetic experiments illustrate approximate distribution transport along horizontal trajectories. On resized MNIST, we use the same construction to generate images from Gaussian inputs with fewer controls than pixels.

items.title: A Unified Bregman Projection Framework for Solving Multi-Split Multiple-Set Implicit Convex Feasibility Problems
items.summary: We study the multi-split multiple-set implicit convex feasibility problem (MSMS-ICFP), in which the constraint sets are generated by point-to-set operators and the feasibility conditions are imposed both in the original space and in several image spaces connected by bounded linear operators. We analyze the generalized proximity function, built from weighted Bregman distances and Bregman projections, introduced by Censor and Dey. For translation-type point-to-set operators, we establish the continuity and Lipschitz continuity of the corresponding Bregman projections, the continuous differentiability of the proximity function with an explicit formula for its gradient, and global and local Lipschitz estimates for this gradient. We then propose a generalized simultaneous projection gradient algorithm. In the nonconvex case, the gradient norms of the iterates converge to zero and every accumulation point is stationary. When the proximity function is convex and the solution set is nonempty, the iterates converge in norm to a solution, with an $O(1/k)$ rate for the proximity values, an $O(1/\sqrt{k})$ rate for the gradient norms, and a linear rate under a quadratic growth condition. Cyclic and block-iterative variants are also analyzed. Numerical experiments, including a cooperative sensor network localization problem, illustrate the theory and show that, in contrast with frozen-set implicit projection methods, the proposed gradient schemes remain convergent when the translation operators are expansive.

items.title: Geometric ergodicity of Gibbs samplers for linear mixed models with several heavy-tailed random-effect components and unknown tail parameters
items.summary: Linear mixed models with heavy-tailed random effects are widely used for robust Bayesian analysis of longitudinal data. We study the three-block Gibbs sampler for such models when the random effects are split into several components, such as random intercepts and slopes, each with its own scale and its own scale mixture of normals, when the tail parameters have priors on finite grids and are drawn jointly with the latent weights, and when the random-effects design is rank deficient, as when some subjects contribute a single observation. We give sufficient conditions for geometric ergodicity that attribute the rank deficiency to the components that cause it, and show that, under conditions on the gamma priors on the precision parameters, they hold for Student-t and slash random effects with individual weights, any grid of tail parameters and any design. The result extends to random-effect vectors whose coordinates share a weight, for subject-specific designs with known shape matrices. It justifies Monte Carlo standard errors for regression coefficients, log-scales and posterior probabilities of the tail parameters. Simulations show that the scale and the tail parameter can mix much more slowly than the regression coefficients, and an analysis of beta-HCG data illustrates the methods.

items.title: Data-Dependent Probability Estimation via Sample Amplification
items.summary: Can we estimate the probability of an event chosen after seeing the data, without using any fresh samples? Its empirical probability can be arbitrarily misleading, while learning the entire distribution to constant accuracy requires $Θ(d)$ samples on a domain of size $d$. We show that $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d})$ samples suffice for constant mean squared error, provided the rule choosing the event is known. More generally, our estimator handles arbitrary $[0,1]$-valued queries and runs in polynomial time given evaluation access to the rule. This sample complexity matches the known lower bound up to logarithmic factors and resolves the open question posed by Feldman, Kale, Raman, Talwar, and Tewari (arXiv:2610.41244). Our estimation framework relies on a new combination of sample amplification (arXiv:1904.12053 and arXiv:2201.04315) with distribution learning via online optimization. Our estimator achieves mean squared error $O(d^{3/4}/n)$ when $d\leq n$ and $\widetilde{O}(d^{1/4}/\sqrt{n})$ when $d>n$. We complement this with a lower bound of $Ω(\min\{1,\sqrt{d}/n\})$ on the mean squared error. Using our framework, we also design an efficient estimator for data-dependent queries on Gaussian distributions with unknown mean and identity covariance. Finally, we show that a smoothed variant of the problem is much (exponentially) easier. For discrete distributions, if the sample size is chosen uniformly from $\{n,\ldots,2n-1\}$, then $n=O(\log d)$ suffices for constant mean squared error.

items.title: Expressive Shallow Networks for Physics-Informed Learning: Why Curvature-Aware Optimization and FP64 Are Not Enough
items.summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often struggle with high-frequency and high-order partial differential equations (PDEs) due to optimization stiffness and spectral bias, despite possessing sufficient approximation capacity. Existing remedies, including modified feature representations, domain decomposition, higher floating-point precision, and curvature-aware optimizers, can improve convergence but largely act as workarounds for optimization difficulties arising from deep architectures rather than addressing their underlying source. We investigate Physics-Informed Shallow Universal Polynomial Networks (PI-SUPNs), which replace deep nonlinear compositions with learnable polynomial expansions, retaining high approximation capacity within a shallow computational graph. On a high-frequency Helmholtz benchmark, PI-SUPNs are the only architecture to successfully recover the solution, while all competing models fail even under FP64 precision and curvature-aware optimization. However, experiments on higher vibrational modes of a fourth-order Euler-Bernoulli beam reveal that architectural improvements alone are insufficient: accurate solutions require the combination of PI-SUPNs, FP64 precision, and curvature-aware optimization. Additionally, Allen-Cahn experiments show that PI-SUPNs achieve lower solution and derivative errors at reduced computational cost, with more favorable loss landscapes than competing architectures. We also establish quasi-local approximation properties and spline-based convergence bounds for SUPNs. Our results show that shallow network architectures are an important mechanism for improving physics-informed trainability, but accurate solutions to the most challenging PDEs can still require FP64 precision and curvature-aware optimization.

items.title: Cliques, Quasi-Cliques, and Bicliques in Random Graphs: Sampling and Algorithms
items.summary: We study the algorithmic problem of finding dense subgraphs - cliques, quasi-cliques, and bicliques - in Erdős-Rényi random graphs. While the extremal structure of cliques in $G(n,1/2)$ is well understood, efficiently locating large cliques remains a central algorithmic challenge. We introduce a new perspective on this problem: the classical Grimmett-McDiarmid greedy algorithm implicitly defines a near-uniform sampler over cliques of size $(1-o(1))\log n$. Building on this observation, we develop a sampling-based framework for finding larger cliques. In particular, for every $η>0$, we give an algorithm that finds a clique of size $(1+η)\log n$ in time $n^{(η^2/2+o(1))\log n}$ - the first smooth trade-off between clique size and running time in this regime, improving on the previously best-known running time of $n^{(1/2+o(1))\log n}$. We further show that improved sampling algorithms for cliques of size $(1+η)\log n$ translate into faster algorithms for finding a maximum clique. Beyond cliques, we give a deterministic algorithm that enumerates all maximum $γ$-quasi-cliques in $G(n,p)$ in time matching their count up to lower-order factors, and extend this to random bipartite graphs $G(n,n,p)$, establishing new concentration bounds for quasi-bicliques together with analogous enumeration algorithms. Finally, we study unbalanced bicliques in $G(n,n,p)$. For each $s \in [n]$, we obtain a concentration bound on the largest $t = t_{\max}(s)$ for which an $(s,t)$-biclique exists, and show that when $s = ω(\log n)$, a simple greedy algorithm finds an $(s,(1-o(1))t_{\max}(s))$-biclique in linear time with high probability - demonstrating that greedy is near-optimal in this regime.

items.title: Adaptive Precision Incomplete Matrix Factorization
items.summary: Incomplete factorizations are widely used to precondition Krylov subspace methods for solving large sparse linear systems. Recent work has explored computing approximate factorizations in low precision, but using only one uniformly low precision limits the achievable accuracy and can degrade the quality of the preconditioner. We propose adaptive precision incomplete factorization algorithms in which we store each entry of the factors in a precision chosen according to its magnitude and a target accuracy. We present a rounding error analysis showing that the adaptive precision threshold-based incomplete LU and incomplete Cholesky factorizations achieve a backward error of the order of the target accuracy. We also discuss how to incorporate pivoting and scaling and how to perform the triangular solves with the adaptive precision factors. Finally, we explain how the approach applies to memory-limited incomplete Cholesky factorizations by using the magnitude of the largest dropped entry as the target accuracy. Numerical experiments on a wide range of matrices from the SuiteSparse collection show that adaptive precision can substantially reduce the storage required by the factors without degrading the quality of the preconditioner and improve the storage-weighted iteration count and overall storage required compared with uniform 64-, 32-, and 16-bit factorizations.

items.title: Motion Mamba 2.0: Autoregressive Diffusion Mamba for Long-Horizon Humanoid Control
items.summary: Long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation is essential for interactive animation and humanoid robotics, where an agent must respond to changing instructions and spatial goals while moving. Existing autoregressive diffusion methods generate motion incrementally, but bounded attention caches limit access to distant history, while repeated denoising introduces substantial inference overhead. We present Motion Mamba 2.0, a Mamba-based root-body diffusion architecture that integrates local attention, resumable recurrent states, and persistent content memory (PCM) for long-horizon controllable motion generation. PCM transforms compressed motion history from Mamba recurrent states, together with state changes and text-conditioned features, into dynamically updated content slots accessible to local attention. To enable efficient inference, we further develop an execution scheme tailored to this architecture, combining CUDA Graph replay, fused kernels, and execution-flow simplification while preserving the canonical history update. Evaluations on retargeted HiPHI demonstrate accurate terminal control over rollouts of up to 39.52 s, while short-horizon comparisons on BONES Seed and retargeted HumanML3D show that the model also retains strong spatial control and text-motion matching. On an RTX 4090, the optimized execution reduces median complete-window latency from 1685.35 to 276.14 ms, achieving a median paired speedup of 6.138times while preserving identical outputs and committed states in the tested rollouts. Moreover, we conduct extensive real-world evaluation on the Unitree G1, demonstrating sequential text-guided action composition, expressive motion, and interactive locomotion through keyboard and mouse control.
