Closed-form benchmarks revised after public error reporting reach 92.5% verified validity, compared with 29.3% across six multi-step suites that nevertheless already supply 161 verified complex tasks. Rubric suites fail through mismatches between prompts and reference checklists, whereas execution harnesses add incomplete state assertions, shared-channel leaks and grading-time collisions. Across confirmed defects, 71.7% withhold credit from compliant solutions while 28.3% permit shortcut passes, indicating that raw leaderboard ceilings understate frontier capability on many practical tasks. Grading committed patches inside a fresh container cuts confirmed runtime bypasses from 14.7% in shared containers to 2.7% (a 5.5x drop, and 0% in read-only or static suites), showing how targeted maintenance restores existing benchmarks at low cost. As the initial milestone of the long-term Benchmarks' Last Exam initiative, this synthesis launches sustained expansion across wider benchmark coverage and deeper evaluation-quality dimensions so that pursuing leaderboard gains directly advances genuine model capability.

items.title: Automating Multi-View Quality Assessment of 3D Annotation Layouts
items.summary: Text labels provide descriptive information about elements in visual scenes. In 3D visualization, the arrangement of these labels and their connections to target locations forms an annotation layout. Assessing layout quality supports comparisons between alternative layouts. However, existing quality measures often focus on specific layout properties and may not fully reflect human judgments of overall quality. Moreover, a layout may appear clear from one viewpoint but suffer from occlusion or clutter from another. To address these issues, we propose a multi-view quality assessment method based on a multimodal large language model (MLLM). We fine-tune a compact MLLM using structured supervision from human ratings to predict a rating for each quality dimension in each view. These ratings are aggregated into view-level and sample-level quality scores. To support training and evaluation, we construct the Annotation Layouts with Quality Assessment (ALQA) dataset, containing 3,216 layout samples from 1,072 3D objects across 13 categories. Each layout is rendered from 5 predefined viewpoints, and each view is independently rated by 3 human raters across 5 quality dimensions. On ALQA, our method agrees more closely with human reference scores than the evaluated MLLM baselines, and a user study demonstrates strong agreement with human preferences in layout ranking.

items.title: Sketch2TikZ: Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning for Converting Hand-Drawn Sketches to Executable TikZ
items.summary: Automatic digitization of hand-drawn sketches into editable formats is crucial for modern document workflows and LaTeX integration. Converting sketches into executable TikZ code provides a structured representation of diagrams, but remains challenging due to noisy and ambiguous inputs, which hinder reliable interpretation and limit the effectiveness of token-level supervision for ensuring global diagram validity. To address these challenges, we propose Sketch2TikZ, a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes sketch-to-code generation via a sequential multi-reward strategy, combining Code-Structure ($\mathcal{R}_{cs}$), OCR ($\mathcal{R}_{ocr}$), CleanDIFT ($\mathcal{R}_{cd}$), and Self-Similarity ($\mathcal{R}_{ss}$) rewards to enforce textual, visual and structural correctness. We evaluate Sketch2TikZ on the SkeTikZ and FlowChart-3B benchmarks using metrics including compilation success rate (CSR), image similarity, code similarity, and character similarity. Our method achieves near-perfect compilation success and improves visual and textual alignment over strong open-source baselines, while remaining competitive with proprietary GPT-based vision-language models. Extensive ablations demonstrate that curriculum-based reward scheduling is critical for reducing reward interference, stabilizing training and mitigating proxy over-optimization. Overall, our results highlight the effectiveness of reference-aware, multi-objective reinforcement learning for structured diagram generation from noisy sketches.

items.title: Potential emergence in LLM agents: a statistical physics perspective
items.summary: There has been significant recent interest in understanding the behaviour of LLM agents from the perspective of human preferences or corpus statistics. In this paper we propose agent states as intermediate variables through which post-training can be measured and predicted. From a statistical physics perspective, we study the emergence of a global potential which governs the transition of state in LLM agent reasoning. We introduce a partition function to model the ideal KL-regularised transition distribution and track potential structure, mean reward and state entropy. We demonstrate our approach in two Qwen3.5-9B tasks: safety-test selection and physics-reasoning auditing. We observe that the potential structure strengthens during post-training as predicted from our framework, while joint changes in reward and state entropy provide consistency evidence. States thus provide a quantitative description of how post-training organises agent behaviour.

items.title: Circular Predictive Coding Unlocks Effective Depth
items.summary: Predictive coding networks perform credit assignment through an energy minimization process. Despite their ability to train models with arbitrary network topologies, they have mostly been used to train feedforward architectures to match the performance of backpropagation. However, they fail to do so when the models become too deep, because error signals become unstable or vanish as they travel through many layers. We address this limitation with circular networks, which get their depth directly from the energy minimization, rather than from stacking layers. Formally, we prove that convergence to an equilibrium of the energy functional of a circular predictive coding network approximates the fixed-point iteration process of a deep equilibrium model, showing that circularity alone suffices to unlock effective depth. Empirically, we show that circular models (i) outperform other predictive coding models of the same size on image classification tasks, matching the accuracy of state-of-the-art predictive coding ResNets and VGG networks despite having substantially fewer parameters; (ii) solve constraint satisfaction problems that require many steps of iterative reasoning, a task not feasible with feedforward models at all, reaching 99.3% test accuracy on Sudoku-hard via nested energy minimization loops; and (iii) scale to autoregressive language modeling by training a circular transformer on TinyStories and WikiText-103, before out of reach for predictive coding models. These results have direct implications for physical neural networks, where computational depth can be traded for recursion on a fixed-size circuit.

items.title: Quantum-Informed Regularized Poisson Learning for Graph-Based Semi-Supervised Classification
items.summary: We introduce IPQSSL, a quantum-informed regularized Poisson framework for graph-based semi-supervised classification under scarce labels. Local graph feature contexts are QR factorized, lifted to unitary encodings, and processed by a shared variational circuit whose measurements yield node wise diagonal weights that stabilize a symmetrized Poisson system. We establish positive definiteness of the symmetrized, regularized operator under explicit spectral conditions and derive a Hermitian, block encoding compatible formulation that separates the classical NISQ oriented implementation from a future fault-tolerant pathway. Across seven benchmarks spanning tabular data and a citation network, the effect of regularization is dataset- and budget-dependent: IPQSSL improves over the Poisson baselines on Iris and Wine at all but the single-label budget, reaching 0.946 accuracy on Iris at ten labels per class and at every budget on German Credit, where, however, all methods remain below the majority class rate. Original Poisson remains preferable on Breast Cancer, Heart Disease, Optdigits, and Cora, with the deficit narrowing as the label budget grows on the two largest graphs. Ablations attribute the gains to diagonal stabilization rather than variational training. The result is a resource transparent bridge between Poisson graph learning and quantum linear algebra, with an explicit empirical delineation of when diagonal regularization helps.

items.title: Tasklets: A Unit-Test Benchmark for Language Model Architectures
items.summary: We introduce Tasklets, a benchmark of small synthetic tasks for evaluating the computational capabilities of language model sequence-mixing layers. These tasks probe foundational capabilities such as recall, sequence manipulation, and state tracking. Such tasks are widely used in architecture research, but differences in task selection, formulation, and evaluation make comparisons across studies difficult. Tasklets brings these tasks together, organizing them by the capabilities they test and providing a shared setup for evaluating how different architectural layer types learn fundamental computations. We compare a broad range of layer types through controlled experiments with small models. Our task implementations and evaluation code support reproducible, low-cost testing of new architectural proposals: https://github.com/zaydzuhri/flame/tree/tasklets.

items.title: Adapting AI Weather Foundation Models to a Changing Climate
items.summary: AI weather foundation models learn from historical archives, while the climate distribution encountered during deployment continues to evolve. This growing model--climate mismatch motivates continual adaptation without repeated full-model retraining, but the structure of weather forecast errors determines how such adaptation should be performed. We develop an online adaptation framework that exploits two complementary error structures: geographically persistent biases and flow-dependent errors that vary with the atmospheric state. Analysis of Aurora-1.3B reveals strongly concentrated forecast-loss sensitivity in its decoder, motivating flow-dependent corrections within fixed low-dimensional sensitivity subspaces. A residual memory tracks persistent errors remaining after this correction, while a variable-wise online gate controls the contribution of the persistent component. We evaluate Aurora-1.3B using ERA5 from 1959--1968 for offline initialization and a strictly chronological 1969--2022 stream for online evaluation, with updates restricted to previously available verification targets. For 2-metre temperature, distributional departure from the historical reference, measured directly from ERA5, is associated with larger frozen-model errors and greater adaptation gains, while the adapted model maintains more stable skill across evaluation periods. Across 69 output fields and five lead times from 6 to 72 hours, our method reduces MSE and MAE by 6.90\% and 6.45\%, respectively, relative to $δ$-Adapter, the strongest of six online adaptation baselines.

items.title: PromptTTSD: Controllable Text to Spoken Dialogue Synthesis with Open-Ended Text Descriptions
items.summary: Spoken dialogue synthesis aims to generate multi-turn conversational speech from dialogue scripts while maintaining speaker consistency and contextual appropriateness. However, existing models largely lack fine-grained controllability, which is critical for capturing the dynamic, context-dependent style shifts in natural conversations. While prompt-based TTS has enabled such control for single-speaker speech, existing datasets heavily rely on predefined tags, which fundamentally limits their capacity to capture open-ended styles. To address this gap, we propose a scalable pipeline for extracting conversational speech from multi-narrator audiobooks, featuring an improved two-stage alignment algorithm to preserve dialogue continuity, paired with LLM-based extraction of style descriptions directly from narrative text. We release PromptDialog, a large-scale multi-speaker conversational speech dataset comprising 8,383 hours of Chinese speech and 120 hours of English speech, with open-ended style descriptions for 79% of utterances. We further introduce PromptTTSD, a spoken dialogue synthesis model built via a prompt-aware fine-tuning strategy that integrates style prompts into text-speech interleaved sequences. PromptTTSD is an open-source spoken dialogue synthesis model that supports both zero-shot voice cloning and natural language style control. Experiments demonstrate that PromptTTSD not only maintains strong fundamental synthesis capabilities but also achieves competitive open-ended style control compared with proprietary models, and substantially improves contextual appropriateness in multi-turn dialogues.

items.title: Block Search Conditioned on Features for Sequential Quantum Data Encoding
items.summary: Sequential quantum data encoding is addressed through the joint selection of input features and encoding blocks within a fixed quantum register. At each step, a new feature, a block of operations, its placement, and its rotation weights are selected together from training data, extending the incremental construction of Q-FLAIR. With direct-loss selection (RAW), nine to twelve features were retained in four qubits across five new Bars and Stripes datasets. Under the same final calibration, mean changes relative to the calibrated Q-FLAIR reference were +5.53 percentage points in balanced accuracy, -15.83% in binary cross-entropy (BCE), and +7.79% in area under the ROC curve (AUC). The prespecified success criterion was met in four of five datasets and for the mean paired differences. These results were obtained by comparing complete procedures under a common cap of 32 operations.

items.title: Leakage-Free Is Not Confounder-Free: What a Patient-Level Split Cannot Certify About a Medical Imaging Benchmark
items.summary: Patient-level splitting is the standard safeguard against subject leakage in medical imaging evaluation, but it cannot remove a confounder that every fold inherits: an acquisition variable aligned with the diagnosis across the whole cohort. We present a five-question audit of a candidate confounder: how well it predicts the diagnosis, whether it can be decoded from the images, whether diagnostic scores depend on it, whether the image adds predictive value beyond it and how much discrimination survives once it is controlled. We apply it to DMR-IR, the public dataset on which most machine-learning results in breast thermography rest. On 236 patients under a strict patient-disjoint protocol, the acquisition date alone predicts malignancy at AUROC 0.980, above the best of nine imaging arms (0.949), because benign and malignant patients were recruited in different years. The acquisition year is decodable from the pixels among patients who share a diagnosis, largely through a global thermal offset outside the breast, yet only one arm, the one pooling every frame of a visit, demonstrably carries it into its diagnostic score. No arm improves on the date on paired folds, and once the date is controlled, discrimination either collapses or survives only on comparisons the benchmark cannot attribute. The dataset contains only eight cross-label same-date pairs, from ten patients, which limits reliable evaluation within recorded acquisition-date groups. A second, independently acquired cohort, whose dominant channel is patient age, returns the same audit outcome from a different confounder. Mitigation may suppress such a confounder, but without cross-label acquisition support no evaluation on the benchmark can certify that what remains is pathology.

items.title: Do DeepONet Trunk-Basis Preconditioners Need Training?
items.summary: Trunk-basis (TB) preconditioners build the coarse space of a two-level Schwarz preconditioner from the trunk functions of a trained deep operator network (DeepONet), restricted to subdomains. Their effectiveness has been attributed to spectral bias since networks learn low frequencies first, complementing a smoother that removes the high-frequency error. Spectral bias, however, is a property of training, whereas a randomly initialized trunk with a smooth activation is already smooth. We therefore ask whether TB preconditioners need training. In one dimension, we prove that on each subdomain the span of untrained trunk functions is close to the space of low-degree polynomials under suitable nondegeneracy assumptions. Numerically, for the Poisson equation and three-dimensional linear elasticity with constant coefficients, untrained TB and piecewise polynomial coarse spaces of equal dimension yield close conjugate gradient iteration counts, while training with the standard \(\ell^2\) loss sometimes increases them. Training can improve iteration counts when high-contrast coefficients make the low-energy modes non-smooth, and if the loss measures the error in the energy norm. For the Poisson equation with contrast \(10^5\), energy-trained TB coarse spaces need fewer iterations than piecewise polynomials of equal dimension, whereas \(\ell^2\)-trained ones do not. For a topology-optimized elastic cantilever with contrast \(10^6\), the energy-trained TB space enriched with the rigid-body modes gives the fewest iterations at larger coarse dimensions. This suggests that for neural operator-based hybrid solvers, a network's inductive bias and training objective should match the solver.

items.title: PRISM: Validation-Free Online Batch Selection for LLM Fine-Tuning via Preconditioned Conic Ghost Matching
items.summary: Online batch selection lowers the cost of fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) by replacing each candidate batch with a smaller informative subset. Existing selectors typically depend on a held-out validation or proxy set, or else rely on Euclidean facility-location objectives over unpreconditioned gradients whose diameter-shifted similarities are distorted by heavy-tailed gradient norms and cross-layer anisotropy. We introduce PRISM (Preconditioned Ray-Isotropic Submodular Matching), a validation-free online batch selector that aligns candidate gradients in a factored second-moment metric and casts subset construction as conic facility location over positive ray projections. Computing the required pairwise geometry through factored preconditioned ghost inner products avoids materializing per-example parameter gradients, while the conic objective remains normalized, nonnegative, and monotone submodular---guaranteeing a $(1-1/e)$ greedy approximation whose additive error scales with total batch gradient energy rather than the worst-case outlier diameter. Assigning each candidate to its best-aligned selected ray induces closed-form radial projection weights that automatically shrink orthogonal or noisy examples toward zero. We derive a nonconvex convergence bound showing that optimization error is governed directly by the conic representation cost. Across four LLM fine-tuning configurations spanning 1.5B to 8B parameters, PRISM outperforms full-batch training, Euclidean facility location, and zeroth-order selectors, and rivals or surpasses validation-guided baselines without held-out data.

items.title: Unlocking Heterogeneous Accelerator Flexibility in AI Data Centers: Sizing and Workload Allocation
items.summary: AI data centers are an emerging electricity demand, but limited local grid capacity could delay their connection and expansion. While existing operational strategies consider spatio-temporal workload flexibility, few studies address the strategic sizing and allocation of diverse accelerator archetypes with different capital and energy-efficiency trade-offs. This paper unlocks the flexibility potential of heterogeneous accelerators by jointly sizing and allocating different AI workloads (training, delay-tolerant batch work, and online inference requests) across sites and hours to meet the time-varying grid constraint at minimum cost. Workload-specific throughput and energy coefficients link these decisions to facility power. In a representative two-site case, heterogeneous sizing reduces daily cost by 6.5% relative to spatio-temporal scheduling with fixed capacity. When evaluated using workload-specific performance, a capacity design based on workload-averaged hardware coefficients costs 7.7% more than the proposed design. The proposed design also eliminates the envelope violations of an unconstrained design at a 0.25\% daily cost increase. These results show how hardware heterogeneity and workload flexibility jointly shape economical, grid-compliant capacity plans.

items.title: Minimax-Optimal Small-Loss Regret in Online Convex Optimization and Applications to Contextual Search and Online Inverse Optimization
items.summary: We give small-loss regret bounds for online convex optimization (OCO), using one subgradient per round. Let $Δ_T^\star$ denote the cumulative loss of the best fixed decision in hindsight, measured relative to the per-round minima. Our algorithm achieves the regret bound $O(1+\sqrt{Δ_T^\star})$ without knowing $Δ_T^\star$, up to domain and gradient-scale factors. The bound is minimax optimal, including its domain dependence, on $\ell_p$ balls for every $1\le p\le\infty$. No smoothness or condition bounding gradient norms by loss values is assumed, and neither loss values nor the time horizon are needed. Algorithmically, we extend the metric-update revocation of Gupta et al. (2026), originally developed for online inverse optimization, to general OCO using the follow-the-regularized-leader framework and a mixture of multiple base learners. We also apply our algorithm to contextual search and online inverse optimization. In $d$-dimensional contextual search with comparison flips of unknown bias $κ>0$, we obtain minimax expected cumulative absolute error $Θ(\sqrt{d}/κ^2)$ under Euclidean normalization using polynomially many arithmetic operations, resolving an open question of Liu et al. (2021). For online inverse optimization with the Euclidean unit-ball utility domain, our algorithm bounds the regret relative to observed actions by $O(\sqrt{d}+d^{1/4}\sqrt{D_T})$, where $D_T$ is their cumulative suboptimality; this matches the regret rate of Gupta et al. (2026) when $D_T=0$. Our guarantee extends to other utility domains; for example, on the probability simplex, the bound improves to $O(\log(d+1)+\sqrt{D_T\log(d+1)})$.

items.title: WEIR: Watershed Exploration and Drift-Aware Prefix Shrinkage for Multi-Turn Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Multi-turn language model agents often receive only a single binary reward at the end of a long interaction trajectory, making it difficult to separate decisive decisions from routine steps or estimate accurate intermediate values. Prefix-tree methods improve sample efficiency by merging trajectories that share action histories, yet two structural flaws remain: naive pooling mixes stale off-policy outcomes into critic targets with fixed weights, and uniform or entropy-driven branching wastes continuations on dead-end states whose outcome is already settled. We introduce WEIR (Watershed Exploration and Intrinsic-Drift Shrinkage), an actor-critic reinforcement learning framework grounded in a Doob turn-variance conservation identity. WEIR maintains a cross-iteration canonical action-prefix tree with exponentially discounted visit counts and trains a prefix-conditioned critic toward a minimax drift-aware shrinkage target that adapts from single-trajectory returns at rare nodes to pooled empirical means at dense nodes. Using the same pre-update critic, WEIR allocates rollout budgets across tasks via Neyman stratification $B_q \propto \sqrt{\hat{p}_q(1-\hat{p}_q)}$ and directs within-task branches to watershed forks where high survival-headroom uncertainty coincides with steep value cliffs. Across four multi-hop QA benchmarks, ALFWorld, and WebShop on Qwen2.5-3B/7B-Instruct, WEIR achieves $32.18\%$ and $37.85\%$ average QA exact match and $84.83\%$ and $87.81\%$ ALFWorld success rates, outperforming CAPO by $1.50$--$3.74$ points while generating $28$--$29\%$ fewer rollout tokens than chain sampling.

items.title: TITAN: DRL-Based Dynamic Scheduling and Resource Allocation for Tactile Internet
items.summary: Tactile Internet (TI) applications require ultra-reliable, low-latency tactile communication alongside video traffic. However, tactile Quality of Service (QoS) requirements vary with the interaction context, making fixed resource allocation inefficient. In this paper, we propose TITAN (Two-Timescale Integrated Tactile Internet over 5G Access Networks), a dynamic scheduling and resource allocation (SRA) scheme. TITAN receives time-varying tactile QoS profiles from a higher-layer module and adapts SRA to the current QoS profile and network state. A deep reinforcement learning-based agent splits the available network bandwidth between tactile and video streams at a slow timescale, while a fast-timescale scheduler allocates resource blocks among active user equipment. Through simulations, we show that TITAN simultaneously satisfies both tactile and video QoS targets and achieves a performance gain of 7.64 percentage points (pp) in the joint satisfaction rate over the best-performing static SRA baseline.

items.title: Can Language Models See the Circuit in Pixelated RFIC Passives?
items.summary: The emergence of inverse-designed, pixelated passives for microwave and millimeter-wave applications has been a major development in the field of RFIC design. These devices, which appear to be QR-code-like in structure, exist in a generalizable, high-dimensional design space that includes conventional passive topologies. However, these structures are naturally unintuitive for designers, and failures or deviations in performance are difficult to debug. In this work, we ask whether a frontier language model can understand, predict, and edit the responses and layout structure of pixelated passives. The agent, run with all tools disabled, is first asked to read layouts on 18x18 and 27x27 tile grids and, in a single reply, predict the input impedance and loss of the structure from 20-100 GHz. On eight GA-synthesized layouts and five random fills, the predicted Smith-chart locus follows full-wave simulation results closely, with a systematic shift that places features about 16% lower in frequency than EM. On multipath loop structures it identifies notches successfully but shows a smaller frequency bias, about half that of an ideal transmission-line model that ignores bends. The agent is then asked to debug seven designs that fail their specification, and given a budget of five EM simulations and at most twelve changed tiles, it is able to improve all seven and bring five designs within specification. These experiments suggest language models can serve as an interpretability and debugging tool for traditionally non-intuitive inverse-designed passives.

items.title: Bringing AI Assistance to the Beznau Nuclear Power Plant: A Hierarchical System of LLM Agents for Reactor Monitoring
items.summary: Beznau Unit 1 in Switzerland, in operation since 1969, is the most experienced nuclear reactor still running worldwide. Five decades of incremental modernization have left its monitoring systems, alarm logs, variable catalogs, technical specifications and investigation reports in separate silos that were never designed to be queried together. As a result, investigating a core instrumentation anomaly means slow, manual gathering of knowledge scattered across databases, documents, and experienced colleagues. We present a hierarchical multi-agent assistant built on large language models (LLMs) to support these investigations and reduce the need for tedious manual searches in SAP systems. An orchestrating agent breaks down an engineer's question and hands the parts to specialized sub-agents, each with read-only access to one source. Domain expertise is written as natural-language procedures that plant engineers can read, review and revise. The system is strictly advisory, with every answer traced back to its sources. We also report organizational lessons from introducing agentic AI into a culture built on safety, traceability and conservative change. Beyond the technical architecture, the Beznau case study examines how an assistant can be introduced into a setting where evidence must be traceable, changes carefully reviewed, and operational decisions retained by plant personnel, paving the way for the responsible use of agentic AI in industrial plant monitoring.

items.title: Vega-Fafnir: Is Greedy Decoding the Same Decoding? Where Rounding Noise in Speculative Verification Comes From and What Removing It Costs
items.summary: Serving engines treat the ways of running a greedy language model as interchangeable: cached or not, padded or not, alone or batched, one token or several verified at once (speculative decoding). In finite precision they round differently. We measure how often the greedy text of Qwen3-0.6B (bfloat16, 128 new tokens, GSM8K and ARC prompts) differs from a reference that decodes one token per pass. Verifying 4 guessed tokens per pass changes 60% of 150 prompts and padding changes 68%; every first divergence has a top-1 minus top-2 logit gap of 0.375 or less. A split of the noise shows that cache entries written by multi-token passes are about as noisy as the multi-token pass itself. A margin gate (fall back to one token when the gap is below a bound calibrated on separate GSM8K prompts) whose fallback reads that cache does not help: 58 of 100 prompts differ, against 61 of 100 for plain verification. Rebuilding the cache with one-token passes leaves 0 of 100 different but costs 7.2 model passes per token, against 1.0 for the reference. Fixed-width decoding makes drafted and plain decoding identical (0 of 100 prompts differ) at 0.75 passes per token. On shifted MMLU and HellaSwag prompts the rebuild gate leaves 0 of 60 different, plain verification 48 of 60. On 138 further and shifted prompts the bound was exceeded at 0.6% of positions and missed 0 of 309 flips. One GPU, one drafter, small models.

items.title: Altair-Nidhogg: Which Model-Merging Theories Hold for a One-Pass Decision Encoder? Soups, Task Arithmetic, TIES and DARE Against Joint Training and Prediction Ensembling
items.summary: Laya is a small model that answers a multiple-choice question in one pass: each option has a name and a written description. A new skill costs a training run, so we test whether published recipes for merging fine-tuned models (weight averaging, task arithmetic, TIES, DARE) work for it, and whether the theories behind them hold. All 156 models start from one released checkpoint: four plain fine-tunes, five specialists (each adds one kind of training row), joint fine-tunes on all rows, and prediction ensembles. Items are held-out, synthetic and LLM-labelled. In-family, each skill is scored on new items of its own kind, and "kept" is the share of a specialist's gain over the plain fine-tune. Averaging four specialists keeps 52% [38, 64] with +1.7 points of general accuracy; adding the full vectors keeps 42% [3, 63] with -9.0; TIES, which trims and resolves sign conflicts, keeps 64% [50, 76] with +1.5; joint fine-tunes, which see all the rows, keep 120% [104, 162] and 116% [104, 149]. DARE does not repair the full sum (-0.4 points), and ensembles of the models' predictions keep 26% to 54% depending on how they are combined. Swapping the seed of one specialist moves the average by up to 8 points (23 for the full sum). Of 10 predictions fixed in advance, 1 held, 1 held partly, 7 failed and 1 could not be tested. Out-of-family (benchmark questions, code-mixed tickets), the four-way average, joint models and ensemble stay within 2.6 points of the plain fine-tune, but full-vector sums lose up to 7.7. Labels are LLM-made, data synthetic, one base model.

items.title: GameScrub: Learning HUD Removal from Real Gameplay with Recovered Targets
items.summary: Gameplay videos are a rich source of experience for learning virtual-world dynamics, yet their frames contain heads-up displays (HUDs) that follow interface rules rather than scene dynamics. Removing HUDs would make this footage directly usable for learning world dynamics. However, training a removal model requires paired clips with and without HUDs, whereas real recordings contain only HUD-overlaid footage. Existing work synthesizes pairs by compositing HUD graphics onto HUD-free footage, requiring a separately curated clean corpus and producing HUDs that only approximate real ones. Models trained on such pairs leave 40 to 50% of real HUD elements untouched. We instead recover pseudo-clean targets directly from real recordings by inpainting HUD regions with a pretrained video diffusion model. Preventing HUD traces from leaking into recovered targets is challenging because latent video autoencoders mix information across mask boundaries. Our training-free recovery pipeline, GameScrub-Data, pre-fills HUD regions with flow-guided background estimates before encoding, excludes HUDs from scene conditioning, and confines restoration to masked regions through pixel-space compositing. The resulting pairs train GameScrub, a video diffusion removal model that handles diverse HUDs without inference-time masks or clean reference images. On the in-the-wild Game2World benchmark, GameScrub achieves an artifact-adjusted removal score of 71.95, compared with 57.86 for the strongest reference-free GameCleaner configuration, and removes 90.06% of annotated HUD elements versus 59.07%. These results demonstrate that real recordings with recovered targets can support effective HUD removal, advancing HUD-free gameplay data for world models and controllable video generation.

items.title: Alliance Rupture and Repair in Simulating Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Dialogues
items.summary: In cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), routine work can strain the client-counselor working alliance, and the counselor must then notice the rupture, repair it, and adapt the work that follows. Existing CBT simulators model client resistance and follow structured treatment plans, but rarely track alliance state or allow counselors to repair ruptures over multiple turns and revise their plans accordingly. We present ALLY, a simulation framework that brings alliance rupture, repair, and replanning into ongoing CBT dialogue. Each client has a hidden alliance state that governs how openly the client engages. Like a real counselor, the counselor agent sees only the dialogue. It must notice when the client pulls back or pushes against the work, repair the rupture, and replan the rest of the session around what it has learned. Automatic evaluation shows that ALLY's counselors are closer to real CBT counselors than those of existing public synthetic datasets in strategy flow and emotional dynamics, and that ALLY is rated highest overall in counseling quality (CTRS) and interpersonal skill (FIS-T). An expert evaluation with 20 licensed therapists also finds the simulated ruptures plausible and the repairs and replanning largely appropriate.

items.title: On the Limits of Observability for Evaluating Coverage in Machine Unlearning
items.summary: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of any requested subset of training data while preserving utility on the remaining data. Empirical evaluations measure predictive accuracy and infer training-set membership (MIAs) from model outputs or intermediate activations. However, by focusing on selected forget sets, these evaluations can overlook Coverage, the range of requests a method can fulfill. To assess this coverage, we first conduct a stress test of observability with 502 retrained models, finding that hidden embeddings reveal known deletions missed in predictions. To characterize capacity limits on coverage, we show that distinguishing all $n$ singleton deletions with linear scores can require a shared representation of rank $Ω(\log n)$. We further extend the bound to arbitrary subsets and show when partial deletion can appear complete. Building on this analysis, we propose CEO, a framework for evaluating unlearning coverage under limited observability. Its compositional color-shape benchmark makes forgetting and retained utility measurable from the full output distribution and provides a leave-one-out retraining oracle for each target. From a fixed number of oracle observables, we estimate empirical target coverage, the fraction of targets reliably flagged when deleted and rarely flagged under any other deletions. To recover missed deletions, CEO further expands each observable representation into high-dimensional activation space with the frozen encoder of a SAE trained on the original model. Extensive experiments of 20 baselines shows that even on this simple synthetic task, only retraining from scratch covers all deletion targets.

items.title: When Visually Rich Documents Meet Multi-Vector Retrieval for Region-level Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary: Visually rich documents (VRDs) convey knowledge through textual, visual, and layout information that text-centric Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Text-RAG) struggles to fully exploit. Recent Vision-RAG approaches enable retrieval and generation directly from document images, retaining this multimodal information. However, earlier Vision-RAG methods commonly adopt coarse retrieval representations and full-page visual contexts, which can obscure local evidence and introduce substantial redundancy and computational overhead. To address these challenges, we propose MV-VisRAG, a region-level Vision-RAG framework that uses semantically complete regions for both document representation and visual augmentation. Specifically, MV-VisRAG first constructs these regions through a ContentAdaptive Regionalization module. It then encodes them into local region vectors and a page-level global vector using a VLM-based retriever trained through multimodal reconstruction pretraining and retrieval fine-tuning. With this compact multi-vector representation, MV-VisRAG performs late-interaction retrieval and estimates region contributions from the resulting matching scores. These contributions guide the selection of relevant regions, which are then rearranged into a compact visual context for generation. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate retrieval and generation gains over corresponding baselines, while region-level augmentation substantially reduces visual tokens and computational cost. Our code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xandery-geek/MV-VisRAG.

items.title: From Tokens to Pixels: Training-Free Guided Upsampling of Frozen CARL Features for Hyperspectral Imaging
items.summary: Camera-agnostic foundation models such as CARL map spectral images from arbitrary sensors into a shared feature space, but deliver their features only on a token grid at one eighth of the input resolution. The usual bilinear interpolation blurs material boundaries over about one token and rounds off corners. We investigate how much spatial accuracy image-guided upsampling recovers for frozen CARL features without training the encoder or the upsampler. We compare joint bilateral upsampling (JBU), a guided filter and the pretrained AnyUp, each with the hyperspectral image or an RGB rendering as the guide. A hyperspectral ColorChecker dataset acquired specifically for this study, with model-independent reference geometry measured to sub-pixel precision, serves as the evaluation benchmark. JBU with the hyperspectral guide raises the Boundary IoU from 13 to 67 % and reduces the effective edge width of the features from 38 to 4 px, close to the resolution of the raw spectra. The effect occurs in all 24 patches of the ColorChecker and replicates on an additional recording. On placenta and oral cavity images, the feature edges also become markedly qualitatively sharper. For sharp, high-contrast boundaries, JBU is the most accurate and most economical method. On tissue with softer transitions, the pretrained AnyUp yields qualitatively sharper contours. An analysis of 78 simulated band configurations shows that the gain persists in every configuration as long as the head matches the configuration. Image-guided upsampling is thus a simple, training-free step for applications that use CARL frozen with linear heads.

items.title: Open CDLM: A Benchmark and Library for Continuous Diffusion Language Models
items.summary: Reliable comparisons of continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) require evaluating both model fit and the distribution of generated text. Two common practices leave this goal only partially addressed. Likelihood-based evaluation often reports a variational upper bound on discrete negative log-likelihood, whose slack can confound comparisons. Generated-sample-based evaluation commonly combines generative perplexity with within-sequence unigram entropy; both scores can remain favorable even when a sampler produces the same text on every draw. We introduce \textbf{Open CDLM}, a benchmark for evaluating CDLMs and their samplers, and describe the design of an accompanying open-source library to support reproducible comparisons. For likelihood-based evaluation, we clarify which comparisons of model fit are supported by reported perplexity bounds and how those conclusions depend on the evaluation procedure. For sample-based evaluation, we use \textit{Kernel Text Discrepancy} (\textbf{KTD}) to compare collections of generated and real texts, alongside diagnostics for diversity, validity, and coverage. In controlled OpenWebText experiments, replacing a collection of texts with copies of a single selected passage improves both conventional generation scores. MAUVE detects the resulting collapse, and its response to other perturbations depends on the text representation and the type of perturbation. This work marks the beginning of Open CDLM as an open-source project for CDLM research. We will maintain and extend the library over time and welcome contributions from the community.

items.title: Fix Where It Fails: Root-Cause-Guided Agentic Harness Optimization for Scene Graph Generation
items.summary: Scene graph generation (SGG) aims to detect objects in an image and predict the relationships between them. The standard PredCls, SGCls, and SGDet settings show how much performance drops without ground-truth boxes and labels, but not where or why a model fails. Knowing this would allow fixing a model where it fails, without retraining. We propose RoHa-SGG (Root-cause-guided Harness optimization for SGG), which extends agentic harness optimization to SGG. It optimizes the harness, the inference code around a frozen SGG model. RoHa-SGG has two main LLM agents. A root-cause analysis (RCA) agent finds the components where the model fails and diagnoses why, and a proposer agent searches for a harness that fixes these causes. We evaluate RoHa-SGG on Visual Genome and PSG with representative two-stage, one-stage, and multimodal-LLM SGG models. The analysis shows that the components where ground-truth triplets are lost differ across models and datasets. RoHa-SGG improves every metric on all five model-dataset combinations. Graph-constrained R@100 and mR@100 rise by up to 15.8 and 26.4 points for the multimodal LLM and by up to 3.6 and 10.1 points for the two-stage and one-stage models. With root-cause guidance, the harness search reaches the final score of an unguided search up to three times faster.

items.title: PaMuk-Bench: A Parallel Multilingual Multitask Benchmark for Vision-Language Tasks
items.summary: While vision-language models (VLMs) currently obtain notable results for highly-studied languages, e.g. English, they exhibit significant performance drops in certain low-resource languages, especially due to the lack of annotated datasets. To this end, we propose PaMuk-Bench, a novel parallel multilingual multitask benchmark for vision-language tasks. Our benchmark includes a set of over 10K curated English prompts that are translated into six languages: Arabic, Danish, French, Hindi, Italian, Romanian. Parallel translations, which are obtained via a semi-automatic process, along with accompanying generated and retrieved images enable the comparative development and evaluation of VLMs across a wide range of tasks: text-to-image generation, image captioning, content-based image retrieval, image generation difficulty estimation, image retrieval difficulty estimation. We empirically show that zero-shot English and multilingual pre-trained VLMs compare consistently worse than their fine-tuned counterparts, confirming that PaMuk-Bench is a valuable resource that can drastically reduce the language gap across a variety of VLM architectures and tasks. PaMuk-Bench is available at https://github.com/ghesil/pamuk_bench.

items.title: EchoAlign: Echocardiography foundation model with multilevel report alignment
items.summary: Echocardiography assesses the structure and function of the heart. Cardiologists read each study across several standard views and report the findings visible in those views by cardiac structure. AI foundation models can learn to analyze these studies from clinical reports, reducing annotation burden and supporting clinical interpretation. However, existing models are trained by pairing each video with the full clinical report, including structures and findings its view does not show. This mismatch lets a model associate a finding with incidental or spurious signals rather than its visual evidence, which limits accuracy, anatomical grounding and clinical trust. Here we introduce EchoAlign, a vision-language foundation model developed on 2.87 million echocardiographic videos and images from 159 clinical centers. EchoAlign aligns each cardiac structure, video and study with its report text, and a visibility matrix restricts supervision to the views that actually depict each structure. We compare it with five public foundation models on 0.47 million test videos across ten unseen external datasets from more than 25 clinical centers. EchoAlign achieves the highest mean AUROC of 0.890 (95% CI, 0.881 to 0.897) for classification and the highest mean quadratic weighted kappa of 0.530 (95% CI, 0.511 to 0.544) for severity grading. Across 62 clinical findings, EchoAlign provides one model that detects findings, grades their severity, estimates measurements and segments cardiac structures.

items.title: PhiJEPA: Denoising Latent Predictions for Visual Representation Learning
items.summary: Can a predictor trained to infer hidden image regions still help a world model plan when part of an object disappears from view and the visible context is blurred? We introduce PhiJEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture that adapts PhiNet's two-stage prediction to masked Transformers. From sparse, photometrically corrupted context, a Transformer block predicts hidden tokens of an independently corrupted teacher view. A token-wise MLP then maps these predictions to clean teacher tokens. Controlled ablations show that the combined objective improves dense features over the tested one-stage alternatives. Pre-trained on ImageNet-1K with $5.6\times10^{19}$ training FLOPs, PhiJEPA achieves 69.3 mIoU on linear PASCAL VOC segmentation, exceeding the evaluated I-JEPA and DSeq-JEPA checkpoints in segmentation accuracy, with 25\% fewer training FLOPs than I-JEPA. It also improves hidden-region segmentation over Simple I-JEPA (49.1 vs.\ 44.3 mIoU). As an application, we use the frozen encoder in DINO-WM on PushT, and reuse the pre-training predictor, which JEPAs usually discard, to complete occluded tokens without fine-tuning. In open-loop planning with simultaneous object occlusion and Gaussian blur ($σ=2$ pixels), predictor completion raises success from 33\% to 65\%, compared with 25\% for Simple I-JEPA with its predictor and 40\% for iBOT with pixel inpainting. Together, these results support two-stage latent prediction as an efficient approach to learning visual representations that remain useful under photometric degradation and support completion under partial observation.

items.title: Beyond a Single Human Demonstration: Learning from Scored Trajectory Alternatives for End-to-End Driving
items.summary: Human driving logs record only one trajectory per scene, leaving other feasible driving choices without explicit trajectory targets or quality labels. This limits supervision for end-to-end planners that generate and refine multiple candidate trajectories. Meanwhile, conditioning refinement on a large vision-language model adds substantial online inference cost. We propose DriveSTA, which extends autoregressive proposal generation and proposal-conditioned residual flow refinement with scored trajectory alternatives. For each training scene, we generate alternatives offline through smooth deformations of the recorded trajectory and evaluate their simulated execution against logged traffic. Diverse, high-quality alternatives supervise distinct proposals and define residual targets for quality-guided denoising, while candidates spanning the full score range train a scorer to assess driving quality. A shared joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), adapted through masked video-feature prediction, encodes observed frames once and provides temporal context for both refinement and scoring. On NAVSIM v1 Navtest, DriveSTA ranks first among the compared planners trained on NAVSIM data alone. With expanded training data, DriveSTA-Scale achieves state-of-the-art results among the compared methods on Navtest and closed-loop HUGSIM, while reducing mean planner forward-pass latency by 73% relative to ChainFlow-VLA in matched evaluations.

items.title: Deep Cross-Division Network for Product-and-Ratio Feature Interactions in Industrial Ranking
items.summary: Learning effective feature interactions is essential for industrial recommender systems. DCN and DCNv2 efficiently automate polynomial feature crossing. However, their cross layers construct interactions using only non-negative integer powers of the input features, with the maximum degree controlled by network depth. Consequently, they cannot directly represent the reciprocal terms required for ratios, rates, and normalized counts unless such features are explicitly provided as inputs. We introduce DCDN, a Deep Cross-Division Network that augments a DCNv2-style cross layer with a division branch. DCDN jointly learns product, ratio, and mixed product-ratio interactions. We characterize the representable interactions as multivariate Laurent polynomials and show that a $K$-layer DCDN generates Laurent monomials of $\ell_1$-order up to $K+1$, with signed degree between $-K$ and $K+1$. We evaluate DCDN against a production-optimized neural-ranking baseline built around DCNv2 and supplied with manually engineered ratio features. Replacing the DCNv2 block with DCDN allowed us to eliminate the entire class of manually engineered ratio features from the model input, reducing the number of input features by $40.1\%$. DCDN is deployed in the production ranking stack of a major short-video service. In a live A/B test on this service, DCDN increased likes by $3.25\%$, shares by $16.26\%$, total view time (TVT) by $0.33\%$, and clicks to open fullscreen by $0.38\%$; all changes were statistically significant. The number of shown videos decreased slightly ($-0.24\%$). These results demonstrate that DCDN can improve user engagement while eliminating reliance on manually engineered ratio features. Our code is publicly released at https://github.com/rw404/DCDN.

items.title: PGS-PCQA: Perceptually Gated Synthetic Supervision for No-Reference Point Cloud Quality Assessment
items.summary: Existing no-reference point cloud quality assessment (NR-PCQA) methods perform well within individual datasets but generalize poorly across datasets. We identify insufficient distortion coverage in training data as a key cause: on unseen distortion types, models rank severity levels near chance or even in reverse. We propose perceptually gated synthetic supervision for no-reference point cloud quality assessment (PGS-PCQA), an NR-PCQA model trained with synthetic distortion ranking. It builds a synthetic distortion bank from source reference point clouds and uses within-type severity ranking as supervision in addition to the source mean opinion scores (MOS), requiring no subjective scores for the synthetic samples. Since higher severity does not always mean lower perceived quality, a perceptual gate softens the ranking targets of pairs with small perceptual differences in rendered views. The synthetic supervision is used only during training and needs no target-domain data. In a single training run on SJTU-PCQA, PGS-PCQA achieves Spearman rank correlation coefficients (SRCCs) of 0.709 on WPC and 0.751 on BASICS. The corresponding published DSP-PCQA scores are 0.595 and 0.723. Under reference-disjoint cross-validation, PGS-PCQA achieves SRCCs of 0.955 on SJTU-PCQA, 0.934 on WPC, 0.906 on BASICS, and 0.791 on LS-PCQA Part I. In the exclusion experiment, the reported scores for the reduced synthetic bank represent 58-65% of the full-bank SRCC gain relative to training without the bank. Code is available at https://github.com/Fan-QY/PGS-PCQA.

items.title: Breaking the Barrier of Hard Samples: A Data-Centric Approach to Synthetic Data for Medical Tasks
items.summary: Data scarcity and quality issues remain significant barriers to developing robust predictive models in medical research. Traditional reliance on real-world data often leads to biased models with poor generalizability across diverse patient populations. Synthetic data generation has emerged as a promising solution, yet challenges related to these samples' representativeness and effective utilization persist. This paper introduces Profile2Gen, a novel data-centric framework designed to guide the generation and refinement of synthetic data, focusing on addressing hard-to-learn samples in regression tasks. We conducted approximately 18,000 experiments to validate its effectiveness across six medical datasets, utilizing seven state-of-the-art generative models. Results demonstrate that refined synthetic samples can reduce predictive errors and enhance model reliability. Additionally, we generalize the DataIQ framework to support regression tasks, enabling its application in broader contexts. Statistical analyses confirm that our approach achieves equal or superior performance compared to models trained exclusively on real data.

items.title: Self-Supervised Continuous-Time Depth Learning and Ego-Motion Estimation from Asynchronous Events
items.summary: Event cameras register brightness changes pixel by pixel with microsecond precision, whereas the dense depth that could supervise them is costly to acquire and exists only at isolated instants. Condensing the stream into frames eases learning, but at the expense of the very timing that sets event sensing apart. We propose a self-supervised approach in which each event is assigned its own depth in continuous time, and the camera motion is recovered from the same observations. Supervision arises from geometry: lifted into 3D by its predicted depth and displaced by the camera motion at the instant it fired, an event should coincide with others produced by the same edge, so any misalignment exposes an error in depth or motion. Differentiable rendering then turns these per-event estimates into dense depth maps at target times within each window, faithful to the events behind them. On MVSEC, the approach outperforms prior event-only self-supervised methods in most sequences and depth ranges, with the widest margins at night, and recovers camera rotation more accurately than an earlier unsupervised event-based method. Ablations isolate the roles of local spatiotemporal context, the temporal backbone, and the alignment objective. These results position motion-compensated event alignment as a principled source of supervision for continuous-time depth and ego-motion estimation.

items.title: How Many Bytes Has a BPE Model Seen? Estimating Byte-Token Exposure in Pretraining from Corpus Statistics and Embedding Norms
items.summary: Byte-level BPE vocabularies retain 256 single-byte fallback tokens. When converting such a model into a pure byte-level model, these tokens provide the starting embeddings. How much training have they received? We estimate byte-token exposure in Qwen3.8 using two independent routes. First, we tokenize 540 MB of public corpora covering 40 domains and 33 languages, then combine per-domain token shares with assumed pretraining mixtures. Single-byte tokens account for 13 to 36% of tokens, mostly ASCII; genuine UTF-8 fallback bytes (0x80-0xFF) account for 0.15 to 0.27% under mainstream mixtures, or about 2 billion occurrences per trillion pretraining tokens. Fallback rates vary by four orders of magnitude across languages, reflecting how well each script is covered by the vocabulary. Second, we analyze embedding and output-matrix row norms for four open models, using untrained padding rows as a zero-exposure baseline and ordinary tokens with known frequencies for calibration. In all four models, the 13 bytes that cannot occur in valid UTF-8 remain at initialization, while every legal high byte lies in a high-frequency band. For Qwen3.8, the norm-based estimate agrees with the corpus estimate within a factor of four. The norm-frequency relation eventually folds, so inversion is useful only as a model-specific, order-of-magnitude estimate. No private data were used.

items.title: The Assistant Persona Differs Across Languages in Activation Space
items.summary: Large language models behave differently across languages, and are noticeably less safe in lower-resource languages. This gap is well established behaviorally, but not mechanistically. Directions in activation space, including the assistant persona direction, are almost always extracted from English and assumed to generalize across languages. We extract the assistant persona direction in 31 languages in Qwen3-32B, and find that the resulting axes differ substantially: their cosine similarity to the English axis ranges from 0.378 to 0.911. Moreover, each language's assistant persona direction and its magnitude are correlated with the language's resource level. We also find that the model's default assistant state is farther from the helpful assistant pole in lower-resource languages. Finally, steering against a language's own axis amplifies persona-based jailbreak more than steering against the English axis. These results indicate that the model does not carry a single assistant representation across languages. More broadly, the assistant persona may need to be an explicit target of multilingual alignment.

items.title: Solar-Conditioned Flow Matching for Multitemporal Aerial Visible-to-Infrared Image Translation
items.summary: Aerial visible-to-infrared (V2IR) image translation provides scalable thermal data across the full diurnal cycle. However, existing methods predominantly learn a static mapping within narrow acquisition windows. As the thermal state evolves throughout the day, a single visible image may correspond to multiple plausible IR appearances, making V2IR translation an inherently multitemporal task. This letter proposes solar-conditioned latent flow matching (Solar-Flow), which upgrades aerial V2IR translation from static mapping to multitemporal generation. First, we design three computable physical factors, namely the solar elevation, the thermal phase clock (TPC), and the flight altitude. The TPC counts the elapsed heating and cooling hours on a continuous 24-hour axis anchored at sunrise, so the thermal state stays well defined even at hours without training samples. Second, we inject the condition into every Transformer block of a pretrained flow matching generator through adaptive layer normalization. This design preserves translation fidelity and enables multitemporal generation. Finally, we construct a paired aerial V2IR dataset covering 14 hour groups. Solar-Flow achieves multitemporal generation on this dataset, where a single visible image is translated into plausible IR images at multiple times of day, even at hours that were never seen in training.

items.title: Turnout: Adaptive Attention Switching for Efficient Reasoning
items.summary: Post-hoc transformer linearization replaces the key-value cache of full attention, which grows linearly with generation length, with a fixed size state. This change reduces memory consumption but often hurts accuracy. In reasoning tasks, which require long generations, this effect is especially pronounced. In this work we introduce Turnout, a method that mitigates accuracy loss as a result of linearization, while maintaining its memory-reduction benefits. We apply post-hoc linearization to a pretrained full-attention model, training a linear path through distillation while leaving the original full-attention path unchanged. During response generation, the resulting hybrid model retains both paths and uses a learned policy to control when each layer switches from full to linear attention. We train the policy with reinforcement learning using a reward that balances answer correctness and memory use. Empirical evaluation of our method shows that the learned adaptive policy achieves a better accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier on reasoning tasks compared to fixed switching and static hybrid baselines.

items.title: Constraint-Aware Anticlustering Decomposition for Certifying Pairwise-Constrained Clustering
items.summary: Certifying the quality of feasible solutions to large-scale minimum sum-of-squares clustering with pairwise must-link and cannot-link constraints remains challenging, as it requires strong lower bounds on the optimal objective value. We propose a decomposition framework that partitions the data points into smaller subsets, called anticlusters, and solves the induced clustering subproblems to obtain a certified optimality gap for the original problem. To preserve pairwise information, we introduce the Constrained Anticlustering Problem (CAP), which assigns each connected component of the constraint graph to a single anticluster while seeking geometrically representative subsets. We formulate CAP as a mixed-integer second-order cone program and develop a variable neighborhood search heuristic to construct high-quality decompositions. The resulting lower bound remains valid even when the induced subproblems are not solved to global optimality. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets with up to approximately 4,000 observations show that our approach can achieve mean optimality gaps below 1% at a modest computational cost.

items.title: Trained on Harm, Still Refusing: A Training-Time Defense for Code Generation
items.summary: Fine-tuning enables safety-aligned code language models to adapt to diverse downstream tasks. However, training on untrusted data can severely undermine their ability to refuse harmful requests. Notably, we find that models comply with harmful requests even though harmfulness information remains highly decodable from their internal representations. Moreover, an initial preference for refusal does not necessarily translate into sustained refusal behavior throughout generation. Together, these findings reveal a critical gap between recognizing harmful requests and consistently refusing to fulfill them. To address this gap, we introduce SAFEHOLD, a novel provider-enforced defense framework that preserves safety alignment during harmful fine-tuning by treating refusal as a sustained generation process rather than a single response decision. Specifically, SAFEHOLD preserves the aligned model's full-vocabulary response distribution at the initial generation position through decision-boundary anchoring, while supervising the complete refusal sequence through refusal-path reinforcement. We conduct extensive experiments evaluating safety, utility, and internal mechanisms. SAFEHOLD reduces average ASR by 72.03 percentage points relative to undefended fine-tuning, outperforming five SOTA defenses by 24.32 to 70.87 percentage points. Meanwhile, it improves average HumanEval pass@1 by 10.24 percentage points over undefended fine-tuning, while maintaining an average XSTest over-refusal rate of only 2.73 percent. Overall, these results demonstrate that SAFEHOLD effectively mitigates safety degradation during harmful fine-tuning while preserving benign-task utility.

items.title: Typhoon OCR 2: From Thai Document Transcription to Multilingual, Multi-Task OCR
items.summary: Typhoon OCR 1.5 focused on reading Thai documents. However, in real-world workflows, users often need to extract specific information or preserve the structure of an entire page for further processing. Typhoon OCR 2 handles both tasks in a single model, with prompt-driven extraction and structured full-page parsing. Full-page parsing covers Thai, English, and Chinese. We release compact 2B and 0.8B models adapted from open document parsers through supervised fine-tuning on curated Thai and public multilingual data, followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with task rewards and a rule penalizing unfinished responses. Among evaluated open models, Typhoon OCR 2 2B scores highest on Thai MDPBench (80.7 versus 68.9 for Typhoon OCR 1.5) and on ThaiOCRBench (59.91 versus 40.45), which covers recognition, extraction, and document understanding. The 2B model remains close to its base on English olmOCR-bench (84.7 versus 84.4) and on OmniDocBench, which evaluates English and Chinese together (90.97 versus 91.03). On MDPBench, GRPO reduces the mean share of pages with repetition loops for the 2B model from 3.2% to 0.7%, with a smaller and statistically uncertain score gain for the 0.8B model. We release the model weights, Python package, and evaluation suite.

items.title: Learning Unknown Oscillators From Bandit Feedback
items.summary: We study semi-bandits driven by unknown oscillators. Each round, a learner selects two of four reward channels and observes their individual rewards. Frequency errors change future reward rankings and the resulting measurements. We show when committing to one fitted oscillator lets its greedy choices expose prediction errors. Our controller bounds reward loss (regret) over a continuous confidence set and holds the longest block within budget. An online regression policy gathers observations when the check fails. Regret grows at a square-root rate, up to logarithmic factors, across all frequencies and extends to two competing oscillators. On 96 fresh synthetic instances, checked commitment uses 49 fits instead of 1,023, with 1.5% higher mean regret than fitting every round. Matched isolated timings give a 4.69-fold speedup. The confidence sets also certify trajectory regret.

items.title: Alignment without Transfer: Tokenization Impacts Cross-lingual Representations during Multilingual Language Model Pretraining
items.summary: Tokenization represents one of the most crucial steps in mulilingual NLP pipelines. Yet, tokenizers routinely under-allocate vocabulary to low-resource languages. While improved allocation leads to better performance, it remains poorly understood how tokenization shapes cross-lingual representations and transfer during pretraining. To address this, we pretrain 39 mono- and bilingual 1B decoder-only models on FineWeb2-HQ across English, German, French, Arabic and Chinese, varying only the tokenizer. Our results demonstrate that improved vocabulary allocation (i) substantially raises cross-lingual representation alignment in early-to-mid layers, an effect that prior work measuring only the output layer could not observe, (ii) increases cross-lingual parametric knowledge sharing in feed-forward neurons, supported by correlational and causal evidence, and (iii) an alignment-transfer dissociation, where cross-lingual transfer remains essentially unchanged despite higher alignment. Moreover, transfer is significantly lower for cross-script bilinguals even under fair vocabulary allocation, indicating that the script barrier is not merely a tokenizer artifact. All of our checkpoints and code are publicly available.

items.title: Which Dwarf Is This? Doppeldwarf-306 and Near-Identical Instance Retrieval
items.summary: Most established instance-retrieval benchmarks emphasise landmarks; small sculptures from visually similar series offer a complementary challenge. We introduce Doppeldwarf-306: 1,691 openly licensed photographs of 306 bronze dwarf statues in Wrocław, Poland, many made in themed series that share one style, with the photographer of each image recorded. With no training, nearest-neighbour search over frozen DINOv2 features names the right statue first for 93.1% of leave-one-out queries, and the best of thirteen backbones from seven pretraining paradigms reaches 94.7%. Accuracy falls slowly as candidates are added: for DINOv2, by about 0.8 points each time their number doubles. A natural design for a phone guide compares a photograph only with statues near the user. In simulation this helps, but less than an equal number of randomly chosen statues does, so random subsampling overstates its value; a permutation test ties the penalty to the real layout (p = 0.005). Used as a weight instead of a filter, location raises DINOv2 from 93.4% to 98.7% for a simulated user 25 m from the statue. With the query's photographer withheld, learned local-feature matching raises DINOv2 accuracy from 81.8% to 85.5% and also improves DINOv3. Comparing the two best candidates cuts DINOv2's false acceptance of unknown statues from 38.3% to 19.6% at 90% known acceptance.

items.title: Efficient Natural Language to Temporal Logic Translation for Real-Time Physical AI
items.summary: Robots can be controlled to perform tasks with guaranteed correctness when the task instructions are stated in a formal language. Large language models (LLMs) have been widely used to allow users to provide such instructions in natural language (NL), by translating NL into formal language. When deploying such translators on a robot, however, we face limited computing and energy resources, while offloading computation or data to the cloud may be infeasible or undesirable. Yet an LLM is a general-purpose text generator, whereas a formula in a fixed formal language fragment follows a well-defined syntax. We therefore ask whether text generation is needed at all. For the formal language of linear temporal logic (LTL), we show that this translation can instead be broken down into answering a set of questions with pre-defined answers. We then construct a System-One model, a recent class of NL-based classifier, to provide such answers and enable us to translate a natural language instruction into an LTL instruction. On three benchmarks, our translator matches or exceeds the accuracy of the best local LLMs available, at up to one order of magnitude lower runtime and energy consumption. We show that it generalizes to unseen atomic propositions and temporal patterns.

items.title: Verifying and Strengthening Neural Tangent Kernel Theory
items.summary: Writing Neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory explains why very wide neural networks trained by gradient methods converge in the lazy-training regime. Its standard proof combines matrix concentration, random Gram matrices, continuous-time dynamics, spectral perturbation, and a bootstrap argument, but has lacked machine-checked verification. We present a Lean\~4 formalisation for two-layer networks, proving an end-to-end theorem: for a smooth bounded activation (instantiated with $σ=\tanh$), frozen biases, paired $\pm 1$ initialisation, and explicit width conditions, gradient flow exists uniquely with probability at least $1-δ$, and $$ \|r(t)\|^2 \leq \|y\|^2 e^{-λ_0 t/2}. $$ The sole data assumption is population NTK non-degeneracy, $λ_0>0$. Initial coercivity, kernel drift, the movement bootstrap, the residual ODE, and flow existence and uniqueness are formally proved. The formalisation also sharpens the standard analysis in two ways. First, replacing the conventional matrix-Bernstein variance proxy with the classical row-covariance proxy yields estimated concentration-width certificates for $\tanh$ that are $36$--$53\times$ smaller at $(m,d)=(16,8)$ and $94$--$121\times$ smaller at $(32,16)$. Lean certifies the inequality; the ratios are numerical. Second, the network Hessian has operator norm $Θ(\sqrt{p})$ on the sup-norm parameter ball (a paper calculation), preventing the expected $O(1/\sqrt{p})$ linearisation bound via sup-norm Taylor estimates. An $L^2$ parameter geometry resolves this issue. Required widths remain polynomial but far beyond practical scales, limiting applicability.

items.title: Practical insights into controlling exponential concentration in quantum machine learning
items.summary: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models are often limited by exponential concentration, where quantum observables become insensitive to input variations as system size increases. In this work, we provide a comparative empirical study of this phenomenon across Fidelity Quantum Kernels (FQK), Projected Quantum Kernels (PQK), and Quantum Extreme Learning (QEL), within a unified observable-based framework based on expectation-value variance. We investigate how measurement locality, entanglement, and circuit expressivity shape concentration across different architectures. Global fidelity-based kernels exhibit strong concentration driven by Hilbert space dimensionality, whereas local-observable approaches reduce but do not eliminate this effect. In PQK and QEL, concentration is primarily governed by entanglement and quantum dynamical expressivity, with reservoir depth emerging as a key factor in QEL architectures. We further study bandwidth scaling as a general mechanism for controlling encoding expressivity across all models. Our results indicate that bandwidth scaling effectively reduces concentration in moderate regimes by restricting the effective expressivity of the encoding, though this protective effect diminishes in highly expressive structural settings.

items.title: From Manufacturing Event Logs to Simulation: Enabling SMEs with Agentic AI for SimPy Simulation Generation
items.summary: High expertise and cost barriers exclude small and medium-sized enterprises from discrete-event simulation (DES). We introduce GenAI4SimPy, a multi-agent framework powered by Qwen 3.6 (27B), an open-weight large language model, that automates end-to-end DES generation from manufacturing event logs to executable SimPy models through tool-augmented reasoning and human-in-the-loop validation. Evaluated on three execution blocks from a public smart factory dataset, the framework achieved a mean absolute percentage error of 7.9\% and coverage of failure rate for all three blocks and of throughput for two of three. A fidelity paradox was observed: accurate process-level parameters did not ensure system-level behavioral fidelity, with flow-time and throughput errors driven by misinterpreted observation-window truncation and absent system-level calibration. These results demonstrate that local open-weight models can perform DES generation at accuracy comparable to cloud-based alternatives, while identifying parameter extraction as necessary but insufficient for behavioral validity. Source code and results are available at https://github.com/RaikoPipe/genai4simpy

items.title: Cannot Wait to Verify: Parallel Drafting to Eliminate Verifier Idle Time in Speculative Decoding
items.summary: Autoregressive inference in large transformer models is limited by token-level sequential execution, resulting in high latency and low GPU utilization. Speculative decoding (SD) mitigates this bottleneck by introducing a draft-and-verifier model. However, the drafting stage remains sequential, leaving the verifier idle and underutilizing compute. To address this, we propose a plug-and-play drafting adaptive drafting method that parallelizes inference across transformer layers during draft generation. Starting from a shared hidden state, our approach evaluates multiple layers in parallel and verifies consistency by measuring divergence in hidden-state space. Layer-wise draft states are accepted when deviations are small; otherwise, a correction step is applied. By exploiting redundancy across transformer layers, our method accelerates draft generation and improves hardware utilization without modifying architectures or requiring retraining. Experimental results on NLP tasks show that our method speeds up the drafting stage by up to $1.65\times$ with minimal degradation in accuracy, while maintaining the same performance as SD.

items.title: PathOPEN: A pathologist-curated histopathology dataset for visual question answering
items.summary: PathOPEN is a histopathology dataset for visual question answering. Two clinical pathologists selected 157 cases with 229 available original images and wrote open-ended, five-option multiple-choice and close-ended (yes/no) questions. They supplied both a correct and a wrong answer for 201 of the 309 open-ended questions. Each case records the organ, pathology category and regional anatomy, and each image records its magnification. The dataset includes 6,870 augmented images and four manifests that select subsets to improve balance by individual metadata field. Five additional pathologists and two vision-language model judges rated items with scoring rubrics, and six models answered questions zero-shot across the three formats. The metadata support subgroup evaluation, and the paired answers can be used to construct preference examples.

items.title: ROSWORLD: When Digital Task Competence Meets Physical Execution
items.summary: Computer-use agents now solve most desktop tasks through direct software input, but a robot using the same computer must turn GUI knowledge into physical contact with a keyboard and mouse. We introduce ROSWorld, a benchmark that couples a physically simulated robot workstation to a live OSWorld desktop, so that a robot and a desktop agent pursue the same goals under the same official evaluators. The evaluated model receives observations only from the workstation camera views and operates the peripherals through either a single-arm rigid probe or dual-arm dexterous hands. Across five frontier models and 40 tasks in ten applications, models that complete 31-39 tasks on the desktop complete at most 23 with the probe and 28 with the hands. Paired trajectory analysis shows that models adapt their interaction strategies toward keyboard input, yet physical execution frequently fails through missed presses, incorrect targets, and unintended contacts. ROSWorld makes the gap between knowing what to do on a computer and physically doing it measurable.

items.title: Cecilia: Towards Layout-Inclusive Optical Music Recognition
items.summary: Reconstructing an editable music score requires musical events, sung text and the instructions that organise them on the page. Existing recognition targets often omit part of this information, while direct MusicXML prediction repeats substantial structural markup. We introduce Cecilia, a compact representation of canonicalised MusicXML that retains musical content, lyric attachments and layout instructions.
