items.summary: Complex social systems are often characterized by a deep interconnection between individuals' opinion formation and their decision-making processes. In this chapter, we show how these two dynamics can be incorporated within a unifying game-theoretic coevolutionary model for actions and opinions. We present the main theoretical results concerning the convergence of the coevolutionary model, and its recent extensions to incorporate further features of real-world social systems. Then, we focus on the problem of controlling such a coevolutionary model. In particular, we present two distinct approaches: i) introducing a committed minority in the population, and ii) broadcasting information to some target individuals. For both of these methods, we discuss their implementation and provide theoretical guarantees on their performance. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed control methods on different case studies, illustrating their implementation on simple academic examples, as well as exploring their performance in realistic scenarios using network structures inferred from real-world data. In summary, this chapter provides an overview of the mathematical approaches developed to model a population of individuals with coevolving actions and opinions, providing effective tools to study and, ultimately, control this complex socio-technical system.

items.title: Running-Time Lower Bounds under FPT $\neq$ W[1]
items.summary: We revisit running-time lower bounds historically based on the Exponential Time Hypothesis. Our case study asks how much of their quantitative content can be recovered under the assumption FPT $\neq$ W[1]. The reductions encode the choice of a clique in few bits and control the target parameter in terms of that encoding. This makes a sufficiently fast algorithm for the target problem yield a fixed-parameter algorithm for deciding whether a graph has a clique of the requested size. We obtain twelve lower bounds for deterministic algorithms across graph, string, and integer feasibility problems, including bounds that hold under structural restrictions. In several cases the same function of the parameter appears in the exponent as in the historical bound, with the additional requirement that the cutoff for any prescribed saving in the exponent be computable.

items.title: Preconditioning for quadratic matrix optimization via constraint reshaping
items.summary: We study quadratic optimization over orthogonality or symplectic constraints, a problem arising in eigenvalue computation, subspace analysis, and reduced-order modeling. Ill-conditioned problems have a wide positive Hessian spectrum at a minimizer, which slows first-order Riemannian methods. Existing preconditioned-metric approaches choose a Riemannian metric, which determines the resulting Hessian spectrum. We instead redesign the problem itself to find the narrowest possible spectrum. We reshape the constraints into equivalent formulations that preserve the optimal value and the solution set, giving a family of preconditioned problems parametrized by positive constraint weights. We derive a closed form for the positive Hessian spectrum in terms of these weights. Minimizing the condition number then reduces to a linear program (LP) in the logarithms of the weights. The LP attains a globally optimal design within the paired equal-block family, and its strong duality gives matching lower bounds on the condition number. On tested instances, the optimized formulation substantially reduces the local condition number, with returned spectra matching predictions on both orthogonal and symplectic instances. We also benchmark the design against Lagrangian and left-right preconditioned metrics. The method thus provides an exact, optimization-based alternative to heuristic preconditioned metrics.

items.title: Guided Cuckoo Filter: Full-Pipeline Insertion Optimization
items.summary: Cuckoo filters are widely deployed as space-efficient alternatives to Bloom filters, supporting fast lookups, insertions, and deletions. However, their insertion cost grows steeply at high load factors because the standard insertion procedure is entirely unguided: it places each fingerprint into whichever candidate bucket happens to be tried first, and when both candidates are full, it displaces a random victim in a random walk. These blind random choices occur at two distinct stages of the insertion pipeline, the initial placement decision and the eviction victim selection, yet each stage can be independently replaced with a guided, informed decision. We propose the \emph{Guided Cuckoo Filter}, which optimizes the entire insertion pipeline by steering both stages. At the placement stage, the filter compares the occupancy of both candidate buckets and inserts into the less loaded one, applying the power-of-two-choice principle to reduce how often eviction chains are triggered. At the eviction stage, the filter preferentially displaces the most recently inserted element, whose alternate bucket carries latent randomness that shortens the resulting chain. Because these two guided decisions target orthogonal bottlenecks, eviction frequency and eviction chain length, their benefits compose multiplicatively. Experiments on cuckoo filters with $2^{22}$ slots confirm that the fully guided insertion reduces per-insertion kicks by up to $3.1\times$ at 96\% load and cumulative total kicks by 63\% at the practical capacity ceiling of 95\% load, with negligible computational overhead.

items.title: High-Order Area-Preserving Runge--Kutta Methods for Surface Diffusion Flow of Curves
items.summary: We propose a class of high-order area-preserving Runge--Kutta (RK) methods for the surface diffusion flow of curves, a curvature-driven geometric flow that decreases the perimeter while conserving the enclosed area. By coupling the parametric finite element approximation of the classical BGN formulation with symplectic RK time discretisation, we rigorously prove that the fully discrete scheme unconditionally conserves the enclosed area of curves. This conservation arises solely from the intrinsic symplectic structure of the RK methods, without introducing any additional constraints, auxiliary variables, or Lagrange multipliers to enforce structure preservation. To attain high temporal accuracy, we adopt $q$-stage Gauss RK methods, which are symplectic and yield order $2q$ (e.g., $q=1,2,3$). The resulting fully implicit, strongly nonlinear system is solved efficiently via an equivalent discrete formulation combined with a monolithic damped Newton iteration. Extensive numerical tests on various evolving curves validate the theoretical findings, confirming exact area preservation, high-order temporal convergence, and favorable mesh quality, while the Newton iteration count rapidly decreases to fewer than 8 per step, demonstrating the robustness of the tailored solver.

items.title: Asymptotic Bounds for Codes in Toroidal Distance
items.summary: The toroidal distance naturally describes the geometry of codes over \(\mathbb Z_q\), where distances are measured modulo \(q\). In this paper, we study asymptotic bounds for codes in \(\mathbb Z_q^n\) under the toroidal metric. We first derive an explicit asymptotic lower bound from the classical Gilbert--Varshamov bounds for the Hamming and Lee metrics, which serves as a baseline for comparison. We then develop a saddle-point approach for the toroidal metric, which yields an asymptotic Gilbert--Varshamov lower bound and an asymptotic Hamming-type upper bound. For \(3\mid q\), we embed ternary Hamming codes into \(\mathbb Z_q^n\) and obtain another asymptotic lower bound for the toroidal metric. In addition, we derive an asymptotic lower bound for Maximum Toroidal Distance (MTD) codes. We compare these lower bounds with the baseline and prove that they are nontrivial in the corresponding parameter ranges. Finally, we compare the asymptotic bounds numerically.

items.title: Feedback-Free FDD Cell-Free Massive MIMO With Sparse AP Activation and Dual-Mode Precoding
items.summary: This correspondence enables practical frequency-division duplex (FDD) operation in cell-free massive MIMO via two mechanisms. Sparse access-point (AP) activation reduces downlink pilot overhead to enable coherent detection, while angle-reciprocity precoding steers beams using only uplink-estimated angles, eliminating channel feedback entirely. A load-adaptive dual-mode optimizer further enhances performance: closed-form signal-to-leakage-and-noise-ratio precoding for high-load rate boosting, or semidefinite relaxation for low-load power minimization. Simulations verify its superiority over existing feedback-free FDD solutions in spectral and energy efficiency, and its robustness to angle errors, reciprocity mismatch, and multipath.

items.title: Below Three: A 2.8027-Approximation for Moldable Precedence Scheduling
items.summary: We study makespan minimisation for nonpreemptive moldable jobs with arbitrary precedence constraints on identical processors. Each job runs on a chosen number of processors that remains fixed throughout its execution. Allocating more processors to a job can shorten its execution, but may increase total work and delay other jobs. We assume nonincreasing processing times, nondecreasing work, and a convex duration--work relation after dominated allocations are removed. This model includes jobs with concave speedup, for which Jansen and Zhang obtained a $3.291919\ldots$-approximation. Independently and concurrently with our work, Chen obtained a $3.016208\ldots$-approximation for the full convex model and a $2.973912\ldots$-approximation for concave speedup. We give a deterministic polynomial-time $2.8027$-approximation for the full convex model and every number of processors. Our result breaks the factor-three barrier for this model and also improves the approximation guarantee for concave speedup.

items.title: Self-Orthogonal MDS Principal-Ideal Codes
items.summary: We investigate Euclidean self-orthogonality and the generalized Reed--Solomon (GRS) property for coefficient-vector codes generated by a monic polynomial $g$ and its shifts $xg,\ldots,x^{k-1}g$, of length $n=r+k$ and dimension $k$, where $°g=r$ and $3\le k\le r$. We give a complete classification, over any algebraically closed field, of the generators for which these codes are both self-orthogonal and GRS. Such generators have either distinct roots in a geometric progression satisfying explicit order and scalar conditions, or a single repeated root in certain positive characteristics. In particular, only finitely many generators occur for fixed $r$, $k$, and characteristic. We determine their maximal self-orthogonal lengths, show that the corresponding maximal-length codes are cyclic or negacyclic, and obtain exact generator counts over finite fields, together with the least fields of definition. In contrast, when $3\le k<r$, we prove that every algebraically closed field supports infinitely many pairwise monomially inequivalent self-orthogonal non-GRS maximum distance separable (MDS) codes in this family. Consequently, arbitrarily many such codes can be realized over a common finite extension of any prescribed finite field, while remaining inequivalent and non-GRS over its algebraic closure.

items.title: Time-independent equivalent matrix representation for time-domain boundary element analysis of large-scale 3D acoustic problems
items.summary: This paper proposes a time-independent equivalent matrix representation for large-scale three-dimensional (3D) acoustic analysis with the time-domain boundary element method (TDBEM). In conventional TDBEM, pair-dependent retarded times couple spatial interactions to historical boundary data, causing substantial storage and history-convolution costs. The proposed representation decouples compressible spatial interactions from propagation history, allowing reuse of the same compressed spatial representation across propagation delays and throughout time marching without additional temporal interpolation of the kernel. For conventional space-time discretizations, blockwise low-rank compression yields the compressed equivalent matrix method in the $\mathcal{H}$-matrix format (CEM-$\mathcal{H}$), with dynamic cluster-pair tracking to skip inactive interactions during wavefront propagation. For low-frequency, long-wavelength problems with a bounded number of nonzero time-lag matrices, the framework is extended to the $\mathcal{H}^2$-matrix format (CEM-$\mathcal{H}^2$) using delay-consistent partitioning, shared coupling matrices, and nested cluster bases. Under sparsity and bounded-parameter assumptions, storage and per-step cost of CEM-$\mathcal{H}^2$ both scale as $O(N_s)$, excluding preprocessing. Numerical results agree well with conventional TDBEM and semi-analytical reference solutions. For CEM-$\mathcal{H}$, the storage requirement for a sphere with $N_s=20,480$ is reduced from approximately 349.0 GB to 1.6 GB, with a speedup of approximately $45.4\times$. For CEM-$\mathcal{H}^2$, simulations with up to $N_s=1,310,720$ are performed in the low-frequency, long-wavelength regime. A million-degree-of-freedom underwater-vehicle model is also analyzed. These results demonstrate the capability of the proposed framework for large-scale 3D transient acoustic analysis using TDBEM.

items.title: Quasi-orthogonality is a geometric property
items.summary: Quasi-orthogonality is one of the key ingredients for proofs of optimal convergence rates for adaptive mesh refinement methods (Carstensen, Feischl, Page, and Praetorius, arXiv:1312.1171). The work of Feischl (arXiv:2008.12198) proposed a relaxed quasi-orthogonality that follows directly from the inf-sup stability of the underlying problem discretization. The proof uses an intricate connection to the stability of $LU$-factorization of matrices. Recently, Gantumur (arXiv:2609.16265) presented a vastly simplified argument based solely on Hilbert space arguments. Building on this idea, we show that quasi-orthogonality is a purely geometric property of a set of points. This property is checked for a large class of Petrov-Galerkin methods for monotone, non-linear equations.

items.title: Fast Computation of Lowest Common Ancestor in Version Control Commit Graph
items.summary: The problem of finding the lowest common ancestor in the commit graph arises when a user wants to merge two (or more) development branches: for example, to add their own development into a common branch. At that moment, the version control system must determine the merge base - the common ancestor of the latest commits of the branches, in order to show the mutual difference between the branches. The problem is complicated by the fact that the commit graph is not a tree but an arbitrary acyclic graph. Moreover, if there is no common ancestor, searching for one may require traversing the entire graph. Traversing a graph with several million vertices takes tens of seconds, which becomes noticeable to users. We show that the commit graph has additional structure - supporting branches - and that this can be used to speed up the algorithm. By extracting supporting branches, the graph can be preprocessed and the search for the lowest common ancestor can be significantly accelerated. Moreover, if removing the supporting branches decomposes the graph into connected components of bounded size, the lowest common ancestor query can be answered in time comparable to searching for a common ancestor within a single component only. We present an algorithm running in time $O(δ_Gm_c + n_s\log^2 n_s + m_s\log n_s)$ and requiring $O(d)$ preprocessed data per vertex, where $δ_G$ is the maximum out-degree of a vertex in $G$, $n_c$ and $m_c$ are the maximum numbers of vertices and edges in a connected component formed after removing the supporting branches, $n_s$ is the number of supporting branches, $m_s$ is the number of edges in the reachability graph between the supporting branches, and $d$ is the maximum number of supporting branches adjacent to any single component.

items.title: Material optimization of optical properties of particulate products by transition matrix method and sequential global programming
items.summary: Material optimization of nanoparticle assemblies, such as structurally coloured photonic crystals, attracts increasing interest. We combine the transition matrix method (TMM), which avoids spatial discretization of particles and surrounding medium, with sequential global programming (SGP) to optimize optical properties of particulate products by iteratively assigning predefined catalogue materials to individual particles. We derive exact separable models, reproducing the fully coupled objective under single-particle material changes, and computationally accessible first-order correct approximations for general continuously differentiable objectives. These approximations aim to capture the nonlinear, potentially nonconvex dependence on individual material variables beyond their local first-order behaviour. Within SGP, globally minimizing the particle-wise subproblems can yield substantial improvements in few outer iterations, including steps away from unfavourable stationary points, as previously demonstrated for discrete dipole approximation-based SGP. The construction exploits the decomposition of the TMM system matrix into a material-dependent block-diagonal and a material-independent coupling matrix, while the state and adjoint problems remain fully coupled. Applications include extinction, scattering quantities, and colour objectives. In a 35-particle extinction minimization problem, the objective decreases by 31.0% in 13 iterations. A fine-grid evaluation of the fully coupled objective shows that no tested single-particle material change improves the final design. For a 627-particle photonic crystal, chroma increases by 58.4-122.1% for different particle diameters in 17-42 iterations. The optimized designs favour absorbing material in layers away from the incident light, consistent with experimental findings.

items.title: X Hedging: towards an eXplainable artificial intelligence option Hedging framework
items.summary: We propose X Hedging, an alternative to the Deep Hedging framework that addresses computational and explainability limitations of neural-network-based hedging strategies. Deep Hedging leverages neural networks to learn flexible hedging policies but relies on opaque models and typically requires large training datasets, which can complicate interpretation and limit its effectiveness in data-constrained settings. X Hedging takes a step toward addressing these limitations by replacing neural networks with tree ensemble methods, specifically LightGBM, to estimate hedging strategies. This design provides a computationally efficient alternative while preserving strong hedging performance and moving toward more user-centered explainability. To integrate LightGBM into a reinforcement-learning-style hedging framework, we introduce an optimization approach that sequentially trains tree-ensemble models while introducing stochasticity through random training orders. In controlled experiments, X Hedging achieves performance comparable to Deep Hedging while offering greater user-centered explainability, improved computational efficiency, and substantially higher robustness when training data are limited. The numerical results demonstrate that tree-ensemble methods provide an effective computational alternative to neural networks for data-driven dynamic hedging.

items.title: Optimal Impure $(r,δ)$-Quantum Locally Recoverable Codes with Explicit Minimum Localities
items.summary: Quantum locally recoverable codes with $(r,δ)$-locality ($(r,δ)$-qLRCs) are quantum error-correcting codes in which $δ-1$ erased qudits can be recovered by accessing only $r$ other qudits. The minimum locality of a qLRC is the least $r$ such that it has $(r,δ)$-locality. This paper aims to construct optimal impure $(r,δ)$-qLRCs with disjoint recovering sets and explicit minimum localities, where the optimality is measured by the Singleton-like bound of Guruswami, Kshirsagar, and Trivedi (GKT-optimal). Such qLRCs have particular advantages in recovering as many quantum erasures as possible while operating in parallel and with minimal qudit access overhead. We first characterize the recovering sets and the minimum locality of any CSS code by local relative distances, which are relative minimum distances of punctured codes with respect to shortened codes. We then construct impure qLRCs as CSS codes from nested pairs of generalized monomial-Cartesian codes. Grouping the monomials by their degree in the last variable, we reduce both their minimum distances and their local recovery to nested pairs of codes in the remaining variables, and the coordinates with the same values of these variables form disjoint recovering sets. In this way, we obtain four infinite families of GKT-optimal impure $(r,δ)$-qLRCs with disjoint recovering sets, and determine their minimum localities and the recovering sets attaining them for every admissible $δ$, except for a partial range of $δ$ in one family. These minimum localities need not be monotone in $δ$. In particular, two of the families contain GKT-optimal impure subfamilies of CSS codes CSS$(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C})$ with $(r,δ)$-locality for some $r<n-δ+1$ at values of $δ$ for which $\mathcal{C}$ has no classical $(r',δ)$-locality for any $0<r'<n$, where $n$ is the length of $\mathcal{C}$.

items.title: Kernel Compensation and Quasi-Newton Iteration for Nonlinear Non-Hermitian Eigenproblems in Photonic Crystals
items.summary: We extend the kernel-compensated eigensolver developed in our previous work from Hermitian to non-Hermitian nonlinear eigenproblems arising in dispersive photonic crystals. A mimetic finite-difference discretization preserves the discrete curl--divergence complex, and three-dimensional discrete Fourier transforms provide matrix-free realizations of the curl and divergence blocks. The isotropic inverse dielectric coefficient is stored through the material-edge indices, so its value and derivatives can be updated without assembling a Maxwell matrix. Kernel compensation is characterized by a fixed unitary block diagonalization, which remains exact for the nonlinear problem. At each outer step, a right Generalized Davidson iteration solves the non-Hermitian linearized eigenproblem. The exact derivative of a simple eigenvalue branch is expressed through its left and right eigenvectors. To avoid a second eigensolve, we replace the left eigenvector by the available normalized right eigenvector and obtain a right-Rayleigh quasi-Newton update. We prove that the exact left--right Newton iteration is locally quadratically convergent at simple roots, whereas the proposed iteration with exact inner eigenpairs has an explicit linear error factor and is at least quadratic when the derivative defect vanishes. A spectral regularity estimate bounds the gradient appearing in the derivative defect.

items.title: Trading Before a Committed Rebalance
items.summary: An institution must complete a portfolio adjustment, but traders who prepare inventory for it can choose whether to participate. We study how public forecasts affect the institution's cost in a Bayesian execution game with optional activation, transient impact, and uniform-price terminal completion. The curvature of equilibrium cost as a function of the posterior target mean determines the value of information. In the scalar model, information benefits every fixed participation roster. Optional supply can reverse this ranking at entry, at full participation, and in a smooth interior with lognormal activation costs. For centered scalar targets, information weakly lowers cost relative to no information, strictly when the posterior mean is nonzero with positive probability. Centered Gaussian precision gains are always beneficial. An exact symmetric finite-population equilibrium identifies how information resolution and individual strategic size interact near entry. A portfolio extension gives a matrix criterion for the fixed-roster ranking, which can fail under general cross-impact. Even with isotropic execution, shared activation allows equally accurate signals about target magnitude and composition to have opposite execution values under one unchanged prior. Intraday ETF price data is used to characterize target uncertainty and trading conditions without identifying activation or institutional costs.

items.title: Beyond geometric lattices: pseudo-atoms and redundant join representations in the face lattice of the permutohedron
items.summary: We study the lattice obtained from the poset of ordered set partitions (the Fubini poset), ordered by merging adjacent blocks, by adjoining a bottom element of rank -1. It is the face lattice of the permutohedron. We look at it from the point of view of geometric lattices: it is graded, atomic and coatomic in the strong sense that every element is a meet of coatoms, but it is not semimodular. Its atoms are the $n!$ permutations, and its elements of rank one, which we call pseudo-atoms, are the edges of the permutohedron. Describing ordered set partitions by chains of subsets, the cuts, we show that the rank is modular whenever the meet is above $\bot$, while the join of two distant atoms can have large rank, so that the rank of the join is a metric on permutations. An element has a unique representation as a join of atoms only up to rank one; above it, irredundant representations have sizes ranging from two to the rank, and the redundancy of an element is its number of atoms minus two. The Möbius function is that of an Eulerian lattice, the Whitney numbers are the face numbers of the permutohedron, and the characteristic polynomial has the alternating coefficients of the geometric case, but only $\bot$ and $\top$ are left-modular, so the lattice is not supersolvable. We show that it is CL-shellable, we exhibit EL-labelings for $n\le5$, and we compare the independent sets of Raz arXiv:2307.05005 (v3, Jan. 2026) with irredundant families and with the matroid of the vertices of the permutohedron. Replacing ordered set partitions by partial flags of subspaces of $\mathbb F_q^n$ gives a $q$-analogue, whose Möbius function is $(-1)^{\mathrm{rk}+1}q^κ$, with $κ$ the number of pairs of elements in a common block at $q=1$, and whose characteristic polynomial and Betti numbers are polynomials in $q$.

items.title: Safeguarded Learning-Assisted Nonlinear Conjugate Gradient Methods
items.summary: A learning-assisted framework for Nonlinear Conjugate Gradient (NCG) methods is developed in which lightweight online prediction is used to support, rather than replace, the classical optimization process. The proposed approach retains the standard two-term NCG structure and introduces two independent online extreme learning machine models. The first model predicts an NCG coefficient during restart recovery or when persistent stagnation is detected, whereas the second model is used only after a line-search failure in finite precision arithmetic to propose a bounded correction to the deterministic fallback step size. Neural predictions are accepted only when they satisfy deterministic numerical safeguards, including descent, scale, and out-of-distribution requirements; otherwise, the corresponding deterministic recovery or fallback mechanism is retained. Both learning models are updated online using quantities already generated along the optimization trajectory and therefore require no additional function or gradient evaluations for training. These learning frameworks are applied to six well-known classical NCG methods, producing corresponding low-storage learning-assisted variants with deterministic safeguards. Numerical experiments on 480 CUTEst test problems show improved robustness for all six variants at broadly comparable evaluation costs. A PDE-constrained conductivity-identification example further illustrates the potential of the proposed approach to reduce evaluation costs and computational time for problems with expensive function and gradient evaluations. These findings suggest that restricted online learning can improve the robustness and computational performance of classical NCG methods while preserving their low-storage structure and deterministic optimization safeguards, and is particularly promising when function or gradient evaluations are expensive.

items.title: Norm-equation methods for structured group-penalized regression
items.summary: Group-penalized regression with correlated predictors requires block updates for which familiar group soft thresholding formulas are generally inapplicable. Although proximal-gradient methods can solve such updates directly, their computational cost depends on the penalty and the design. We develop a norm-equation framework for a Euclidean group penalty combined with a finite, closed, convex, positively homogeneous within-group penalty. Each nonzero block minimizer is characterized by a unique scalar root, evaluated through strongly convex inner problems without enumerating sparsity or fusion patterns. Valid inner subgradients provide computable bounds on the scalar function and the block Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) error. These bounds allow scalar-search decisions and acceptance of approximate updates without solving every inner problem to high accuracy. Accounting for gradient changes during a cyclic sweep then gives a computable global KKT bound. Combined with standard stochastic-score and restricted-curvature conditions, this bound leads to a regularization-scaled stopping rule under which approximate estimators retain the usual estimation and prediction rates. Experiments with sparse-group and fused sparse-group regression show that computational performance depends strongly on the inner solver, with coordinate-descent and dual implementations offering advantages over direct proximal methods in some highly correlated settings.

items.title: Intent-Defined Radio: A Goal-Native Architecture for Next-Generation Wireless Networks
items.summary: Wireless systems are becoming harder to operate because service goals are increasingly expressed in outcome-oriented terms, while radio platforms still expose mainly low-level configurations and protocol-specific controls. This mismatch makes it difficult to translate latency, reliability, throughput, and continuity requirements into coherent radio behavior. This article argues for Intent-Defined Radio (IDR) as a new system abstraction for next-generation wireless networks. Rather than treating the radio stack as a fixed mechanism set to be manually engineered and then tuned, IDR connects explicit service goals to executable radio behavior within a constrained design space by leveraging the capacity of large language models (LLMs). We position IDR relative to programmable radio, intent-based networking, and learning-based protocol design. We also present two simulation studies using Intent2MAC to illustrate the design loop, demonstrating executable MAC synthesis and offline refinement guided by evaluation feedback. The results show improved service satisfaction at a throughput cost and improved remote-control performance when random contention is replaced by distributed urgency-based arbitration. We finally discuss the open challenges in intent specification, evidence, hardware execution, interoperability, and lifecycle cost, and outline a staged path toward deployment.

items.title: Computing Optimal Non-stationary Policies for the Probabilistic Reach-Avoid Problems
items.summary: We develop and analyze an algorithm for computing optimal non-stationary policies for probabilistic reach-avoid problems. The objective in probabilistic reach-avoid problems is to maximize the probability of reaching a goal without visiting predefined avoid states. Prior work has focused on computing optimal stationary reach-avoid policies. Stationary policies use the same action distribution whenever a given state is visited. This paper shows that stationary reach-avoid policies may be suboptimal and non-stationary policies may outperform them in reach probability by a margin arbitrarily close to one. To compute optimal non-stationary policies, we reduce the reach-avoid problem to a constrained average-reward Markov decision problem and propose an algorithm to compute lottery-based policies from a standard linear program formulation. We prove that the lottery-based policies are optimal and show that they are simple to compute, analyze, interpret, and implement. The numerical experiments confirm that the lottery-based policies can outperform state-of-the-art stationary policies even in complex domains.

items.title: When and why can integral constraints improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks?
items.summary: Adding constraints obtained by integrating governing equations to the loss has been reported to improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in several applications, but mathematical understanding of these benefits remains limited. For several partial differential equations (PDEs), we derive stability estimates for losses with and without integral constraints. The comparison reveals that in certain parameter regimes, the standard loss has very weak control over specific error components, and that the integral constraints restore uniform control of these components. This explains when and why the constraints improve accuracy. Finally, numerical experiments support this interpretation. In parameter regimes where the standard loss is predicted to have weak control over those components, the two losses indeed show clear differences in accuracy. Conversely, in regimes where the standard loss retains sufficient control, both losses yield similar accuracy.

items.title: Planning Width Is Hard to Approximate Even Given the Unique Optimal Plan
items.summary: For each fixed $k$, iterative-width search finds optimal plans in polynomial time on tasks of bounded tuple-chain width, but the approximability of planning width has remained open even when an optimal plan is supplied. When all optimal plans visit the same state sequence, we characterize set and chain width as hitting numbers of competing states. We construct positive-precondition STRIPS tasks with a supplied unique optimal plan, a single reachable goal state, binary branching, and constant-size actions. Every reachable state lies on a goal-reaching execution at most one action longer than optimal, yet distinguishing width $1$ from $Θ(N)$, where $N$ is the number of atoms, is NP-hard for set, chain, and goal-admissible width. Unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, no polynomial-time algorithm achieves a one-sided approximation factor $o(N)$ or a symmetric factor $o(\sqrt{N})$, and simple estimates attain both orders. For positive-precondition tasks with a supplied unique optimal plan of length at least two, testing set or chain width against a threshold $k\geq 1$ is coNP-complete for each fixed $k$ and $Σ_2^{\mathrm{P}}$-complete when $k$ is part of the input. Both results also hold for goal-admissible width if only one goal state is reachable. On an explicit state graph, a greedy algorithm approximates set width within a logarithmic factor even when optimal plans branch. Thus, knowing an optimal plan does not eliminate the difficulty of certifying substantially smaller width.

items.title: Improved Constants in the Kautz-Singleton Construction for Probabilistic Group Testing
items.summary: We consider the probabilistic nonadaptive group testing problem, in which a uniformly random defective set of size $d$ is to be identified among $N$ items using a binary test matrix. For the explicit Kautz--Singleton construction, it is known that order-optimal scaling $T=Θ(d\log N)$ for high-probability recovery can be achieved in the regime $d=Ω(\log^2 N)$. However, the leading constant in this scaling remains uncharacterized even for standard low-complexity decoders. In this work, we revisit the probabilistic analysis of this construction and improve the leading constant for the COMP decoder, as well as establishing the same bound for the DD decoder. Our approach relies on a sharper analysis of the number of distinct roots associated with the defective items, yielding tighter bounds on the decoding error probability. In particular, we show that both COMP and DD achieve vanishing average error probability with $T\le (1/\ln 2+\varepsilon)d\log N$ tests for any $\varepsilon>0$, in the admissible regime $N=q^k$ for some prime power $q = Θ(d)$ and integer $k \ge 2$. For COMP, this leading constant matches that of the random near-constant column weight design, whereas for DD, a gap remains except in the sparse regime $d = N^{o(1)}$.

items.title: Dimension-Free Buffer Bounds for Compressed-Momentum Error Feedback
items.summary: Analyses of error feedback bound the memory buffer through a compressor contraction constant -- $r/p$ for the best rank-$r$ approximation of a $p$-dimensional spectrum -- which survives into the rate. We show it need not appear at all. When the compressed momentum is re-injected into the pre-compression accumulator, the previous compressed momentum $β_1 M_{t-1}$ is an admissible competitor in the projection, and the buffer obeys $\|E_t\|_F \le (1-β_1)\|G_t\|_F + γ\|E_{t-1}\|_F$, free of the dimensions $m,n$ and of the rank $r$. The argument uses only that the compressor is a metric projection onto a closed cone, so it covers top-$k$ selection as well as truncated SVD, holds for every selection from the projection set with no condition on singular-value crossings, and in its trajectory-tracking form assumes nothing about the gradients. In the two-stage template of the standard analyses it replaces a Stage-2 constant of order $p^2/r^2$ by one of order $1$, against $Θ(p/r)$ for the sharpest contraction-based bounds. Transferring the full rate costs a leakage term, which we bound by the step-weighted gradient mass $\sum_{u\le t}η_u\|G_u\|_F$ and show tight up to a factor $\sqrt{2}$; the price is an additive $O(\log^2 T)$ floor, not a slower rate. On BERT fine-tuning at rank ratio $32/768$ the feedback decay costs under $0.008$ validation $F_1$.

items.title: HAVAPlot: A Web-Based Scientific Visualization and Post-Processing Platform
items.summary: This paper presents HAVAPlot, a browser-based framework for scientific visualization and post-processing of numerical simulation data. Operating entirely within the user's browser, HAVAPlot requires no software installation or data uploads while supporting mesh-based and tabular datasets beyond computational fluid dynamics. The framework directly reads native OpenFOAM cases, including polyhedral meshes, ASCII and binary fields, boundary data, and Lagrangian particles, as well as legacy and XML VTK files and tabular datasets. It provides line, contour, and three-dimensional plots; exact polyhedral slicing; boundary extraction; variable calculations; customizable color scales; symmetry mirroring; zoomed insets; streamlines; isosurfaces; particle visualization; and vector PDF/EPS and data export. The underlying numerical algorithms are independently verified. Cell centers and volumes agree with an independent implementation of OpenFOAM's geometric algorithm, while 6.1 million field values across four two-dimensional, axisymmetric, and three-dimensional production cases are reproduced to machine precision. For analytical fields on distorted hexahedral meshes, cell-to-point interpolation exhibits second-order convergence in the interior and first-order convergence at boundaries. Meshes containing 250,000 cells load in at most 1.3 seconds. Applications to an impinging supersonic jet, hypersonic cylinder flow, a hybrid particle-continuum cold-spray nozzle, a three-dimensional gas-bearing film, and supersonic cone flow demonstrate the framework's capabilities.

items.title: An explicit domain-preserving projected Milstein scheme with strong order one for stochastic systems
items.summary: A variety of domain-preserving numerical schemes have been developed for scalar stochastic differential equations and for several classes of multidimensional systems, including those defined on hyperrectangles and positive orthants. To accommodate more general domain constraints, we consider stochastic systems on bounded or unbounded open convex polyhedral domains, where coefficients may exhibit boundary singularities and polynomial growth. Under local regularity, growth and boundary assumptions, we establish well-posedness and integrability estimates for the exact solution. Then we construct an explicit projected Milstein scheme that preserves the domain by applying a Euclidean projection onto a step-size-dependent interior set after each Milstein update. For systems driven by multidimensional commutative noise, we prove strong order-one convergence for the maximum grid error in Lp, for suitable p > 1 and sufficiently small step sizes under additional weighted regularity and stability conditions. The proof combines these integrability estimates with local Milstein consistency, localization and weighted stability, without requiring a priori step-size-uniform moment or boundary inverse-moment bounds for the numerical approximation. Applications to constrained stochastic models and numerical experiments illustrate the observed first-order convergence behavior.

items.title: A decoupled structure-preserving scheme for pressure-driven multispecies tumor growth
items.summary: We propose an Onsager-based scheme for an $m$-species pressure-driven reaction--cross-diffusion system with a common homeostatic pressure. The scheme uses a modified scalar energy structure to update the total density, followed by compatible updates of the individual species. The global nonlinear problem remains scalar, and the species densities sum exactly to the updated total density. We establish unique solvability and show that the scheme preserves species nonnegativity, the pressure bound and total-mass monotonicity and satisfies a discrete energy dissipation law without a time-step restriction. We further develop a predictor--corrector extension to improve temporal accuracy while retaining these structural properties. Numerical experiments verify the accuracy and structure-preserving properties of the proposed schemes and demonstrate their computational efficiency.

items.title: Covering Location Optimization at GPU Speed
items.summary: Large-scale covering location optimization often involves NP-hard combinatorial problems that pose substantial computational challenges in urban facility planning. This paper proposes a GPU-accelerated parallel search framework for the maximal covering location problem, combining device-resident multi-trajectory exploration with lightweight CPU-side coordination. Exploiting the structure of one-swap moves, exact incremental gains are evaluated through sparse coverage representations and tiled CUDA kernels. A hierarchical reduction identifies the best exchange without materializing the full swap-gain matrix, while GPU-resident destroy-and-repair and elite-guided restarts balance intensification and diversification. Computational experiments on nine real-world urban configurations demonstrate consistent improvements over GRASP, achieving a mean relative gap of 0.029\% against published best-known solutions (BKS) and reaching BKS in 50 of 90 independent runs. On the largest urban benchmark, Kings, with 7,730 candidate locations and a budget of 50 facilities, the proposed method reaches BKS in all ten runs using a consumer-grade NVIDIA GTX 1660 Ti GPU, requiring only 45.2 seconds on average to obtain its final incumbent, compared with 99.5 seconds reported for AILS-PR in a high-performance computing cluster environment. The source code and benchmark reproduction scripts are publicly available at https://github.com/Yuntian-Zhang/GPU4CO

items.title: Interference Bounds and Merge-Aware Training Dynamics for Composable Fine-Tuned Models
items.summary: Combining fine-tuned models by composing their parameter updates has become a standard alternative to multi-task training. We formalize composability as a property of a collection of task vectors and prove that the excess loss of the merged model is controlled by an interference functional of the cross-task curvature overlap and the signed alignment of the updates. In the quadratic regime this functional equals the excess loss, giving a criterion that is necessary as well as sufficient and that measures the angle between task vectors in the curvature metric rather than the Euclidean one. Fine-tuning under a curvature-guided regularizer -- constructed from curvature statistics of the kind memory-efficient optimizers maintain -- keeps displacement in the base curvature metric below a ceiling set by the penalty coefficient at every iterate, at the standard $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ non-convex rate. Under a single Loewner comparison between the base statistic and the task curvatures, this control converts into a ceiling on the interference functional, inversely proportional to the penalty coefficient, so that the curvature term of the bound is controlled during training. A first-order term, present because regularized solutions are not stationary for the task loss, is not reduced in the same way. Experiments on an exact non-quadratic model confirm the budget and the ceiling, show the first-order term dominating for strong penalties, and find the curvature-guided penalty slightly better than an isotropic one. In a three-seed transformer study the functional is rank-correlated with merging degradation, but no more strongly than the Euclidean displacement norm.

items.title: ObliGraph: Graph Pattern Query Processing with Full and Differential Obliviousness
items.summary: Graph pattern query is a fundamental primitive in graph databases for retrieving data graphs that match a query graph under various structural constraints. As graph data is increasingly outsourced to third-party cloud servers for scalable query processing, however, both the query graph and the data graphs may leak sensitive structural information through server-side access patterns. In this paper, we study privacy-preserving graph pattern query processing in the outsourced setting, aiming to protect the structures of both the query and data graphs from access-pattern leakage. To this end, we propose $\mathsf{ObliGraph}$, the first oblivious graph search framework that supports multiple classes of graph pattern queries under two privacy modes: $\mathsf{FOS}$ achieves full obliviousness by uniformly evaluating candidate mappings, making the server-side access pattern independent of the structures of the query and data graphs; $\mathsf{DOS}$ further improves query efficiency through pruning while retaining a provable privacy guarantee of differential obliviousness. This design enables a smooth trade-off between stronger privacy and higher efficiency within a single framework. Experiments on real and synthetic datasets demonstrate that $\mathsf{ObliGraph}$ efficiently supports a range of graph pattern queries, achieving substantial improvements while preserving strong privacy guarantees.

items.title: A GPU Interior-Point Solver with Macro-Element Condensation for Equilibrium-Based Plasticity
items.summary: Equilibrium-based conic formulations of elastoplasticity and limit analysis provide statically admissible stress fields but generate large Newton systems whose sparse factorization limits three-dimensional computations. This work develops and analyzes a macro-element condensation tailored to the Newton systems arising from primal--dual interior-point methods. Exploiting four-tetrahedron macro-elements, the method eliminates stress directions and macro-internal traction-continuity multipliers, yielding reduced systems that can be solved using positive-definite factorizations, with estimated reductions of approximately \(4\times\) in dimension and structural nonzeros relative to stress-only elimination. The validity of this elimination is established through global and macro-local nonsingularity conditions. Local nonsingularity is independent of the yield criterion in elastoplasticity, whereas in limit analysis it holds directly for Rankine and is ensured for von Mises through trace-bound augmentation. Numerical results show that, relative to stress-only elimination, the proposed condensation achieves CPU speedups of up to approximately \(2\times\) and reduces peak linear-solver memory by up to \(66.5\%\). We further develop a CUDA Fortran implementation that exploits uniform macro-local blocks through batched routines and uses cuDSS for the reduced sparse solve. This implementation achieves speedups of up to \(13.5\times\) over its CPU counterpart and up to \(87.5\times\) over MOSEK, while successfully solving the largest tested 3D problems that exceed the device-memory capacity of the GPU solver CuClarabel. For elastoplasticity, we also propose a preconditioned conjugate-gradient solver that reduces device-memory requirements relative to the direct GPU solver, at the expense of increased solution time.

items.title: Efficient Privacy-Preserving High-Dimensional Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
items.summary: In the AI era, approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search on vector databases is critical as it supports similarity retrieval over high-dimensional vectors, which is essential for many large language model (LLM) applications. To reduce costs and improve scalability, vector databases are often outsourced to cloud servers, raising privacy concerns for users whose query vectors contain sensitive information. In this work, we study the problem of asymmetric privacy-preserving ANN search, where the vector database is public but user queries must remain private from an untrusted cloud server. To solve this problem, we propose ObliSC, an efficient privacy-preserving search framework that protects query privacy against access-pattern leakage. ObliSC consists of (i) a search base that retrieves ANNs with a strong privacy guarantee of full obliviousness; and (ii) parallel optimization strategies that accelerate candidate retrieval and refinement while preserving full obliviousness and retrieval quality. Experiments on six standard ANN benchmarks show that ObliSC not only achieves efficiency and result quality competitive with baseline methods but also maintains a lightweight index compared with the evaluated privacy-preserving approaches.

items.title: Certified pandigital approximations of $π$, $γ$, $δ$ and $e$
items.summary: In 2004 Erich Friedman asked for the best approximations of $π$, $e$, the Euler-Mascheroni constant $γ$ and Feigenbaum's constant $δ$ that use each of the digits $1, \dots, n$ exactly once, with addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, exponentiation, parentheses and the decimal point. We determine the optimal expressions for $π$, $γ$ and $δ$ for every $n \le 9$, with the digits in any order and in increasing order, and for $e$ when $n \le 6$. The optima are found by exhaustive search and certified by an independent algorithm that encloses every expression rigorously and decides each candidate with Arb and exact arithmetic; a second certified computation covers intermediate values of any size. Twenty-one entries improve the records published before this work; one of them, the optimal formula for $π$ with 1-9 (error $2.81 \cdot 10^{-14}$), was found independently by M. Verheyen, and we prove it optimal. For $e$, whose records come from identities between power towers, we prove that Bamberger's formula is optimal within the natural family of such identities. All code and certificates are public.

items.title: A Nonadaptive Sparse Fourier Transform in Every Dimension
items.summary: Let $G=(\mathbb{Z}/2^a\mathbb{Z})^d$, of order $N=2^{ad}$. Given point-query access to any complex signal $X$ with Fourier transform $\hat{X}$ over $G$, we provide a randomized algorithm that constructs a $k$-sparse estimate $\widetilde{X}$ via non-adaptive queries such that, with large probability, $\|\widetilde{X}-\hat{X}\|_2^2 \leq C \cdot \|H_k(\hat{X})-\hat{X}\|_2^2$, for an absolute constant $C>0$, where $H_k(\cdot)$ denotes the best $k$-sparse approximation. The constant $C$ can be improved to any desired $1+\varepsilon$ by either supplying a constant-factor estimate on the $k$-sparse tail norm or allowing an arbitrarily small additive error term $δ\|\hat{X}\|_2^2$ on the right-hand side. With a supplied tail estimate, we can also satisfy an $\ell_\infty/\ell_2$ heavy hitters guarantee. For fixed $δ$, the number of samples is $O((k/\varepsilon^2)(\log N)\log(k/\varepsilon))$, and the recovery algorithm requires a polynomial in $(k/\varepsilon)\log N$ exact operations. The algorithm naturally extends to $G=(\mathbb{Z}/b^a\mathbb{Z})^d$ for any fixed integer $b>1$.

items.title: Variational integrators for time-dependent Lagrangian systems on Lie groups
items.summary: We develop fixed-step variational integrators for time-dependent Lagrangian systems on Lie groups, derive their reduced dynamics, and analyze their long-time behavior by backward error analysis. We derive the continuous Euler-Lagrange equations, energy balance, and Noether conservation laws, and construct time-indexed discrete Lagrangians using retractions, with the midpoint-Cayley scheme treated explicitly. On their regularity domains, the resulting phase-space maps are symplectic. For left-invariant discrete Lagrangians, they reduce to Lie-Poisson maps that preserve coadjoint orbits and, when $G$ is connected, every Casimir function. A variational error analysis establishes second-order accuracy of the midpoint-Cayley method. We also construct an exactly symplectic, projectable extension on $T^*(\mathbb R\times G)$ whose formal modified Hamiltonian is affine in the momentum conjugate to time and admits symmetry reduction. Under uniform analyticity, coefficient bounds, and domain-containment assumptions, optimal truncation yields exponentially accurate interpolation and near-conservation of the modified extended Hamiltonian over exponentially long intervals. For a connected attitude network on $SO(3)^N$ with damping and uniformly positive, non-increasing coupling weights, we prove local asymptotic stability of the static consensus set for the continuous dynamics and exact preservation of total spatial momentum by the discrete scheme. Numerical experiments on the network and on a time-dependent rigid body on $SO(3)$ illustrate second-order convergence and the extended energy balance.

items.title: Subexponential Algorithms for Continuous Euclidean $k$-Means in Subpolylogarithmic Dimension
items.summary: Given $n$ points in $\mathbb{Q}^d$ and an integer $k$, the continuous Euclidean $k$-means problem asks for $k$ centers in $\mathbb{R}^d$ that minimize the sum of squared distances from the input points to their nearest centers. In one dimension, the problem can be solved in polynomial time by dynamic programming. In higher dimensions, the algorithm of Inaba, Katoh, and Imai [SoCG 1994] runs in polynomial time when both $k$ and $d$ are fixed. Mahajan, Nimbhorkar, and Varadarajan [TCS 2012] showed that the problem is NP-hard even in the plane when $k$ is part of the input, answering a question of Dasgupta [2008]. In this paper, we give a deterministic exact algorithm for continuous Euclidean $k$-means. For arbitrary $k$ and $d=(\log n)^{o(1)}$, the algorithm runs in $O^*(2^{o(n)})$ time and uses polynomial space. Aman, Karthik C. S., and Punna [ESA 2024] asked whether the $2^n$ time bound for Euclidean $k$-means can be improved in high dimensions. Our result gives an affirmative answer to the corresponding question in subpolylogarithmic dimension.

items.title: DS3M: Deep structured state space models for nonlinear system identification on modern hardware
items.summary: Neural state-space identification learns dynamical models from measured inputs and outputs. SUBNET combines this task with an encoder that estimates initial states from short measurement histories. Its continuous-time version requires many successive neural-network evaluations during numerical integration, resulting in slow training speed which is a major limitation for practical use cases. We propose deep structured state space models (DS3M), which combine compact nonlinear dynamical components in parallel and in series. Custom GPU kernels implemented with Triton reduce the launch and memory overhead of their sequential evaluation. We explain this construction, describe a port-Hamiltonian variant, and present various benchmark comparisons of accuracy and training time.

items.title: A fast iterative solver for lopsided Sylvester matrix equations
items.summary: A generalization of the factored alternating direction implicit algorithm is introduced that makes use of type $(p, q)$ Zolotarev rational functions to apply unequal numbers of left and right shifts. Convergence properties of the algorithm are discussed, as well as a method for computing shift parameters. Several applications are highlighted where the generalized method is useful, including in the solving of a collection of shifted linear systems, for discretizations that involve left and right operators that are not equally amenable to inversion, and for Sylvester matrix equations with differently-sized, differently-structured, or differently-conditioned coefficient matrices.

items.title: Formally Verified Semidefinite Programming
items.summary: We present a formally verified Rust implementation of a first-order semidefinite programming solver, a nontrivial piece of numerical software. We wrote the solver by hand and then directed Claude to generate the entire verification in Verus, an automated theorem prover for Rust programs. We discuss the algorithm underlying the solver, its implementation in Rust, and our pragmatic approach to proving it correct in Verus.

items.title: Small-Gain Analysis of Robust Event-Triggered Extremum Seeking for Scalar Maps
items.summary: We study a sample-and-hold implementation of gradient extremum seeking for a scalar quadratic map in which the control signal is refreshed only when an event occurs. The event generator acts on the demodulated gradient signal as it is actually measured, rather than on its averaged version, and contains a strictly positive offset, following the small-gain philosophy for robust event-triggered control. Rather than invoking averaging theorems, we work directly with the exact dynamics of the parameter estimation error. In the scalar setting, the demodulated gradient has an explicit sinusoidal structure, which is exploited through a change of variables that absorbs the zero-mean oscillatory perturbation, together with a quadratic Lyapunov function and the persistence of excitation of the probing signal. For a sufficiently fast dither, the estimation error is shown to decay exponentially to a residual neighborhood of the origin whose size is quantified by the dither amplitude and frequency, and by the relative threshold and the offset of the event generator. All constants, including the input-to-state stability gain of the extremum seeking loop, the admissible dither frequency and the positive lower bound on the time between two consecutive events, are given in closed form, so that Zeno behavior is excluded. A simulation example illustrates the results.

items.title: Optimal Robust Community Detection
items.summary: We study community detection in the sparse two-community stochastic block model when an adversary may corrupt a small constant fraction of the edges of the observed graph. For every choice of parameters above the Kesten-Stigum threshold and every $\varepsilon > 0$, we give a nearly-linear-time algorithm which estimates the communities with accuracy within $\varepsilon$ of the information-theoretically optimal accuracy, while tolerating a small constant fraction of adversarially corrupted edges. Previously, efficient algorithms with optimal accuracy were known only in the absence of corruptions, while robust algorithms either achieved only weak recovery or approached optimal accuracy only in the limit of large signal-to-noise ratio. Our algorithm is simple: approximate the second eigenvector of the nonbacktracking matrix, using a semidefinite program to cope with the corruptions, and use it to initialize belief propagation. Along the way, we show that in the absence of corruptions, belief propagation initialized at this eigenvector achieves optimal accuracy, resolving an open problem of Zdeborová in the two-community case. The proof of this fact is short and independent of our robustness results--its key ingredient is a local characterization of the second eigenvector of the nonbacktracking matrix in terms of constant-depth nonbacktracking walks.

items.title: Robust BUG dynamical low-rank integrators based on the Euler-Maruyama method for stochastic differential equations. Part I: a closed-moment approach
items.summary: In this work, we introduce Euler-Maruyama-based Basis-Update & Galerkin (EM-BUG) dynamical low-rank integrators for stochastic differential equations (SDEs). These integrators extend the standard BUG integrator to the Euler-Maruyama scheme by incorporating diffusion directions into the augmented physical basis and exploiting the second moment to update the physical basis independently of the new Brownian increments. This construction avoids the inversion of the reduced second-moment matrix and allows us to derive convergence estimates that are robust with respect to small eigenvalues. We establish preservation of positive semidefiniteness, exactness with respect to Euler-Maruyama at full rank, and second-moment stability. Strong and weak convergence estimates show that the time-discretization accuracy of the underlying Euler-Maruyama scheme is preserved up to the low-rank approximation error. We also derive Monte Carlo error estimates recovering the standard sampling rate up to the time-discretization and low-rank approximation errors. Numerical experiments on linear SDEs with additive and multiplicative noise support these theoretical results and demonstrate accuracy comparable to the standard BUG integrator.

items.title: An α-potential linear approximation for LQ differential games
items.summary: Feedback Nash equilibria of infinite-horizon linear-quadratic (LQ) differential games are characterized by coupled algebraic Riccati equations (cAREs), whose numerical solution generally relies on iterative algorithms and can be highly sensitive to their initialization. Motivated by the $α$-potential-game framework, this letter proposes an $α$-potential linear approximation for constructing a systematic, game-dependent initialization. For an N-player LQ game, a reference potential game is constructed. Its equilibrium requires solving only one standard algebraic Riccati equation. The original cAREs are subsequently linearized around this reference solution, yielding a coupled linear system whose solution provides player-specific corrections and hence an approximate feedback Nash equilibrium. The resulting approximation is used to initialize three standard cARE solvers. Numerical experiments on $10^4$ randomly generated two-player games show that the proposed initialization reduces the mean number of iterations. Further experiments for $N=2,\ldots,13$ show that the reduction in iteration count persists as the number of players increases.

items.title: Accelerating Diffusion Maps on a Quantum Computer: Spectral Filtering and Galerkin PDE Solvers
items.summary: Diffusion maps generalize principal component analysis (PCA) to nonlinear manifolds, enabling spectral dimensionality reduction, geometric data analysis, and elliptic PDE approximation on point clouds. For large datasets of size $N$, however, classical matrix operations incur prohibitive $\operatorname{poly}(N)$ scaling, even when extracting low-dimensional spectral features or targeted scalar observables. We introduce a quantum algorithmic framework that bypasses explicit graph-Laplacian assembly by exploiting the symmetric factorization $G = A^T A$ directly at the block-encoding level. Combining Gaussian moment dilation, Laplace-weighted linear combinations of unitaries (LCU), and quantum singular value transformation (QSVT), we implement spectral filters of $A$ to estimate heat-semigroup overlaps, regularized inverse queries, and energy responses, as well as to prepare spectral Galerkin solution states. A common-state construction further allows the block-encoding queries to be used across multiple scalar observables. Under polylogarithmic-cost block-encoding access to $A$ and state-preparation oracles, our heat-overlap algorithm achieves $O(\operatorname{polylog} N)$ gate complexity at fixed normalized precision, confidence, and spectral scale. Ideal statevector simulations validate our discrete circuit constructions, while a matched approximate-counting benchmark demonstrates the quadratic precision advantage of coherent amplitude estimation for energy readout.

items.title: A Modified Quasi-Newton Method for Unconstrained Optimization with Nonpositive Curvature Detection and Structured Complexity
items.summary: We consider the convergence, worst-case complexity, and implementation of R2N, a modified quasi-Newton method for large-scale unconstrained smooth optimization. At each iteration, we compute a step that approximately minimizes the sum of a quadratic model of the objective with an adaptive quadratic regularization, and that results in sufficient decrease. The objective is only assumed to be $C^1$, although second derivatives may be used if they are available. The implementation features a broad range of step-computation strategies, from sparse factorization to matrix-free Krylov methods, that satisfy global convergence requirements. When detected, directions of nonpositive curvature are exploited. Our analysis allows unbounded model Hessians, provided they satisfy a mild growth condition. We derive a worst-case evaluation complexity bound that separates the progress made along positive- and nonpositive-curvature directions. By forcing the regularization parameter to vanish near isolated local minimizers, we obtain superlinear local convergence. The implementation specializes naturally to nonlinear least-squares problems. We provide a modular Julia implementation, and use it in a numerical study on the CUTEst test set that assesses the treatment of nonpositive curvature, the subproblem solver, the update of the regularization parameter, and direct versus iterative subproblem solves. An Armijo-Goldstein line search along nonpositive-curvature directions, MINRES-QLP as subproblem solver, and a regularization parameter driven to zero near a solution form our recommended configuration. With exact second derivatives, R2N is competitive with a trust-region method, solving slightly more problems with fewer objective and gradient evaluations. With convex models, the trust-region method performs as well or better.

items.title: Learning Integer Winding Evolution Times in Quantum Phase Estimation
items.summary: Learning a Hamiltonian evolution time in Quantum Phase Estimation that produces phase distributions with low Shannon entropy circumvents the fundamental limit of digitization error of phase, independent of the number of phase qubits of accuracy. By introducing an optimization loop to minimize the Shannon entropy of measured eigenvalues produced by a QPE quantum circuit, minimum eigenvalue computation accuracy is greatly improved, which we show numerically on quantum magnet models. This technique works because standard QPE has a natural correspondence between entropy of the phase distribution and the analog accuracy of the minimum eigenvalue phase. This introduces for the first time a type of parameter learning to QPE, which makes near term practicality of QPE for fundamental sciences more feasible by using shorter depth QPE circuits.

items.title: Fast and Memory-Light Evaluation of Density-Based Clusterings with the DISCO Index in R
items.summary: DISCO is a recent internal cluster validity index for density-based clustering that, unlike earlier indices, also evaluates the quality of noise labels. The discoCVI package makes DISCO available in R. This article describes the design of the package and a typical workflow, in which DISCO is used to compare clusterings and to choose the parameters of HDBSCAN without ground truth, followed by the implementation introduced in version 0.2.0. DISCO is defined through density-connectivity distances between all pairs of points, so direct implementations store several n-by-n matrices. We show that every quantity DISCO needs can be read off the single-linkage merge tree of the mutual-reachability minimum spanning tree, so that the index can be computed exactly with memory that grows linearly with the number of points, while the running time remains quadratic as in the original definition. The implementation is tested against the previous version, agrees with the original Python implementation to within $3 \times 10^{-13}$, and corrects the score of singleton clusters to match the published definition. In benchmarks, discoCVI is 23 to 138 times faster than its previous version for 500 to 4,000 points and 3 to 9 times faster than the Python reference for 500 to 8,000 points, using a fraction of the memory of both, and it scores 100,000 points in about 50 seconds with less than 200 MB of memory.

items.title: Structure and Complexity of Perfect Functional Representations
items.summary: For given random variables $(X,Y)$, functional representation lemma states that there exists a random variable $Z$ and a deterministic function $g$ such that $Y = g(X,Z)$, and $X$ is independent of $Z$. In other words, $Z$ captures all the information about $Y$ not contained in $X$. We refer to $Z$ as a `perfect functional representation' if it satisfies $I(Y;Z) = H(Y|X)$. We show that the existence of perfect representation depends solely on the conditional distribution $p_{Y|X}$ and define the corresponding conditional distributions as perfectly representable. We provide a necessary and sufficient condition for $p_{Y|X}$ to be perfectly representable. Moreover, we cast the problem of checking perfect representability as a linear program, give an algorithm whose complexity is polynomial in $|\mathcal Y|$ and exponential in $|\mathcal X|$, and prove that deciding perfect representability is NP-complete for rational input matrices encoded in binary.

items.title: Entanglement Geometry Beyond Polygons: Graph-Theoretic Entanglement Inequalities
items.summary: Entanglement entropies of pure multipartite states can be constrained by organizing subsystem cuts as edges (hyperedges) of graphs (hypergraphs). Starting from the one-party entanglement polygon inequality, we derive these constraints from strong subadditivity and pure-state complementarity, with optimal coefficients and explicit equality conditions. Our central result determines, for a distinguished two-party cut and an arbitrary weighted family of cuts, the optimal polygon coefficient: the smallest total weight of the cuts separating a member of the distinguished pair from a remaining party. A refinement involving three mutual information terms gives the exact minimum of the weighted sum at fixed entropies of the two parties and of their union, attained by at most three independent bipartite pure states. This criterion recovers the cycle and complete-graph inequalities and shows that uniform incidence parity, which we prove sufficient for polygon inequalities on hypergraphs, is not necessary. Averaging strong subadditivity over both sides of a bipartition gives a sharp $k$-marginal inequality with coefficient $2\binom{n-2}{k-1}$, and we determine uniformly optimal coefficients for collective hyperstar inequalities. For paths and overlapping hyperchains, the deficits are exact sums of conditional mutual information terms; genuinely multipartite entangled cluster states saturate the hyperchain inequality while the chain inequality remains strict. We characterize pure chain equality states, bound the trace distance to cycle equality states independently of the number of parties and local dimensions, and obtain bond-dimension bounds for matrix product states and sequential-recovery error estimates.

items.title: Near-Quadratic Sample Compression for All VC Classes
items.summary: The sample compression conjecture is a longstanding open problem in learning theory, originating in the work of Littlestone and Warmuth in the 1980s. At its heart is a connection between simplification and generalization: if a predictor consistent with a training sample is defined using only a small part of that sample, then it is likely to generalize. Sample compression schemes formalize this idea, and many natural learning algorithms can be analyzed this way. The sample compression conjecture of Floyd and Warmuth (1995) asserts that every binary concept class of VC dimension $d$ admits a sample compression scheme of size $O(d)$; a weaker conjecture asks only for size polynomial in $d$. Both have remained open: the first bound depending only on $d$, due to Moran and Yehudayoff (2016), is exponential in $d$. We prove the weaker conjecture by constructing a sample compression scheme of size $O(d^2 \log^2 d)$.

items.title: TuringSpace: Grounding Spatial Intelligence in Action with Interactive CAPTCHAs
items.summary: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.

items.title: WAM-Policy: World Action Models with On-Policy Distillation for Quadrupedal Loco-Manipulation
items.summary: Arm-free quadrupeds can perform loco-manipulation, walking on three legs while manipulating with a front leg, yet no existing policy for it follows language instructions. World action models (WAMs) have emerged as effective language-conditioned manipulation policies, but are pretrained for robot arms and sample slowly. WAM-Policy turns one WAM into a quadrupedal loco-manipulation policy via two stages. The first, Cross-Morphology Policy Adaptation and Acceleration, adapts the arm-centric WAM to quadrupeds and distills the transferred policy into a student with one video and two action steps by on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). This student, however, is bounded by its teacher, which only imitates demonstrations. The second stage, Task-Specific Improvement and Merging, therefore tunes the teacher by reinforcement learning (RL) and merges the slow specialists into one few-step student by multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD). On QLM-Bench, ten simulated tasks with 1,000 demonstrations synthesized without teleoperation, the transferred policy reaches 77.0%, and the OPSD student keeps 76.7% while sampling 14 times faster. Task-specific RL and M-OPD lift it to 85.0%. We also deploy the OPSD student on a real Unitree Go2 Air. WAM-Policy thus achieves a stronger quadrupedal policy at a fraction of the inference cost.

items.title: Learning What Actions Change: Action Effect Matching for Dynamics-Faithful World Models
items.summary: World models aim to predict environment dynamics under actions, enabling the prediction of action consequences without executing them in the real world. Yet despite producing increasingly realistic videos, current world models often fail to capture how small action changes affect future observations. This limits their use in tasks such as robotic policy evaluation and model-based planning, where nearly identical actions can lead to qualitatively different outcomes. To address this, we propose AFFECT, an auxiliary training objective for learning the distribution of visual changes induced by action perturbations. Specifically, we inject temporally correlated noise into the actions of a policy trained on task-agnostic human teleoperation. We then train the world model so that its generated videos respond to this noise as the recorded videos do, without requiring repeated executions from the same initial state. Across OGBench simulation and real-world DROID and ALOHA-2 setups, AFFECT makes world-model rollouts more faithful to real outcomes. On DROID, the Pearson correlation between policy success rates in the world model and on the real robot rises from 0.47 to 0.79, alongside up to 23% lower FVD. These gains carry over to planning, where selecting actions with AFFECT-trained world models improves task success by up to 8.3%.

items.title: WM^MLLM: Turning MLLMs into World Models
items.summary: Video world models keep the world in the context of a generator, so a revisit is synthesized again and earlier edits can drift or disappear. We present WM^MLLM, the first interactive world model built on multimodal large language models (MLLMs), for persistent, editable world generation from a single image. WM^MLLM keeps the world state outside every generator, as a panorama with a revision history, and lets the MLLMs write it: they turn each request into operations on this state, select where a local edit is written, and check every candidate before it becomes the next state. Image generators only propose views, and video only presents them. Users can walk to new places and return, edit objects through text or a box, place subjects, and change lighting, weather or season. By construction, a revisit at the same revision reproduces the earlier view exactly, a local edit leaves every panorama pixel outside its region unchanged, and each request starts from the result of the previous one. Against six world model baselines on MBench-A, WM^MLLM has the highest mean on all four environment-recovery metrics (Epipolar 91.5 versus 0.1 to 74.0) and completes the most camera round trips (85.3% versus at most 50.9%). It has the best value in all 15 CompBench columns against 15 baselines. On 112 local edits judged blind, selecting the region to write after generation raises completion from 34.8% to 83.0%.
